conformal.blade-basis-persists-under-deg.formal: Let $B$ be any symmetric bilinear form on a real space $W$ of dimension $m$, and let $e_1, \dots, e_m$ be any basis of $W$. Then the $2^m$ blades $e_I = e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_k}$, $I = \{i_1 < \dots < i_k\}$ (ordered geometric products, outer-product blades only for an orthogonal basis), form a linear basis of $\Cl(W, B)$; in particular $\dim \Cl(W,B) = 2^m$ whether or not $B$ is degenerate. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Lem.~2.6]{ButlerT4}; classical, \cite{Chevalley1997}.
conformal.blade-basis-persists-under-deg.technical:
Let $B$ be any symmetric bilinear form on a real space $W$ of dimension $m$, degenerate or not, and let $e_1, \dots, e_m$ be any basis of $W$. Then the $2^m$ blades $e_I = e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_k}$, one for each increasing index set $I$, form a linear basis of $\Cl(W,B)$, so $\dim \Cl(W,B) = 2^m$ in every case.

The fact restates the series' own blade-basis lemma for possibly degenerate forms, which in turn is classical (Chevalley).
conformal.blade-basis-persists-under-deg.lay: A Clifford algebra is built from a space of directions together with a rule for multiplying them. This fact says that the products of distinct basis directions always form a basis for the whole algebra, so an algebra built on m directions has size two to the power m. That stays true even when the multiplication rule is degenerate, with some directions of zero length against every direction.

__notes__.note.conformal.abstract: Projective geometric algebra $\Cl(3,0,1)$ and conformal geometric algebra $\Cl(4,1)$ are the two standard algebras of applied geometric computing, usually presented as independent modelling choices. This note proves that the second is the unique minimal nondegenerate completion of the first. For any real Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q,r)$ of a degenerate form with nondegenerate part of signature $(p,q)$ and radical of dimension $r$, the minimal nondegenerate Clifford completion exists, has signature exactly $(p{+}r, q{+}r)$, and is unique up to an isometry fixing the original space pointwise: existence by adjoining the dual of the radical with the hyperbolic pairing, minimality because each radical direction must pair nontrivially into any completion, the signature forced by Witt splitting of the complement, and uniqueness by the Witt extension theorem. In particular $\Cl(3,0,1)$ completes minimally and uniquely to $\Cl(4,1)$. The completion converts the radical's nilpotent ideal into the unit ideal. No extension gives a radical element an inverse, since its square stays zero; what CGA supplies is a partner $\varphi$ for each radical direction $\rho$ with $\rho\varphi + \varphi\rho = 2$, so the division PGA lacks becomes total at the level of ideals, through the pairing and not through inverses. The embedding carries PGA's translators to CGA's translators verbatim. Every result is proved in full; the note situates the theorem in the series' transport-rule taxonomy and delimits what minimality promises. All computational identities are verified in exact rational arithmetic in an accompanying script.
__notes__.note.conformal.setting-setup: Let $(W, B)$ be a real quadratic space of dimension $m$ with radical $R := \rad(B) = \{\rho : B(\rho, \cdot) = 0\}$ of dimension $r \geq 1$, and nondegenerate induced form of signature $(p,q)$ on $W/R$, so $m = p + q + r$; write $\Cl(p,q,r) := \Cl(W,B)$. The proofs import exactly two results, stated here with their provenance; everything else is proved in this note.
__notes__.note.conformal.setting-setup-2: A \emph{completion} of $(W,B)$ is a quadratic space $(\widetilde W, Q)$ with $W \subseteq \widetilde W$ and $Q|_W = B$ and $Q$ nondegenerate; it is \emph{minimal} if no completion has smaller dimension. Every completion induces a unital algebra embedding $\Cl(W,B) \hookrightarrow \Cl(\widetilde W, Q)$: the inclusion of generators satisfies the Clifford relation, so the universal property gives the algebra map, and the map is injective because a basis of $W$ extends to a basis of $\widetilde W$, whereupon Fact \claimref{conformal.blade-basis-persists-under-degeneracy} sends the blades of $\Cl(W,B)$ to blades of $\Cl(\widetilde W, Q)$ in the extended basis, which are linearly independent.
__notes__.note.conformal.setting-position-series:
This paper is T2 of the series. It relies on two papers of the series. From the root paper T1 \cite{ButlerT1} it takes the element-level lemma that a square-zero element is invertible in no unital extension, the type-N reading of a radical direction and the taxonomy frame of Remark \claimref{note.conformal.relation-transport-rules}, and the representation-independent sharpenings whose scope Remark \claimref{note.conformal.what-minimality-promises-what-it-does} delimits. From the sheaf paper T4 \cite{ButlerT4} it takes the blade-basis lemma for degenerate forms (Fact \claimref{conformal.blade-basis-persists-under-degeneracy}), together with the corank-one square-zero ideal and resolution mechanism of which Proposition \claimref{conformal.nilpotent-ideal-becomes-unit-ideal} is the finite-dimensional, any-corank instance.

Later results do use its completion theorem: the odd-extensions note T14a imports Theorem \claimref{conformal.minimal-nondegenerate-completion} as its Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-minimal-completion-degenerate-algebra-rule}, and \claimref{synthesis.nilpotent-steps-derivative-exponential-and-boost} cites it. The note is otherwise the applied-audience presentation of results whose general versions are proved in T1 \cite{ButlerT1} and T4 \cite{ButlerT4}, and the status table of the capstone T17 \cite{ButlerT17} records it on that basis.
__notes__.note.dark-matter.where-flag-defined-what: Every tower has rungs, the $(1,1)$ ascent adjoining a hyperbolic plane at each floor (Fact \claimref{dark-matter.imported-eight-towers-mod-8-clock}), so at tower level every residue is flaggable (Definition \claimref{obj.dark-matter.witt-flag}) and flaggability selects nothing. The flag counts no towers; it orients them (the section “The arrow counted”), and it equips them: a flag on $H_{k}$ is equivalently the complex structure $J_{k}$ on the complexification $H_{k} \oplus I_4H_{k}$ (the plane $H_{k} \otimes \C$, with the field theory's imaginary unit $I_4$, which commutes with every vector of the plane) whose $-I_4$ eigenline is the annihilated half (it lives in the complexification, since no real endomorphism squaring to $-1$ has the two real null lines as eigenlines), and the ladder pair's number operator generates a $U(1)$ commuting with the rest of the rung. So every flagged tower carries rung-level abelian charges, one per rung, whatever its ground type, as this tower's derived content acquires its $U(1)$ from three ladder pairs \cite{ButlerT12}.
__notes__.note.odd-extensions.setting-machine-veri:
Every computational identity asserted in this note has been verified in exact rational arithmetic by the script \texttt{verify\_T14a.py} \cite{ButlerVerifyT14ext}, which imports the series' shared library \texttt{GA.py} and uses its basis-blade engine; no floating point anywhere. The script indexes generators from zero, so its $e_{0}, \ldots, e_{5}$ are the text's $e_{1}, \ldots, e_{6}$. Eighty-six checks, all passing, in nine parts.

\emph{Part A: the volume element.} Centrality and the sign $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2+q}$ on every diagonal signature of dimensions one, three, five and seven; the four signs of Corollary \claimref{odd-extensions.four-extensions-oriented-pair}; commutation of $\omega$ with the added generator; Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(iii) and the identities behind (i) and (ii), with the specific sign assignment of (i), over every odd signature of dimensions three and five; and the dimension of the centre, two over every odd signature of dimension at most five and one over every even signature of dimension at most six.

\emph{Part B: doubling and complexification.} For the two doubled extensions, the central idempotents $(1 \pm \omega)/2$, the two ideals of dimension sixteen, the action of $e_{5}$ as $+s\,\omega'$ and $-s\,\omega'$ on them with $s = e_{5}^{2}$, and the shadow meeting the even subalgebra exactly in its even part; for the two complexified extensions, the spanning of all thirty-two dimensions by $\Cl(p,q) + \omega\,\Cl(p,q)$ and $\omega^{2} = -1$ central.

\emph{Part C: where the mirror sits.} For all four extensions, the pairwise anticommutation and the squares of the bivectors $e_{\mu}e_{5}$, the generated subalgebra equal to the even subalgebra, the shadow of dimension sixteen meeting it in dimension eight, and the squares of $\omega e_{\mu}$ (reversed in the complexified cases, unchanged in the doubled ones); for $\Cl(2,3)$, the intersection equal to $\Cl^{0}(1,3)$.

\emph{Part D: the rung.} In $\Cl(2,4)$, the signatures $(2,3)$ and $(4,1)$ generated by $e_{i}e_{6}$ and $e_{i}e_{1}$, both generating the even subalgebra of dimension thirty-two; $\omega_{6}$ even, $\omega_{6}^{2} = -1$, commuting with every even element and anticommuting with every vector; the copies of $\Cl(1,3)$ and $\Cl(3,1)$ inside the even subalgebra.

\emph{Part E: the clock and the paths.} The residues of the four extensions, of the oriented pair and of the odd towers' representatives; the residue preserved by conformal completion; the centres of the four extensions of dimension two with the signs that separate the reversed pairs, and the centre of the rung of dimension one; the enumeration of sign-change walks from $(1,3)$ to $(3,1)$, exactly one, with $(0,4)$ a dead end.

\emph{Part F: the frozen point and the ascent's pair.} On exact rational instances of $I = a\,e_{+} + b\,e_{-}$ with $Q(I) = 3$, $-3$ and $0$: the orthogonality of the Lorentz frame and $w$ to $I$, $Q(w) = -Q(I)$; the signatures $(1,4)$, $(2,3)$ and $(1,3;1)$ of $I^{\perp}$ by exact congruence; $w = I$ and $I^{2} = 0$ in the null case; the opposite signs and anticommutation of $I$ and $w$; the generation of all sixty-four dimensions by $I^{\perp}$ with $I$ when $Q(I) \neq 0$; in $\Cl(1,3;1)$ the nilpotent generator, its anticommutation with the Lorentz frame, the sixteen-dimensional ideal and its vanishing square; and the signature $(1,3)$ of the Lorentz frame in all three cases.

\emph{Part G: the transport on the wall.} In the projective-to-conformal paper's model of the completion of $(1,3;1)$: the signature $(2,4)$ by exact congruence; the rank-five linear system for the image of the partner and its unique null solution $c = 0$; the norm $2ab$ of $aI + b\varphi$ on instances of both signs and zero; the invariance of the norm under rational boosts and the swap, the image staying orthogonal to the Lorentz frame; the centres of the two intermediate algebras; and the null pair $v, v^{*}$ in the root paper's normalisation, its identification with the canonical frame, and the norms $\pm\alpha\beta$ and orthogonality of $\alpha v \pm \beta v^{*}$.

\emph{Part H: the two negative results.} The canonical null frame in the rung's diagonal basis; $B = I \wedge \varphi = -e_{+}e_{-}$ with $B^{2} = 1$, commuting with the Lorentz bivectors and vectors and anticommuting with $e_{\pm}$; the rational rotor $5/4 + (3/4)B$ unit, fixing the Lorentz frame, scaling $I$ by $4$ and $\varphi$ by $1/4$, moving a frozen point along its hyperbola; the mirror's $I^{\perp}$ signatures $(4,1)$ and $(3,2)$ on the same instances; the two-by-two rule; the common presentation of $\Cl^{0}(1,4)$ and $\Cl^{0}(4,1)$; and the squares and factorisations of the bare fifth generator.

\emph{Part I: the wall in the cosmological constant.} In four dilation gauges and at seven rational values of $\Lambda$ including zero: the Gram $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1,-\Lambda/3)$ of $I_{\Lambda}^{\perp}$ and its corank at $\Lambda = 0$ only; the gauge independence of the dying eigenvalue; the exact crossing slope $-1/3$ in the parametrisation by $\Lambda$; the signatures $(2,3)$ and $(1,4)$ on the two sides; the rescaled dying entries $\pm 1/3$ and the exceptional signatures; $\Lambda\,(G^{-1})_{ww} = -3$ in every gauge with $w_{0} = a\,I_{0}$; the total signature $(2,4)$ on both sides with the complement's sign switching; the five-dimensional span at the wall and the signature of the Lorentz frame with $I_{0}$ and $\varphi$; and the general hyperplane model of Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.exceptional-algebra-residue-completion-both-sides}(iii) for five signatures $(p,q)$ and five values of $t$.

What the script does not check: the isomorphism types $\Mat(2,\HH)$ and $\Mat(4,\R)$ of the two oriented shadows (Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-representatives-dimension-nearest-four-types}, imported; the note uses that they differ and, in Corollary \claimref{odd-extensions.copy-theorems-blind-spot}, which type belongs to which tower), the frozen-point geometry (Facts \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-frozen-point} and \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-frozen-point-degenerate-algebras}, imported; the script checks the algebra of a vector of each norm sign in the rung, not that the parallel tractor is that vector), the algebra-map properties of Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexification}(i) and (ii) (argued in the text; the script checks the identities they rest on and the four extensions in detail), the identification of the MacDowell-Mansouri translation part with the bivectors $e_{\mu}e_{5}$ beyond the signs of their squares, the reversal of the tractor norm under $g \mapsto -g$ (Proposition \claimref{odd-extensions.two-towers-one-curved-universe}(i), argued in the text; Part H checks its consequences from the reversed signature declared as input), and the transitivity of the boosts on each level set of the norm (Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.transport-constrains-frozen-point-only-through}(iii), argued in the text; Part G checks invariance under particular boosts).
__notes__.note.odd-extensions.two-bits-compared: The root paper's Rule 2 leaves a sign free too, the square of the generator adjoined to a type-C obstruction, and records that the completed algebra forgets it. The sign left free here is of a different kind. The completed algebra, the rung $\Cl(2,4)$, forgets it in the same way; but the intermediate algebra of Theorem \claimref{odd-extensions.are-ascents-pair-signed} remembers it, the doubled $\Cl(1,4)$ against the complexified $\Cl(2,3)$, because the base $\Cl(1,3)$ is even-dimensional and exactly one of the two single extensions changes the parity of $q$ (Lemma \claimref{odd-extensions.volume-element-odd-dimension}). So the sign of $\Lambda$ is a geometric datum with an algebraic witness one level below the rung, and the witness is what the section “The rung's even subalgebra is the anti-de Sitter algebra” used to separate the oriented towers.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-one-dimensional-exten: The physical algebras of the series are even-dimensional and simple. A Kaluza-Klein extension adjoins one direction, and the algebra becomes odd-dimensional, where the volume element is central and the type-C question is live. The first result places the obstruction exactly.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-position-series: This note is a companion to T17 of the series, the capstone \cite{ButlerT17}, and closes Direction 7 of its forward ledger. Every algebraic input is the root paper T1 \cite{ButlerT1}: the classification and the centre (its Theorem 2.5 and Lemmas 2.6, 2.7), the existence and outerness of type C (Theorem 3.6), the Rule 2 machinery (Proposition 5.2, Lemmas 5.3 and 5.4, Theorems 5.5 and 5.7, Remark 5.8), Rule 1's Morita triviality (Theorem 7.1), and the parking of the clock (Proposition 7.4); the note's Lemma \claimref{rule2.even-subalgebra-one-dimensional-extension} is the one standard fact it proves for itself. Theorem \claimref{rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-square} is the note's contribution to T1's own subject: the two rules, compared there as amplifications of the whole algebra and of an even half, coincide on every one-dimensional extension of an even-dimensional algebra, where the even half is the base. The naming of $\Cl(2,4)$ as the conformal completion and of its spinors as twistors is the root paper's and the twistor paper T9's \cite{ButlerT9}. The residue set $\{2, 6\}$ is the dark-matter paper T14's \cite{ButlerT14}, whose reading of the signature convention as indexical is what Corollary \claimref{rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-one-real} needs. The primer T0 \cite{ButlerT0} carries the classification table in the form the note quotes. In the paper series the capstone's ledger row is its only consumer; in the store, later results build on its theorems: \claimref{synthesis.positive-energy-selects-rule-2-sign}, \claimref{synthesis.rule-2-fusing-plane-lorentzian}, \claimref{synthesis.mirror-extensions-causal-convention}, \claimref{synthesis.oriented-causal-towers-mirror-pair-every-window} and \claimref{synthesis.macdowell-mansouri-is-the-frozen-point-reduction-of-five-dimensional-chern-simons}.
__notes__.note.rule2.abstract: The capstone's forward ledger leaves one direction unowned: a physical system whose natural algebra carries a central splitting, so that Rule 2 of the transport principle, ideal fusion by one adjoined generator, is exercised by nature rather than by the classification table. This note supplies two, and the theorem behind both. Of the two one-dimensional extensions of an even-dimensional nondegenerate Clifford algebra exactly one carries the type-C obstruction, spacelike when $p - q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ and timelike when $p - q \equiv 0$, the other having complex type; each ideal of the obstructed extension is a copy of the base; and the Rule 2 repair by a generator of the opposite sign is exactly the Rule 1 ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$: the two adjoined directions span its hyperbolic plane and carry its ladder pair, and the even half that Rule 2 amplifies is the base algebra itself. Applied to the physical lineage: the five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein algebra $\Cl(1,4)$ splits, its two ideals are the two inequivalent five-dimensional Dirac representations, the fifth-direction reflection is the outer exchange, and the fusion is the conformal algebra $\Cl(2,4)$ or its spatial twin $\Cl(1,5)$, the bit the algebra forgets being whether the parity becomes a boost or a rotation. Applied to the plane: $\Cl(2,1)$ splits into the two two-component representations, the four-component fermion of planar electrodynamics and of graphene is the fused algebra, and the parity anomaly is the obstruction's physical face. Twenty-four exact checks verify every identity.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-setting-what-imported:
The transport principle sorts the zero divisors of a real Clifford algebra into three types and repairs each by a minimal ascent \cite{ButlerT1}. Type C is the deepest: not a direction without a partner but a splitting of the algebra itself into two ideals, along the central idempotents $\varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$ built from the volume element, which no inner automorphism can exchange. Its repair, Rule 2, adjoins one generator, fuses the ideals into a simple algebra, and renders inner the very symmetry whose absence defined the obstruction. The capstone \cite{ButlerT17} records that every other direction of the programme has an owner among the series' papers, and that this one does not: no paper of the series exhibits a physical system whose natural algebra is split, with Kaluza-Klein extensions the named candidates. This note takes the row.

The claim is modest and the standard is the series'. What is proved here is algebra: where the obstruction sits among the one-dimensional extensions of an even-dimensional algebra, what its ideals are, and what its repair is. What is physical is imported as Facts with provenance: that odd-dimensional gamma matrices come in two inequivalent representations, that a single planar fermion breaks parity through an induced Chern-Simons term while a doubled one does not, that graphene's low-energy theory is that doubled fermion, that a five-dimensional fermion shifts a Chern-Simons level by half the sign of its mass. The note's contribution is the identification: those two representations are the two ideals, the parity that relates them is the outer exchange, the doubling is the fusion, and the fused algebra of the physical lineage is the conformal algebra the series has used since its root paper. the section “What has been exercised, and what has not” says exactly what has been exercised and what has not.

Notation follows the root paper: $\Cl(p,q)$ has $p$ generators of square $+1$ and $q$ of square $-1$, $n = p + q$, $d = p - q \bmod 8$ is the clock residue, $\omega = e_1 \cdots e_n$ is the volume element, $\Cl^0$ is the even subalgebra, and $\hat{a}$ is the grade involution. The series labels this world's algebra $\Cl(1,3)$ (time of square $+1$), residue $6$; the dark-matter paper explains why the labelling is a convention and what changes hands under its reversal \cite{ButlerT14}, and Corollary \claimref{rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-one-real} below is where that reversal bites. Below, ``spacelike'' and ``timelike'' name generators of square $-1$ and $+1$ respectively, the series' convention; in the mirror's convention the names swap and the mathematics does not.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-five-dimensional-kalu: Take the physical algebra $\Cl(1,3)$ with generators $e_0$ (square $+1$) and $e_1, e_2, e_3$ (square $-1$), spacetime pseudoscalar $\gamma = e_0e_1e_2e_3$ with $\gamma^2 = -1$, and adjoin one spacelike direction $e_4$, $e_4^2 = -1$: the algebra $\Cl(1,4)$ of a five-dimensional spacetime with one extra spatial dimension, which is what a Kaluza-Klein reduction on a circle sees pointwise.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-machine-verification:
Every computational identity asserted in this note has been verified in exact rational arithmetic by the script \texttt{verify\_T17\_rule2.py}, which imports the series' shared library \texttt{GA.py}: its basis-blade Clifford engine, exact ranks, and exact congruence signatures; no floating point anywhere. Twenty-four checks, all passing, in six parts.

\emph{Part A: the extension theorem.} On every even-dimensional nondegenerate $(p,q)$ with $2 \leq p + q \leq 6$, the volume element of each one-dimensional extension is tested for centrality and its square computed: the spacelike extension is type C exactly when $p - q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, the timelike one exactly when $p - q \equiv 0$, the other has complex type, and the residue sets are $\{2, 6\}$ and $\{0, 4\}$. The Lorentzian alternation with its complex-type complement in dimensions $3, 5, 7, 9, 11$, and the three named cases.

\emph{Part B: the even subalgebra.} The map $e_i \mapsto e_i\nu$ on $(1,3)$ and $(2,0)$ with both signs of $\nu^2$: relations, evenness, and the generated dimension $2^n$.

\emph{Part C: the Kaluza-Klein algebra.} Centrality and square of $\omega$, the idempotent identities, $\gamma^2 = -1$ and $\omega = \gamma e_4$; rank $16$ of $a \mapsto \varepsilon_\pm a$ on the blades of $\Cl(1,3)$ and of each ideal; $\varepsilon_\pm e_4 = \mp\varepsilon_\pm\gamma$; the reflection as $\hat{\cdot}\circ\Ad_{e_4}$, its action on $\omega$ and on $\varepsilon_\pm$.

\emph{Part D: the two fusions.} In $\Cl(2,4)$ and $\Cl(1,5)$: the sixteen matrix-unit products, the non-centrality of $\varepsilon_\pm$, the trivial centre; $\Ad_\nu$ and $\Ad_{\nu e_4}$ on every generator; $(\nu e_4)^2 = \pm 1$; the ladder relations of $(\nu, e_4)$ in $\Cl(2,4)$ and the signature $(0,2)$ in $\Cl(1,5)$; the residues; the Rule 1 projectors $ff^*$, $f^*f$ commuting with $\Cl(1,3)$ and the corner of dimension $16$.

\emph{Part E: the plane.} The same programme for $\Cl(2,1)$: the splitting, the ideal dimension $4$, $\varepsilon_\pm e_t = \mp\varepsilon_\pm e_xe_y$, both fusions with their matrix units, inner grade involution and inner reflection, $(\nu e_x)^2 = \mp 1$, the complex type of $\Cl(1,2)$ and of $\Cl(4,1)$, and the residues.

\emph{Part F: the square in general.} On the grid of Part A: the obstructed extension is type C, the opposite-sign repair is $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ at the same residue with a hyperbolic adjoined plane carrying a ladder pair, the same-sign repair sits two residues away with a definite plane, and every repaired algebra has trivial centre.

What the script does not check: the physics imported as Facts \claimref{rule2.imported-gamma-matrices-odd-dimension}, \claimref{rule2.imported-five-dimensional-chern-simons-shift}, \claimref{rule2.imported-parity-anomaly}, and \claimref{rule2.imported-graphenes-two-valleys-doubling} (the note identifies structures, it does not recompute effective actions); the isomorphism $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$ and the rest of the classification table beyond the dimension counts and centres it computes (imported); the group-theoretic restriction of Remark \claimref{note.rule2.twistor-five-dimensional-spinor} (standard); and the eleven-dimensional module counts of Remark \claimref{note.rule2.eleven-dimensions-reality-spinors} beyond the split-versus-complex verdict of Part A.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-one-dimensional-exten: The dark-matter paper's oriented and causal residues are exactly $\{2, 6\}$ \cite[Cor.~3.11]{ButlerT14}. That the towers carrying matter are exactly the towers whose spacelike extensions obstruct is, at this level, arithmetic ($2 \bmod 4$ twice over); the note records the coincidence without building on it.
__notes__.note.rule2.three-dimensions-matter-below: $n = 5$: $\Cl(1,4)$ is split, $\Cl(4,1)$ complex type. $n = 3$: $\Cl(2,1)$ is split, $\Cl(1,2)$ complex type. $n = 11$: $\Cl(10,1)$ is split, $\Cl(1,10)$ complex type. In the series' own convention the five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein extension of this world is the split one; the planar and eleven-dimensional cases are split in the mirror's convention. Physics done with complex gamma matrices sees the splitting in every odd dimension, as the corollary says it must; what the real form governs is the reality of the spinors, Remark \claimref{note.rule2.eleven-dimensions-reality-spinors}.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-planar-fermions: The second system is the oldest home of the parity anomaly. Take generators $e_x, e_y$ of square $+1$ and $e_t$ of square $-1$: the algebra $\Cl(2,1)$ of a $2{+}1$-dimensional spacetime with time of square $-1$, which is the mirror's labelling in the series' convention (Corollary \claimref{rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-one-real} at $n = 3$: the time-positive form $\Cl(1,2)$ is complex type).
__notes__.note.rule2.eleven-dimensions-reality-spi: Corollary \claimref{rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-one-real} at $n = 11$ says $\Cl(10,1) \cong \Mat_{32}(\R) \oplus \Mat_{32}(\R)$ is split while $\Cl(1,10) \cong \Mat_{32}(\C)$ has complex type. The irreducible real module of the first is $\R^{32}$ and of the second is $\C^{32}$, which is the classical statement that Majorana spinors exist in eleven dimensions with time of square $-1$ and not with time of square $+1$, the reason eleven-dimensional supergravity is written in the former convention. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{KugoTownsend1983, VanProeyen1999}. The note records this as a third physical face of the same theorem, without a section of its own: the Rule 2 repair of $\Cl(10,1)$ is $\Cl(11,1)$ or $\Cl(10,2)$, both $\Mat_{64}(\R)$; the former is the Rule 1 ascent of $\Cl(10,0)$, and the latter is the algebra of the two-time proposals, which the note mentions and does not endorse.
__notes__.note.rule2.setting-what-has-been-exercis:
The ledger asked for a physical system whose natural algebra carries a central splitting. The note has given two, and the theorem that they are instances of: the five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein algebra of this world and the planar algebra of the mirror's convention, each split, each with its ideals the two inequivalent spinor representations that physics has always known about, each with its outer exchange the parity that physics has always known to be anomalous, each with its Rule 2 repair the doubled fermion that physics has always used to restore the symmetry. In the five-dimensional case the repair is the conformal algebra of the series' own root paper, and Theorem \claimref{rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-square} says that this is not a coincidence of the example but the general shape: for the physical lineage, the hyperbolic plane that Rule 1 adjoins is a Kaluza-Klein direction plus the direction that repairs it. Rule 2 has been exercised physically in the sense that the obstruction, the exchange, and the repair are each carried by a measured or standard physical structure, imported here as Facts.

What has not been exercised is dynamics. The note does not derive that a sixth direction exists, nor that the fifth one does; it shows that if a fifth is adjoined the algebra obstructs, and that the repair is the direction the series already had. The forgotten bit is read, not decided: whether the parity of the fifth direction becomes a boost or a rotation is a geometric datum, and the series' choice of $\Cl(2,4)$ rests on the root paper's minimality argument, not on anything here. The planar system exercises the fusion at the level of representation theory and of an induced term in an effective action; it does not make the third direction physical, which in graphene it is not. And the note has used the series' convention where it needed to: the Kaluza-Klein algebra splits in the time-positive form, the planar and eleven-dimensional algebras in the time-negative one, and the complexified statement of Corollary \claimref{rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-one-real} is the convention-free residue.

The row's new state, for the capstone's ledger: owned by this note; the kinematic exercise delivered; remaining, a system in which the fused direction is forced dynamically rather than by the representation theory of the fermions, which is the question of what physical principle selects the sign of $\nu^2$. (Later store results take this up: \claimref{synthesis.rule-2-fusing-plane-lorentzian} shows that no principle on the fused algebra and the extension alone can decide it, and \claimref{synthesis.positive-energy-selects-rule-2-sign} selects $\nu^2 = +1$ by the spectrum condition, given one imported classification.)
__notes__.note.sheaf.setting-clifford-algebras-deg: The Clifford algebra of a possibly-degenerate symmetric form is defined exactly as in the nondegenerate case: for a real vector space $W$ with symmetric bilinear form $B$, $\Cl(W, B)$ is the associative unital $\R$-algebra generated by $W$ subject to $\alpha^2 = B(\alpha, \alpha)$. What must be checked, since the series' fibre papers \cite{ButlerT1} use nondegeneracy freely, is that the linear structure survives degeneracy. It does, by a classical argument of Chevalley \cite{Chevalley1997} which we reprove in the form needed for sheaves: with an explicit model that depends smoothly on $B$.

__notes__.note.sheaf.setting-clifford-algebras-deg: Two classical imports are used repeatedly below and are stated here once, with provenance, per the series' import discipline.
__notes__.note.synthesis.geometric-algebra-as-the-:
\emph{Status: argued, not proved.} The reading is that geometric algebra is the algebra of physics: the least structure that independent distinctions carry once they may depend on order, and the structure nature uses. It rests on the graded ladder (note on the grading of the bit ladder) and on the following evidence, each row a structure the ladder produces and a place where physics found it.
\begin{itemize}
\item The sign bit $-1$ (step 2), read as the rotor of a rotation by $2\pi$ (step 5): spinors change sign under a rotation by $2\pi$ and return after $4\pi$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.spin-double-cover}); neutron interferometry (1975).
\item A plane squaring to $-1$ (step 2): the complex unit of quantum mechanics read as the bivector of the spin plane, or as the pseudoscalar $I_4$ of spacetime (conventions, the unit principle; \claimref{std-algebra.complex-numbers}); Hestenes' reading of the Pauli and Dirac theories.
\item $\Cl(3,0)$ (step 3): spin one half, the Pauli algebra (\claimref{std-algebra.pauli-algebra}); atomic spectra, Stern and Gerlach.
\item $\Cl(1,3)$ (step 3): the Dirac equation and the spacetime algebra (\claimref{std-algebra.sta-matrix}); the electron's magnetic moment, antimatter.
\item The signature, a quadratic form over the bit (step 2; \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}): spacetime of signature $(1,3)$; special relativity.
\item Null directions and their partners (step 3): fermionic creation and annihilation operators (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-basis-car}); the exclusion principle, the periodic table, the stability of matter.
\item The extraspecial group and its representation (steps 2 to 4): the real Pauli group generated by the bit flips and phase flips of $k$ qubits, extraspecial of order $2^{1+2k}$ (the full Pauli group adds a central unit of square $-1$), $\Cl(k,k) \cong \Mat_{2^{k}}(\R)$ on the Fock space (\claimref{std-algebra.fock-representation}); quantum information.
\item Rotors, the even part (steps 3 and 5): rotations and Lorentz transformations act on spinors by rotors; $\mathrm{Spin}(1,3)$ is the symmetry of the matter fields.
\end{itemize}
The argument has two parts and a remark. \emph{Coverage}: signs, a complex unit, spinors (as an algebra), a Lorentzian form and anticommuting fermions appear by step 4; continuous rotations and the $2\pi$ sign of spinors need the completion (step 5). \emph{Economy}: one quadratic form over the bit, with its representation, serves rotations, spacetime geometry, spin, exclusion and the qubit. \emph{Nothing extra}: that no other finite-dimensional associative division algebra is used is a theorem (Frobenius; \claimref{transport.exceptional-division-algebras} for the Clifford side), not evidence; the substantive claim would be that physics needs no non-associative structure, which objection (5) leaves open.

\emph{Objections and limits.} (1) The primitives are chosen; the derivation shows geometric algebra is forced once they are granted, not that nature had to grant them. (2) Universality is cheap: every finite-dimensional associative algebra sits in some $\Cl(k,k)$ because matrix algebras are Clifford algebras, and the same containment holds for matrices; what geometric algebra adds is meaning (grades, blades, the bit structure, the geometric reading of the complex unit), not containment. (3) Formalisms are equivalent: anything stated in geometric algebra can be restated with matrices or tensors, so ``intrinsic to the universe'' is an inference to the best explanation. (4) Bosons: their commutation relations have no finite-dimensional representation; they enter as collective limits on the infinite tower, conditional on the state the series takes there (premise (N$_{+}$)), so they are exactly as derived as the continuum. (5) Octonions: if a non-associative structure (octonions, triality, the exceptional groups) proves fundamental, ``nothing is missing'' fails; today such structures appear in speculative unification schemes. (6) The continuum is a premise, (F4), not a derivation, and its physical source in the series, (N$_{+}$), is itself a premise. (7) Below the reals a rational direction carries square classes (primes) as well as a sign; physics works over $\R$, where only signs survive, but the series' finitist computations over $\Q$ must track them. (8) That every signature is populated is the series' reading, not an established result. (9) Coverage was assembled knowing the physics it covers, so it is weaker evidence than a prediction made in advance.

\emph{What would weaken the reading.} A fundamental role for a non-associative algebra; a bosonic structure that cannot be brought onto the same ladder; a measured spinor phase under a full rotation other than $-1$.
__notes__.note.synthesis.grading-of-the-bit-ladder:
The ladder has four chosen primitives, each a postulate of the foundation, and every other step except the last (argued) is a theorem. The grades are those of the source: \emph{chosen} (assumed), \emph{proved} (a theorem in the store or filed with this note), \emph{argued} (an inference from evidence, not a proof).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[0.] \emph{The bit (chosen: premise (F1)).} One distinction, states $0$ and $1$, combined by comparison, $1 + 1 = 0$: the group $\Z_{2}$, and with the product $1 \cdot 1 = 1$ the field $\mathbb{F}_{2}$. It has no sign: $1 = -1$.
\item[1.] \emph{Independence (chosen, part of (F1); counting proved).} $n$ independent distinctions give the configurations $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ under symmetric difference, $2^{n}$ of them, $\binom{n}{k}$ of grade $k$: the index sets of the blades, with no order and no sign.
\item[2.] \emph{Minimal non-commutativity (chosen: premise (F2)).} A group $G$ generated by the directions and one bit $c \ne 1$, a central extension of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ by that bit, with $e_{i}e_{j} = c\,e_{j}e_{i}$ for $i \ne j$. Proved from it: $c^{2} = 1$ (for $n \ge 2$), every square and commutator lies in $\{1, c\}$, the squares form a quadratic form $q$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ whose polar form is the commutator, the centre, and for even $n$ an extraspecial group; $q$ fixes the type of the algebra (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}; the group statements in the integer-algebra result filed alongside). The sign $-1$, the signature and a plane of square $-1$ appear here, before any addition.
\item[3.] \emph{Superposition over the integers (chosen: premise (F3)).} The algebra is $\Z[G]/(c + 1)$. Proved: it is free of rank $2^{n}$ with basis the blades, $v^{2} = Q(v)$ for integer vectors (the contraction rule as a theorem), and it has the universal property of the Clifford algebra of the $\pm 1$ form over every commutative ring: $\Cl_{\Z}(p,q)$. Over $\Z$ the orthogonal presentation $\Z[G]/(c + 1)$ and the null (Witt) presentation generate different orders, and only the latter contains matrix units (the note on the two presentations over the integers, on \claimref{std-algebra.cl11-matrix}); the Witt pairs need $\tfrac12$, so the qubit reading, $\Cl(k,k) \cong \Mat_{2^{k}}$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.fock-representation}, stated over $\R$), sits at step 4 for the orthogonal presentation.
\item[4.] \emph{Division (proved, no new primitive).} Inverting the vectors that are not null, $v^{-1} = v/Q(v)$ (Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.inverse-of-vector}), forces the coefficients from $\Z$ to $\Q$ and to nothing smaller; null vectors and zero divisors survive except in $\Cl_{\Q}(0,0)$, $\Cl_{\Q}(0,1)$, $\Cl_{\Q}(0,2)$ (the rational counterpart of Theorem \claimref{transport.exceptional-division-algebras}).
\item[5.] \emph{Completion (chosen: premise (F4)).} The coefficients are extended to a complete ordered field. Proved: such a field is Euclidean, every real quadratic space has an anticommuting basis of squares $1, -1, 0$ with invariant counts (Sylvester's law, derived in geometric algebra, \claimref{synthesis.completion-recovers-the-real-clifford-algebras}(iii), which replaced the imported Fact), and every real Clifford algebra of the store is a rational one of a $\pm 1$ form extended by scalars, or a subalgebra of one. The signs need only a Euclidean field; over $\Q$ square classes remain. Completeness proper is used by limits (the exponential of a bivector and $\pi$; the nilpotent exponential of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.nilpotent-steps-derivative-exponential-and-boost} is a finite sum and needs none) and by roots of odd-degree polynomials (for which a real closed field suffices).
\item[6.] \emph{The number systems inside (proved, after (F4)).} $\R$, $\Cl(0,1) \cong \C$, $\Cl(0,2) \cong \HH$ are the only finite-dimensional associative real division algebras (Frobenius, derived in geometric algebra); split-complex and dual numbers and the matrix algebras sit inside, with the classification by $p - q \bmod 8$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.periodicity}); every finite-dimensional associative real algebra embeds in a corner of some $\Cl(k,k)$.
\item[7.] \emph{Bosons (proved in the store, conditional where stated).} Collective pair modes of the infinite tower obey canonical commutation relations in the limit (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.central-limit-of-tower-fluctuation-states-with-the-kernel-unit}); they need step 5 and a state on the tower, and are not a further primitive.
\item[8.] \emph{The algebra of physics (argued).} That nature uses exactly this structure is the argued reading of the companion note, not a theorem.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Where the stored algebra sits.} The store's standard algebra is stated over $\R$ and so sits at step 5; much of its content is already algebraic and holds over $\Q$ or $\Z$ (the blade products, inverses of vectors, the matrix units of $\Cl(1,1)$ over $\Z$), but its statements do not yet say so, and no stored entity assumes the four premises.
__notes__.note.synthesis.two-orders-of-constructio:
The foundation's ladder takes the bit (F1), then one bit of non-commutativity (F2), then superposition over the integers (F3), and reaches $\Cl_{\Z}(p,q)$. Three results filed with this note separate that order of construction from a second one.

\emph{The switch.} Acting on a two-state module by set $v$ and clear $w$ gives $v^{2} = w^{2} = 0$, $vw + wv = 1$, the full endomorphism ring over every commutative ring, and the two directions $v \pm w$ of squares $\pm 1$, with no fraction (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}). On two states, the planes of directions containing two independent operations of square zero are exactly the planes of such pairs, one for each unordered pair of states (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.switch-planes-on-a-two-state-space}).

\emph{The ladder contains no switch over the integers.} $\Cl_{\Z}(p,q)$ has no idempotent other than $0$, $1$, and $ab + ba = 1$ in $\Cl_{R}(p,q)$ forces $2$ to be a unit of $R$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.integer-clifford-algebras-contain-no-switch}). So in the order F1, F2, F3 the direction is the reversible operation (undone, up to the sign, by repeating it), the algebra can exchange the two states, and it contains no test of which state holds and no set or clear until $2$ is inverted, which the step to $\Q$ does. In the other order the tests $vw$, $wv$ and the two irreversible operations are present at once, over the integers, and the reversible directions are their sum and difference. For one switch the first algebra is a subring of index $4$ in the second.

\emph{What is open.} The two orders agree over every ring containing $\tfrac12$. Which the foundation should take is not decided: F2 and F3 stand as filed, and the switch is recorded beside them. A foundation rooted on the switch would replace ``one central sign bit between distinct directions'' by ``each distinction can be set and cleared'', and would have to recover the sign and the anticommutation of distinct switches (the Jordan and Wigner sign), which a single switch does not supply.

\emph{Status.} That the on/off reading is physically significant (the exclusion principle as ``cannot be set twice'') is a reading, argued and not proved. The three results are algebra; none uses a rule of transport and none is evidence for the transport postulate.
__notes__.note.tower.setting-tower-rigidity-frozen: The structural properties of matrix amplification, used repeatedly below, are elementary and are proved here once; the one genuinely imported piece of Morita theory is stated as a fact.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-prior-art:
Two bodies of classical material are used, and neither is claimed.

The structure theory of the real Clifford algebras (the isomorphisms $\Cl(p,q) \cong \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ or $\Mat_k(\mathbb{F}) \oplus \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ with $\mathbb{F} \in \{\R, \C, \HH\}$ determined by $p - q$ mod $8$) goes back to Cartan and to the modern treatments of Atiyah, Bott and Shapiro \cite{ABS1964}, Porteous \cite{Porteous1995} and Lounesto \cite{Lounesto2001}; the quadratic-form background is in Lam \cite{Lam2005} and Chevalley \cite{Chevalley1997}. The computation of the centre and of the sign of $\omega^2$ (Lemmas \claimref{transport.centre} and \claimref{transport.sign}) is folklore, restated here and proved in the primer's toolkit \cite[Section 9]{ButlerT0} because the type-C theorem rests on it. Von Neumann regularity of semisimple rings, on which the exhaustiveness theorem rests, is von Neumann's \cite{vonNeumann1936}; the observation that regularity localises zero divisors at idempotents (Lemma \claimref{transport.regularity-localises-zero-divisors-idempotents}) is elementary and surely known, though we have not found it stated in the Clifford literature in the form used here. The idempotent structure of Clifford algebras is surveyed by Lounesto \cite{Lounesto2001} and, computationally, by Ab{\l}amowicz \cite{Ablamowicz1998}.

The point-level machinery of the type-N section is the \emph{conformal model} of geometric algebra and is thoroughly established. The representation of the points of a quadratic space as null rays in a space two dimensions larger, via the embedding $X(x) = \nO + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\nInf$, together with the realisation of conformal transformations, inversions included, as versors of $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, originates in the program of Hestenes and coworkers \cite{Hestenes2001, HLR2001}, has antecedents in the classical projective-quadric (M\"obius and Lie sphere) constructions of the nineteenth century, was given a comprehensive computational treatment by Dorst, Fontijne and Mann \cite{DFM2007}, is standard in the physics literature through Doran and Lasenby \cite{DoranLasenby2003}, and underlies the algebraic theory of conformal groups via Clifford algebras developed by Angl\`es \cite{Angles2008}. Nothing in the section “Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use” and the section “The completion: the conformal model” is claimed as new. The reader familiar with conformal geometric algebra may skim them for notation; the reader \emph{new} to geometric algebra should begin with the companion primer \cite{ButlerT0}, which develops all of this slowly and with worked examples.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-classification-ce: The taxonomy of the section “A taxonomy of obstructions” rests on three classical inputs, recorded here. The first is the structure theory of the real Clifford algebras, together with the centre and pseudoscalar computations behind it, imported from the primer's toolkit because they are structure theory, the language's side of the division of labour. The second is the regularity lemma, proved here: it is a statement about zero divisors, this paper's subject, and we have not found it stated in the Clifford literature in the form used.
__notes__.note.transport.exotic-embedding-inertnes: $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$ embeds unitally in $\Cl(2,3) \cong \Mat_4(\C)$, an algebra of \emph{half} the dimension of the completion $\Cl(2,4)$: the standard unital embedding $\HH \hookrightarrow \Mat_2(\C)$ ($1, i, j, k$, Hamilton's units, mapped to $I$, $\mathrm{diag}(I_5, -I_5)$, $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&I_5\\I_5&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, the matrix entries read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_5\}$, the centre of $\Cl(2,3)$, whose pseudoscalar $I_5$ is its complex unit, Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}) applied entrywise gives $\Mat_2(\HH) \hookrightarrow \Mat_4(\C)$, and $\Cl(2,3)$ has type $\Mat_4(\C)$ by Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras} ($d \equiv 7$). The embedding is genuine; it is also inert: the ambient quadratic space of $\Cl(2,3)$ is five-dimensional, and by Theorem \claimref{transport.representation-independent-minimality-completion} no normalised conformal chart of four-dimensional spacetime exists on its quadric. The algebra is big enough to contain $\Cl(1,3)$ and too small to resolve it: what a resolution needs is not space for the \emph{elements} but space for the \emph{points}, and points cost two dimensions in the exact balance $(+1,+1)$.
__notes__.note.transport.bit-algebra-forgets: Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified} sharpens the disanalogy with Rule 1 into its correct form. In Rule 1 the signature increment $(+1,+1)$ is unique outright (Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality}). In Rule 2 the \emph{algebraic} completion is likewise unique (there is one fused algebra, $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$), but its geometric realisations are two, and no fusion-internal criterion distinguishes them: the sign $\gamma$ is a genuine geometric datum with no algebraic counterpart. The clock positions differ ($d + 1$ and $d - 1$ mod 8, i.e.\ residues $2$ and $0$, or $6$ and $4$), yet the classification table of Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras} is symmetric about the split residues (positions $0$ and $2$ are both real type, $4$ and $6$ both quaternionic), which is the table-level reflection of the isomorphism proved intrinsically in Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}(3). A canonical choice of $\gamma$, if one is ever wanted, must therefore be imported from structure outside the algebra (an orientation of the ambient geometry), and we record the fact here at the level of algebra only: \emph{the fusion is forced, the sign is free}.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-fusion-theorem: Two lemmas prepare the sharp form of the theorem: the corner algebra cut out by $\varepsilon_+$ is the even subalgebra, and a $2 \times 2$ system of matrix units assembles $B_\gamma$ from that corner.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-one-dimensional-e: The physical algebras the series works with are even-dimensional and simple. Adjoining one direction makes them odd-dimensional, where the volume element is central and the type-C question arises. This subsection places the obstruction exactly among the one-dimensional extensions of an even-dimensional algebra, identifies its ideals, and shows that its Rule 2 repair by a generator of the opposite sign is the Rule 1 ascent of the section “Type N: the isotropic obstruction, and Rule 1”: the two rules, compared in Remark \claimref{note.transport.2-pattern-two-rules-compared} as amplifications of the whole algebra and of an even half, coincide on every such extension, where the even half is the base. Throughout, write $c_u(x) = u x u^{-1}$ for conjugation by an invertible $u$.

The residues $\{2, 6\}$ are also the oriented and causal residues of the dark-matter paper \cite[Cor.~3.11]{ButlerT14}. That the towers carrying matter are exactly the towers whose spacelike extensions obstruct is, at this level, arithmetic ($2 \bmod 4$ twice over); the coincidence is recorded and not built on.
__notes__.note.transport.three-dimensions: $n = 5$: $\Cl(1,4)$ is split, $\Cl(4,1)$ complex type. $n = 3$: $\Cl(2,1)$ is split, $\Cl(1,2)$ complex type. $n = 11$: $\Cl(10,1)$ is split, $\Cl(1,10)$ complex type. In the convention of this paper (time of square $+1$) the five-dimensional extension of spacetime is the split one; the planar and eleven-dimensional cases are split in the opposite convention. Physics done with complex gamma matrices sees the splitting in every odd dimension, as the corollary says it must; what the real form governs is the reality of the spinors.

dark-matter.residue-soldered-invariant-n.technical:
Regard a Clifford algebra together with its generating vector subspace, $(A, V)$, as soldered to a metric: $V$ is the image of the tangent space and $Q(v) = g(v,v)$ for $v \in V$. An algebra isomorphism carrying $V$ onto $V'$ carries one quadratic form to the other, so by Sylvester's law it preserves the signature $(p,q)$ and hence the residue: the residue is an invariant of the soldered algebra.

As abstract algebras, however, residues $0$ and $2$, $3$ and $7$, and $4$ and $6$ coincide at equal dimension: $\Cl(1,1) \cong \Cl(2,0)$, $\Cl(1,2) \cong \Cl(3,0)$ and $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Cl(0,4) \cong \Mat(2,\HH)$, and no isomorphism between the members of a pair carries vectors to vectors. So this world's algebra and the $r = 4$ tower's are the same algebra, and the tower charge belongs to the algebra soldered to the metric, not to the algebra alone.
dark-matter.residue-soldered-invariant-n.lay: Each tower of possible matter is labelled by a number, its residue, which comes from how many directions are time-like and how many space-like. This result shows that the label only has meaning once the algebra is tied to the geometry of spacetime. As bare algebras, some different towers are exactly the same at the same dimension, for example our world's algebra and that of one dark tower. What tells them apart is which elements count as directions, and that is fixed by the metric.

Levels pass: the lay now keeps 'at equal dimension'.

proofs.main: (i): the quadratic form $v \mapsto v^{2}$ on $V$ is intrinsic to $(A, V)$, an isomorphism carrying $V$ to $V'$ carries it to the quadratic form of $V'$, and signature is an invariant of real quadratic forms (Sylvester, \claimref{synthesis.completion-recovers-the-real-clifford-algebras}(iii)). (ii): the abstract isomorphisms are the classical table (\claimref{primer.classification-real-clifford-algebras}) (Theorem \claimref{dark-matter.type-residue-what-each-tower-can} recomputes their invariants: same dimension, centre, division algebra, component count and module dimension for each pair); that none carries $V$ to $V'$ is (i) applied to the differing signatures, and is exhibited directly for the pair $(1,3)$, $(0,4)$: every vector of $\Cl(0,4)$ squares to $-|v|^{2} \leq 0$ while $e_{0} \in \Cl(1,3)$ squares to $+1$, so the image of $e_{0}$ under any isomorphism is not a vector. The script verifies the agreement of the abstract invariants for the three pairs and the sign statements on sampled rational vectors.

dark-matter.two-families-are-two-chirali.technical:
Take a complexified ambient of even dimension $2m$ with a Witt pair $W, W'$ of maximal isotropic subspaces, null blade $f$ and the Fock grading of the spinor module. Every maximal isotropic $U$ has a pure spinor $\psi_U$, unique up to scale and an eigenstate of the pseudoscalar $I$: for $W$ it is $f$, of Fock grade $0$, and for $W'$ it is the top state $v_1 \cdots v_m f$, of grade $m$. Even versors preserve chirality and odd versors reverse it, so the family of $U$, the chirality of $\psi_U$, is invariant under the connected isometry group but not the full one.

There are exactly two families, and since grade-$k$ states have chirality proportional to $(-1)^{m-k}$, the Witt pair lies in opposite families if and only if $m$ is odd. In odd dimension $2m+1$ there is one family: the connected group acts transitively on maximal isotropic subspaces and the spin algebra does not preserve Fock grade parity.
dark-matter.two-families-are-two-chirali.lay: In a space with an even number of complex dimensions, the largest subspaces made entirely of zero-length directions come in two kinds. Each such subspace picks out a special spinor, and the handedness of that spinor decides its kind; rotations keep the kind and reflections swap it. A matched pair of these subspaces is of opposite kinds exactly when half the dimension is odd. In odd dimensions there is only one kind.
dark-matter.two-families-are-two-chirali.typing_note: Kept the edge to the flag proposition, which supplies Witt's transitivity; the versor realisation of isometries is used but not cited by the source, so not added. The paper calls the general result classical (Chevalley), but no imported Chevalley claim is in the store, so no standard-route derivation.

proofs.main:
(i) Existence for $W$: $w_{i}f = 0$ since $w_{i}$ anticommutes with the other $w_{j}$ and $w_{i}^{2} = 0$. Uniqueness: on the grade-$k$ state $v_{i_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{k}}f$, $w_{j}$ acts as zero if $j \notin \{i_{1}, \ldots, i_{k}\}$ and otherwise, using $w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij} - v_{i}w_{j}$ (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-basis-car}; here the $w_{i}$ annihilate $f$ and the $v_{i}$ create, the reverse of the reading suggested there, and the relations are symmetric in the two roles), removes the factor $v_{j}$ up to sign; so the common kernel of $w_{1}, \ldots, w_{m}$ on $S$ is the grade-zero line $\C f$. For $W'$ the same computation with the roles exchanged gives the top state, which every $v_{i}$ annihilates since $v_{i}^{2} = 0$. For a general $U$, Witt's theorem (\claimref{std-algebra.witt-extension}; as in Proposition \claimref{dark-matter.flag-insensitive-residue-no-flag-level}) supplies an isometry $\rho$ with $\rho(W) = U$, and $\rho$ is the twisted adjoint action of a versor $R$ (Lemma \claimref{primer.twisted-adjoint-action}), $\rho(x) = \pm RxR^{-1}$; then $U(Rf) = \pm (RWR^{-1})(Rf) = \pm R(Wf) = 0$, so $Rf$ is a pure spinor of $U$, and it is the only one up to scale because $R$ is invertible on $S$. Chirality: $I$ commutes with every even element, so $I$ acts on each grade as a scalar; explicitly
\[
I \;\propto\; \prod_{i}(v_{i}w_{i} - w_{i}v_{i}) \;=\; \prod_{i}(2v_{i}w_{i} - 1),
\]
and the $i$-th factor is $-1$ on states without $v_{i}$ and $+1$ on states with it, so the grade-$k$ states have chirality $\epsilon(-1)^{m-k}$ with $\epsilon$ the normalisation; every pure spinor, being a versor image of $f$, is a chirality eigenstate by (ii).

(ii) In even dimension $e_{j}I = -Ie_{j}$ for every basis vector (\claimref{std-algebra.pseudoscalar-commutation}), so $I$ commutes with even versors and anticommutes with odd ones; if $I\psi = \chi\psi$ then $I(R\psi) = \pm R I\psi = \pm\chi(R\psi)$ with the sign that of $R$'s parity.

(iii) Both chiralities occur among pure spinors (reflect $W$ in any non-null vector), chirality is constant on each orbit of the connected group by (ii), and the full isometry group, which is the connected group together with one reflection, is transitive by Witt; so there are exactly two orbits, one per chirality. For the Witt pair, $f$ has grade $0$ and the top state grade $m$, so their chiralities are $\epsilon(-1)^{m}$ and $\epsilon$: opposite exactly when $m$ is odd. Odd dimension: $-1$ is an improper isometry ($\det(-1) = (-1)^{2m+1}$) that fixes every subspace, so every orbit of the full group is an orbit of the connected group, and Witt's transitivity gives one family; and on either half $S_{\pm}$ the extra generator $\ell$ acts as the Fock grade parity up to a scalar (script-checked in dimensions five and seven), while the spin-algebra bivector $e_{1}\ell$ anticommutes with $\ell$, so the spin algebra mixes the Fock grades within each irreducible module.

The script builds $I$, $f$ and the top state on the split real forms of dimensions four, six and eight in \texttt{GA.py} and checks that both are eigenstates of $I$ with eigenvalues in the ratio $(-1)^{m}$ exactly (only the ratio is invariant, the sign of $I$ being a convention; the chiralities agree at $m = 2, 4$ and differ at $m = 3$), that $I$ anticommutes with every generator in even dimension and commutes with every generator in dimensions five and seven, and exhibits the exchanging versors with their parities. The classical result, with the general criterion that two maximal isotropic subspaces lie in one family exactly when their intersection has dimension congruent to $m$ modulo two, is Chevalley's \cite[Ch.~III, \S1]{Chevalley1954}, see also \cite{LawsonMichelsohn1989}; only the Witt-pair case is used here, and it is proved here.

odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexificat.technical:
Let $n$ be odd, so the volume element $\omega$ of $\Cl(p,q)$ is central, and let $\Cl^{0}$ be the even subalgebra. If $\omega^{2} = +1$, the complementary central idempotents $(1 \pm \omega)/2$ split the algebra as $\Cl(p,q) \cong \Cl^{0} \oplus \Cl^{0}$, and on the summand of $(1 \pm \omega)/2$ the generator $e_n$ acts as $\pm s\,\omega'$, with $s = e_n^{2}$ and $\omega' = e_1 \cdots e_{n-1}$ the volume element of the shadow. If $\omega^{2} = -1$, then $\omega$ is a central unit of square $-1$ and $\Cl(p,q) \cong \Cl^{0} \otimes_{\R} \mathrm{span}\{1, \omega\}$, the complexification of $\Cl^{0}$ with unit $\omega$.

Separately, the even subalgebra of a one-generator extension is a Clifford algebra of one dimension fewer: $\Cl^{0}(p, q+1) \cong \Cl(p,q)$ and $\Cl^{0}(p+1, q) \cong \Cl(q,p)$.
odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexificat.lay: In an odd number of dimensions, the product of all the basis directions commutes with everything. If it squares to plus one, the algebra falls apart into two identical copies of its even part, the part built from products of an even number of directions. If it squares to minus one, it behaves like the imaginary unit and the algebra is that even part with complex coefficients allowed. The even part itself is always a Clifford algebra of one dimension fewer.
odd-extensions.doubling-or-complexificat.typing_note: Removed the edge to the four-extensions corollary, which the proof mentions only for the script's checks (and which itself uses this theorem, the E301 cycle); added the volume-element lemma, which supplies the centrality of omega the proof uses.

proofs.main: (i) With $\omega$ central (Lemma \claimref{odd-extensions.volume-element-odd-dimension}) and $\omega^{2} = 1$ the elements $P_{\pm} = (1 \pm \omega)/2$ are central, idempotent, orthogonal and sum to one, so the algebra is the direct sum of the ideals $P_{\pm}\Cl$. The map $x \mapsto P_{\pm}x$ restricted to $\Cl^{0}$ is injective, since $\omega$ is odd and $x - \omega x$ can vanish for even $x$ only if $x = 0$, and surjective onto $P_{\pm}\Cl$ because $P_{\pm}y = P_{\pm}(y_{0} \pm \omega y_{1})$ for $y = y_{0} + y_{1}$ split by parity, with $\omega y_{1}$ even; and $P_{\pm}$ is central, so the map is an algebra isomorphism. Finally $\omega = \omega' e_{n}$ with $e_{n}$ commuting with $\omega'$ (it anticommutes with each of the $n - 1$ factors, an even number, \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}), so $\omega^{2} = \omega'^{2}e_{n}^{2}$ and $\omega^{2} = 1$ forces $\omega'^{2} = e_{n}^{2} =: s \in \{\pm 1\}$; then $P_{\pm}\omega' = (\omega' \pm s\,e_{n})/2$ and $P_{\pm}e_{n} = (e_{n} \pm s\,\omega')/2 = \pm s\,P_{\pm}\omega'$, so $e_{n}$ acts on the two summands as $+s\,\omega'$ and $-s\,\omega'$. (ii) With $\omega^{2} = -1$ central, $\Cl$ is an algebra over the field $\mathrm{span}\{1, \omega\} \cong \C$, and the $\R$-linear map $\Cl^{0} \otimes_{\R} \mathrm{span}\{1, \omega\} \to \Cl$, $x \otimes (a + b\,\omega) \mapsto ax + b\,\omega x$, is an algebra homomorphism, injective by the parity argument, and surjective by dimension ($2 \cdot 2^{n-1} = 2^{n}$, \claimref{std-algebra.z2-grading}). (iii) For $e_{n}^{2} = -1$ the elements $e_{i}e_{n}$, $i < n$, anticommute pairwise and square to $-e_{i}^{2}e_{n}^{2} = e_{i}^{2}$, so they generate a copy of $\Cl(p,q)$ inside $\Cl^{0}(p, q+1)$, of the full dimension $2^{n-1}$; for $e_{n}^{2} = +1$ they square to $-e_{i}^{2}$ and generate $\Cl(q,p)$. The script verifies (iii), and the identities behind (i) and (ii) (the sign pairing $P_{\pm}e_{n} = \pm s P_{\pm}\omega'$, the dimensions and the spanning, but not the idempotent identities and not the algebra-map properties, which are argued above), over every odd signature of dimensions three and five, and (i) and (ii) in detail on the four extensions of Corollary \claimref{odd-extensions.four-extensions-oriented-pair}: the idempotents, the two ideals of dimension sixteen, the action of $e_{5}$ as $\pm\omega'$ on them, and the spanning of all thirty-two dimensions by $\Cl(p,q) + \omega\,\Cl(p,q)$ in the complexified cases.

odd-extensions.volume-element-odd-dimens.formal: For $n$ odd, $\omega$ is central in $\Cl(p,q)$ and $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2 + q}$. For $n = 5$ this is $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{q}$.
odd-extensions.volume-element-odd-dimens.technical:
For odd $n = p + q$ the volume element $\omega = e_1 \cdots e_n$ commutes with every generator, since moving $e_i$ through it passes the $n - 1$ other factors, an even number; so $\omega$ is central. Its square is
$\omega^{2} = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2 + q}$: reversing the order of the $n$ factors costs $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$, and the $q$ generators with $Q(e_i) = -1$ contribute $(-1)^{q}$. In dimension five this reads $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{q}$.
odd-extensions.volume-element-odd-dimens.lay: Multiply all the basis directions of an odd-dimensional Clifford algebra together and the result commutes with everything in the algebra. Its square is either plus one or minus one, and this lemma gives a simple formula for which. In five dimensions it is plus one exactly when the number of negative directions is even.
odd-extensions.volume-element-odd-dimens.typing_note: Self-contained lemma with its own proof; it restates content of the primer's centre and sign lemmas, but the source proves it directly, so no edges added.

one-relation.imported-square-roots-real-.formal: The square roots of $-1$ in a real Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ are classified: they fall into finitely many conjugacy classes under the group of invertible elements, distinguished by the trace-like invariants of the algebra's matrix representation, and in $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat(2, \mathbb{H})$ every square root of $-1$ is conjugate to the pseudoscalar (one class; Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.square-roots-of-minus-one}). \emph{Provenance:} \cite{HitzerAblamowiczSangwine2013}. Lemma \claimref{one-relation.odd-square-roots-chiral-phase} below proves the odd case of $\Cl(1,3)$ directly, the general classification being context and not a step of the proof.
one-relation.imported-square-roots-real-.technical:
Imported from Hitzer, Ablamowicz and Sangwine: the square roots of $-1$ in a real Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ fall into finitely many conjugacy classes under the group of invertible elements, distinguished by trace-like invariants of the algebra's matrix representation, and in $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat(2,\HH)$ every square root of $-1$ is conjugate to the pseudoscalar (one class; Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.square-roots-of-minus-one}).

The source uses the general classification as context only; the odd case in $\Cl(1,3)$ that it needs is proved there directly.
one-relation.imported-square-roots-real-.lay: Among ordinary numbers, minus one has no real square root, and the complex numbers give it two. In a Clifford algebra there can be many, and this result from the literature sorts them into finitely many classes, where two roots in the same class differ only by a change of viewpoint. In the algebra of spacetime there is just one class: every square root of minus one is the pseudoscalar seen from another viewpoint.

imported_from.citation: E. Hitzer, R. Ablamowicz, and S. J. Sangwine, Square roots of $-1$ in real Clifford algebras, in Quaternion and Clifford Fourier Transforms and Wavelets, Birkhaeuser (2013) 123--153.

one-relation.imported-witts-extension-th.formal: Let $(V, Q)$ be a nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic not two, and let $\sigma : U \to U'$ be an isometry between two subspaces of $V$ carrying the restricted forms. Then $\sigma$ extends to an isometry of $(V, Q)$. Consequently the isometry group $O(V, Q)$ acts transitively on the subspaces of any one isometry type, in particular on the hyperbolic planes, and in any two Witt decompositions $V = H \perp A$, $H$ hyperbolic of maximal dimension, the anisotropic parts $A$ are isometric (Witt's cancellation theorem). \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Witt1937}; \cite[Ch.~I, \S4]{Lam2005}. It is the whole content of Lemma \claimref{one-relation.third-constant-conversion-constant-between-charts}(ii) and of the uniqueness clause of Proposition \claimref{one-relation.two-capacities-three-consequences}(1); the script exhibits witnesses (hyperbolic planes of $(1,3)$ with isometric complements) and does not check the theorem.
one-relation.imported-witts-extension-th.technical:
Witt's extension theorem: in a nondegenerate quadratic space $(V,Q)$ over a field of characteristic not two, any isometry $\sigma : U \to U'$ between subspaces, for the restricted forms, extends to an isometry of all of $V$. Hence $\mathrm{O}(V,Q)$ acts transitively on the subspaces of any one isometry type, in particular on hyperbolic planes.

A consequence is Witt cancellation: in any two decompositions $V = H \perp A$ with $H$ hyperbolic of maximal dimension, the anisotropic parts $A$ are isometric.
one-relation.imported-witts-extension-th.lay: Witt's theorem concerns a space with a fixed rule for measuring lengths. It says that any length-preserving match between two pieces of the space extends to a length-preserving symmetry of the whole space, so pieces that look alike from the inside are also indistinguishable from the outside. It is a classical result from the 1930s.

imported_from.citation: E. Witt, Theorie der quadratischen Formen in beliebigen Koerpern, J. Reine Angew. Math. 176 (1937) 31--44.
T. Y. Lam, Introduction to Quadratic Forms over Fields, Graduate Studies in Mathematics 67, American Mathematical Society (2005).

rule2.imported-classification-centre-typ.formal: $\Cl(p,q)$ is simple for $n$ even, with centre $\R$. For $n$ odd the volume element is central, $\omega^2 = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^q$, and the centre is $\R[\omega]$: isomorphic to $\R \oplus \R$ when $\omega^2 = +1$ and to $\C$ when $\omega^2 = -1$. $\Cl(p,q)$ contains a nontrivial central idempotent if and only if $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and then the nontrivial central idempotents are exactly $\varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$, exchanged by the grade involution, which is outer on the split algebra: no inner automorphism exchanges the two ideals $\varepsilon_\pm \Cl(p,q)$, each of which is simple. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thm.~2.5, Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7, Thm.~3.6]{ButlerT1}; the table itself is classical \cite{ABS1964, Lounesto2001}.
rule2.imported-classification-centre-typ.technical:
For even $n$, $\Cl(p,q)$ is simple with centre $\R$. For odd $n$, the volume element $\omega$ is central with $\omega^{2} = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^{q}$, and the centre $\R[\omega]$ is $\R \oplus \R$ when $\omega^{2} = +1$ and $\C$ when $\omega^{2} = -1$.

A nontrivial central idempotent exists if and only if $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and then the nontrivial central idempotents are exactly $\varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$. They are exchanged by the grade involution, which is outer on the split algebra: no inner automorphism exchanges the two simple ideals $\varepsilon_\pm \Cl(p,q)$. These facts restate results proved earlier in the series; the table itself is classical.
rule2.imported-classification-centre-typ.lay: This collects basic facts about the structure of real Clifford algebras. In even dimensions the algebra is a single indivisible block. In odd dimensions it may split into two identical blocks, which happens exactly when the number of positive directions minus the number of negative ones leaves remainder one on division by four. The two blocks can then be swapped by reversing the sign of every direction, but never by an internal change of viewpoint.

rule2.imported-gamma-matrices-odd-dimens.formal: In odd spacetime dimension $n$ the complex Clifford algebra has exactly two inequivalent irreducible representations, each of dimension $2^{(n-1)/2}$, related by $\Gamma^M \mapsto -\Gamma^M$ for all $M$ and distinguished by the scalar value of the product $\Gamma^0\Gamma^1\cdots\Gamma^{n-1}$, which is $\pm$ a fixed phase; equivalently, the last gamma matrix is $\pm$ a fixed multiple of the product of the first $n - 1$. \emph{Provenance:} standard; \cite[App.~B]{Polchinski1998}, \cite[\S 3]{VanProeyen1999}.
rule2.imported-gamma-matrices-odd-dimens.technical: In odd spacetime dimension $n$ the complex Clifford algebra has exactly two inequivalent irreducible representations, each of dimension $2^{(n-1)/2}$. They are related by $\Gamma^{M} \mapsto -\Gamma^{M}$ for all $M$ and are distinguished by the scalar value of $\Gamma^{0}\Gamma^{1}\cdots\Gamma^{n-1}$, which is plus or minus a fixed phase; equivalently, the last gamma matrix is plus or minus a fixed multiple of the product of the first $n - 1$. The result is standard and imported from Polchinski and Van Proeyen.
rule2.imported-gamma-matrices-odd-dimens.lay: Physicists represent the directions of spacetime by matrices called gamma matrices. In an odd number of dimensions there are two genuinely different ways to do this, which differ by an overall sign on every matrix. The two can be told apart by multiplying all the matrices together.

rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-o.formal: Let $n$ be odd and consider the two real forms of the Lorentzian algebra in dimension $n$, $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ (time of square $+1$) and $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ (time of square $-1$). Then $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and in each case the other real form has complex type. The two real forms have the same complexification, which is split for every odd $n$: over $\C$, realised as $\Cl(V) \oplus \Cl(V)I_{\hat V}$ with $V$ the $n$-dimensional space and $I_{\hat V}$ the central pseudoscalar of the odd extension $\hat V$ of $V \oplus \R f$ ($f$ one further vector), which squares to $-1$ and commutes with every vector (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), the element $\omega' = \omega$ or $I_{\hat V}\omega$, whichever has square $+1$, is central, and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are its central idempotents. Thus the obstruction is present in every odd Lorentzian dimension; the real form decides whether it is visible as a splitting or hidden as a central complex structure.
rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-o.technical:
For odd $n$ compare the two Lorentzian real forms $\Cl(1,n-1)$, with $Q = +1$ on the time generator, and $\Cl(n-1,1)$, with $Q = -1$ on it. Using the commuting-square theorem on where the obstruction sits among one-dimensional extensions, $\Cl(1,n-1)$ is of type C if and only if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\Cl(n-1,1)$ is of type C if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and in each case the other real form has complex type.

Both forms have the same complexification, which is split for every odd $n$: over $\C$, with complex unit $I_{\hat V}$, the central pseudoscalar of an odd extension of $V \oplus \R f$, whichever of $\omega$ and $I_{\hat V}\omega$ squares to $+1$ is a central involution $\omega'$, and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are central idempotents. So the obstruction is present in every odd Lorentzian dimension, and the real form decides whether it appears as a splitting or as a central complex structure.
rule2.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-o.lay: In an odd number of spacetime dimensions there are two ways to set up the algebra, depending on whether time is given a positive or a negative square. Exactly one of the two breaks into two pieces, and which one depends on the dimension modulo four; the other hides the same feature as a built-in square root of minus one. Over the complex numbers the two choices agree, and the result always splits.

proofs.main: $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ is the spacelike extension of $\Cl(1,n{-}2)$, an even-dimensional algebra with $p - q = 3 - n$, which is $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ iff $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\equiv 0$ iff $n \equiv 3$; Theorem \claimref{rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-square}(a) gives the first claim and the complex type of the other case. $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ is the extension of $\Cl(n{-}2,1)$, $p - q = n - 3$, by a generator of square $+1$, obstructed iff $n - 3 \equiv 0$, i.e.\ $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, complex type otherwise. sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-inclu.formal: Let $B$ be any symmetric bilinear form on $W$, $\dim W = n$, and let $e_1, \dots, e_n$ be \emph{any} basis of $W$ (orthogonality is not assumed and may be unavailable smoothly in families). Then the $2^n$ blades $e_I = e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_k}$, $I = \{i_1 < \dots < i_k\}$ (ordered geometric products; for a non-orthogonal basis they are not the outer-product blades of \claimref{obj.std-algebra.blade}), form a linear basis of $\Cl(W, B)$. Moreover the structure constants of the algebra in this basis are polynomial in the entries $B(e_i, e_j)$.
sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-inclu.technical:
For any symmetric bilinear form $B$ on an $n$-dimensional space $W$, degenerate or not, and any basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of $W$ (orthogonal or not), the $2^n$ ordered products $e_I = e_{i_1} \cdots e_{i_k}$ with $i_1 < \dots < i_k$ form a linear basis of $\Cl(W, B)$, and the structure constants in this basis are polynomial in the entries $B(e_i, e_j)$.

Spanning follows from the rewriting rules $e_j e_i = 2B(e_i, e_j) - e_i e_j$ and $e_i e_i = B(e_i, e_i)$. Independence comes from letting the algebra act on the exterior algebra $\Lambda W$ by $c(\alpha)\,\xi = \alpha \wedge \xi + \iota_{B(\alpha, \cdot)}\,\xi$, which satisfies $c(\alpha)^2 = Q(\alpha)\,\id$ with $Q(\alpha) = B(\alpha, \alpha)$: applied to $1$, each blade gives its wedge product plus terms of lower degree, so the images are triangular and hence independent. Nondegeneracy is never used.
sheaf.blade-basis-degenerate-forms-inclu.lay: A Clifford algebra is built from a space of directions together with a rule for multiplying lengths. This result says that the standard basis of the algebra, made from products of basis directions, still works when the rule is degenerate, so that some directions have zero length against everything, and even when the chosen directions are not perpendicular. The multiplication table depends polynomially, and so smoothly, on the rule.

proofs.main:
The basis statement is \claimref{std-algebra.blade-basis}; its argument is recalled here because the clause on structure constants is read off from it. The blades span, by the defining relations: any word in the generators is reduced to blade form by the rewriting $e_j e_i = 2B(e_i, e_j) - e_i e_j$ ($i < j$) and $e_i e_i = B(e_i, e_i)$, each step lowering the number of inversions or the length, and each step introducing coefficients polynomial in the $B(e_i,e_j)$; this also proves the claim about structure constants, given independence.

For independence, exhibit a module in which the blades act independently. On the exterior algebra $\Lambda W$ define, for $\alpha \in W$,
\[
c(\alpha)\,\xi \;=\; \alpha \wedge \xi \;+\; \iota_{B(\alpha, \cdot)}\,\xi ,
\]
exterior multiplication plus contraction with the functional $B(\alpha, \cdot) \in W^*$. Contraction is an anti-derivation, exterior multiplication by $\alpha$ squares to zero, contraction squares to zero, and their anticommutator is multiplication by the pairing: $c(\alpha)^2 = B(\alpha,\alpha)\,\mathrm{id}$. By the universal property, $c$ extends to an algebra map $c : \Cl(W,B) \to \mathrm{End}(\Lambda W)$. Consider the symbol map $\sigma(x) = c(x)\,1 \in \Lambda W$. For a blade,
\[
\sigma(e_I) \;=\; c(e_{i_1}) \cdots c(e_{i_k})\,1 \;=\; e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k} \;+\; (\text{terms of lower exterior degree}),
\]
since each contraction lowers degree by one while each wedge raises it by one, and the top-degree term takes every wedge. The images $\sigma(e_I)$ are therefore triangular with respect to exterior degree against the basis $\{e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k}\}$ of $\Lambda W$, with unit leading coefficients, hence linearly independent; so the $e_I$ are independent in $\Cl(W,B)$. Nothing in the construction used nondegeneracy, and $c$ is visibly polynomial in $B$.
