synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadrati.formal:
Let $\Cl(p,q)$, $n = p + q \ge 1$, have orthonormal generators $e_{1}, \dots, e_{n}$, with $Q(e_{i}) = +1$ for $i \le p$ and $Q(e_{i}) = -1$ for $i$ in $N = \{p + 1, \dots, n\}$, and for $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ let $e_{S}$ be the increasing product of the $e_{i}$, $i \in S$. Identify the subsets with $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$, addition being the symmetric difference $S \triangle T$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The sign from symmetry.)} Let $x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}$, $n \ge 2$, be elements of an algebra over a field $k$ with $x_{i}x_{j} = c\,x_{j}x_{i}$ for all $i \ne j$, for one $c \in k$, and $x_{1}x_{2} \ne 0$. Then $c^{2} = 1$. Moreover, if only the single relation $x_{1}x_{2} = c\,x_{2}x_{1}$ is imposed ($c \ne 0$), then $x_{1}^{2}x_{2} = c^{2}x_{2}x_{1}^{2}$, so wherever $x_{2}x_{1}^{2} \ne 0$ the square $x_{1}^{2}$ commutes with $x_{2}$ exactly when $c^{2} = 1$. Over a field of characteristic other than $2$, with $c \ne 1$ this gives $c = -1$: the symmetry of the relation and the centrality of the squares each force $c \in \{1, -1\}$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The quadratic form.)} $e_{S}^{2} = (-1)^{q(S)}$ with $q(S) = \binom{|S|}{2} + |S \cap N| \bmod 2$, and $e_{S}e_{T} = \pm e_{S \triangle T}$. The map $q : \mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} \to \mathbb{F}_{2}$ is a quadratic form whose polar form
\[
b(S,T) = q(S \triangle T) + q(S) + q(T) = |S|\,|T| + |S \cap T| \bmod 2
\]
is $1$ exactly when $e_{S}$ and $e_{T}$ anticommute. So the group $\{\pm e_{S}\}$ is a central extension of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ by $\{\pm 1\}$ with commutator form $b$ and squaring map $q$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The radical.)} The radical of $b$ is $\{\emptyset\}$ for $n$ even and $\{\emptyset, \{1, \dots, n\}\}$ for $n$ odd, and $q(\{1, \dots, n\}) = 1$ exactly when the pseudoscalar squares to $-1$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The Gauss sum and the type.)} For any $j$ with $j^{2} = -1$ (a unit bivector of a Euclidean plane, say),
\[
\sum_{S} e_{S}^{2} \;=\; \sum_{S}(-1)^{q(S)} \;=\; \big\langle (1 - j)(1 + j)^{p}(1 - j)^{q} \big\rangle_{0},
\]
and its value is $2^{n/2}$ for $p - q \equiv 0, 2$, $-2^{n/2}$ for $p - q \equiv 4, 6$, $2^{(n+1)/2}$ for $p - q \equiv 1$, $-2^{(n+1)/2}$ for $p - q \equiv 5$ and $0$ for $p - q \equiv 3, 7 \pmod 8$. Define the Arf invariant of a quadratic form $q'$ with nondegenerate polar form on $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m}$ by $\sum (-1)^{q'} = (-1)^{\mathrm{Arf}(q')}\,2^{m/2}$. For $n$ even, $\mathrm{Arf}(q) = 0$ exactly when $\Cl(p,q)$ is a real matrix algebra ($p - q \equiv 0, 2 \bmod 8$) and $\mathrm{Arf}(q) = 1$ exactly when it is a quaternionic one ($p - q \equiv 4, 6$). For $n$ odd, $q$ is nonzero on the radical exactly in the complex case ($p - q \equiv 3, 7$); otherwise $q$ descends to the quotient by the radical, whose Arf invariant is $0$ for a sum of two real matrix algebras ($p - q \equiv 1$) and $1$ for a sum of two quaternionic ones ($p - q \equiv 5$). So the parity of $n$, the value of $q$ on the radical and the Arf invariant determine the type in the classification.
\item[(v)] \emph{(The ascent.)} Add one hyperbolic plane spanned by $e, f$ with $Q(e) = 1$, $Q(f) = -1$, put $\omega = ef$, and take the twisted generators $x_{i}\omega$ of the commuting-copies isomorphism (Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}). For $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ and $B \subseteq \{e, f\}$ the product of the $x_{i}\omega$, $i \in A$, with the blade $e_{B}$ is $\pm$ a blade of $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$, and $(A, B) \mapsto$ its index set is a linear bijection $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} \oplus \mathbb{F}_{2}^{2} \to \mathbb{F}_{2}^{n+2}$ carrying $q_{(p,q)} \perp q_{(1,1)}$ to $q_{(p+1,q+1)}$. The form $q_{(1,1)}$ has Arf invariant $0$, so the $(1,1)$ ascent leaves the Gauss sum's sign, the Arf invariant and the type unchanged (the division-ring clause of Theorem \claimref{tower.rigidity-clock-frozen}); the anisotropic plane $(0,2)$, whose Clifford algebra is the quaternions, has $q = 1$ on its three nonzero elements and Arf invariant $1$; adding it is not an orthogonal sum with the ground form, since the twist by its volume element, of square $-1$, exchanges $p$ and $q$: $\Cl(p, q{+}2)$ carries $q_{(q,p)} \perp q_{(0,2)}$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadrati.technical:
The signs of the squares of the basis blades of a real Clifford algebra form a quadratic form over the two-element field: index the blades by subsets of the generators, so that multiplying blades adds their index sets by symmetric difference, and record a $1$ when the blade squares to $-1$. The associated bilinear form records exactly which pairs of blades anticommute, so the finite group of signed blades is the central extension that this form describes. The form's own invariants recover the classification. In even dimension the anticommutation form is nondegenerate and the Arf invariant, read off from the sign of the Gauss sum $\sum_{S} e_{S}^{2}$, is $0$ for the real matrix algebras ($p - q \equiv 0, 2 \bmod 8$) and $1$ for the quaternionic ones ($p - q \equiv 4, 6$). In odd dimension the radical is spanned by the pseudoscalar: if it squares to $-1$ the algebra is complex, and otherwise the Arf invariant of the quotient separates two real from two quaternionic matrix algebras. The Gauss sum is the scalar part of $(1 - j)(1 + j)^{p}(1 - j)^{q}$ with $j^{2} = -1$, which gives the whole table at once.

Two small structural facts sit underneath. A single commutation coefficient shared by all pairs of directions must satisfy $c^{2} = 1$, because the relation must read the same with the two directions exchanged; and, with only one relation imposed, the same condition $c^{2} = 1$ is what makes the square of a direction central. Either way $c \in \{1, -1\}$, and $c = -1$ needs the separate input $c \ne 1$. These are classical: the classification by the quadratic form is in Ovsienko and in Elduque and Rodrigo-Escudero, and is restated here. In the language of the series, adding a hyperbolic plane, the $(1,1)$ increment of the transport ascent, adds an orthogonal summand of Arf invariant $0$ once the ground generators are twisted by the plane's volume element, so the type never changes up the tower, while the anisotropic plane $(0,2)$, whose algebra is the quaternions, carries Arf invariant $1$; adding it is not an orthogonal sum with the ground form, since the twist by its volume element, of square $-1$, exchanges $p$ and $q$: $\Cl(p, q{+}2)$ carries $q_{(q,p)} \perp q_{(0,2)}$.
synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadrati.lay: Every product of basic directions in these algebras squares either to plus one or to minus one. Writing down which ones give minus one produces a simple yes-or-no table, and that table already knows which kind of number system the whole algebra is built on: ordinary real numbers, complex numbers or quaternions. Adding a pair of directions of opposite type, the basic step the series uses to repair division, never changes that answer; adding two directions that both square to minus one is different, because it also swaps the roles of the existing positive and negative directions.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} Exchanging $i$ and $j$ in the relation gives $x_{j}x_{i} = c\,x_{i}x_{j}$, so $x_{1}x_{2} = c\,x_{2}x_{1} = c^{2}x_{1}x_{2}$ and $(1 - c^{2})x_{1}x_{2} = 0$; since $x_{1}x_{2} \ne 0$ and $c$ is a scalar of a field, $c^{2} = 1$. With only the relation $x_{1}x_{2} = c\,x_{2}x_{1}$, moving $x_{2}$ through $x_{1}x_{1}$ uses it twice: $x_{1}^{2}x_{2} = c\,x_{1}x_{2}x_{1} = c^{2}x_{2}x_{1}^{2}$, so $x_{1}^{2}x_{2} - x_{2}x_{1}^{2} = (c^{2} - 1)x_{2}x_{1}^{2}$, which vanishes, when $x_{2}x_{1}^{2} \ne 0$, exactly when $c^{2} = 1$. In characteristic other than $2$, $c^{2} = 1$ and $c \ne 1$ give $c = -1$. The check verifies the second statement in the normal-ordered model of the algebra with one relation $x_{2}x_{1} = c^{-1}x_{1}x_{2}$ for $c = 2, \tfrac13, -1, 1$ (the square $x_{1}^{2}$ is central exactly for $c = \pm 1$, and these are exactly the values for which the relation reads the same both ways), and in $\Cl(p,q)$ that distinct generators anticommute and every $e_{i}^{2}$ is central.

\emph{(ii)} By Proposition \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}, $e_{S}e_{T} = \pm \prod_{i \in S \cap T} Q(e_{i})\, e_{S \triangle T} = \pm e_{S \triangle T}$, the generators having squares $\pm 1$. Reversing the $k = |S|$ letters of $e_{S}$ costs $\binom{k}{2}$ transpositions, and $e_{S}\widetilde{e_{S}} = \prod_{i \in S}Q(e_{i}) = (-1)^{|S \cap N|}$, so $e_{S}^{2} = (-1)^{\binom{k}{2}}e_{S}\widetilde{e_{S}} = (-1)^{q(S)}$. Moving $e_{T}$ past $e_{S}$ letter by letter gives $e_{S}e_{T} = (-1)^{b(S,T)}e_{T}e_{S}$ with $b(S,T) = |S|\,|T| + |S \cap T|$ (each letter of $T$ passes the $|S|$ letters of $S$, anticommuting with all but the one equal to it, if any). Then $e_{S \triangle T}^{2} = (e_{S}e_{T})^{2} = e_{S}e_{T}e_{S}e_{T} = (-1)^{b(S,T)}e_{S}^{2}e_{T}^{2}$, which is $q(S \triangle T) = q(S) + q(T) + b(S,T)$. The form $b$ is bilinear over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$, since $|S \triangle S'| \equiv |S| + |S'|$ and $|(S \triangle S') \cap T| \equiv |S \cap T| + |S' \cap T| \bmod 2$, and $q(\emptyset) = 0$; so $q$ is a quadratic form with polar form $b$. The group $\{\pm e_{S}\}$ maps onto $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ with kernel $\{\pm 1\}$, central; its commutators are $(-1)^{b}$ and its squares $(-1)^{q}$. The check compares the GA products with the closed forms for every pair of blades in all twenty signatures with $n \le 5$.

\emph{(iii)} $S$ lies in the radical when $b(S, \{i\}) = |S| + [i \in S] = 0$ for every $i$. If $S$ is neither empty nor everything, taking $i \in S$ and $i' \notin S$ gives $|S| \equiv 1$ and $|S| \equiv 0$; $S = \emptyset$ always lies in the radical, and $S = \{1, \dots, n\}$ does exactly when $n \equiv 1 \bmod 2$. Its square is the pseudoscalar's, whose sign is that of Proposition \claimref{primer.sign}.

\emph{(iv)} For $k \ge 0$, $(-1)^{\binom{k}{2}} = \langle (1 - j)j^{k}\rangle_{0}$ (the values for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are $1, 1, -1, -1$, and both sides have period $4$ in $k$). Grouping the subsets by $a = |S \setminus N|$ and $b' = |S \cap N|$,
\[
\sum_{S}(-1)^{q(S)} = \Big\langle (1 - j)\sum_{a, b'}\binom{p}{a}\binom{q}{b'}j^{a}(-j)^{b'}\Big\rangle_{0} = \big\langle (1 - j)(1 + j)^{p}(1 - j)^{q}\big\rangle_{0},
\]
all products taken in the commutative algebra $\mathrm{span}\{1, j\}$. There $(1 + j)(1 - j) = 2$, $(1 + j)^{2} = 2j$, $(1 + j)^{8} = 16$, so with $r = p - q \ge 0$ the product is $2^{q}(1 - j)(1 + j)^{r}$, and $\langle (1 - j)(1 + j)^{s}\rangle_{0} = 1, 2, 2, 0, -4, -8, -8, 0$ for $s = 0, \dots, 7$; with $r = 8m + s$ and $n = r + 2q$ this is the stated table. For $r < 0$ the product is $2^{p}(1 - j)^{|r| + 1}$, and the automorphism $j \mapsto -j$ of $\mathrm{span}\{1, j\}$ turns its scalar part into that of $2^{p}(1 + j)^{|r| + 1}$; since $\langle (1 + j)^{t}\rangle_{0} = 1, 1, 0, -2, -4, -4, 0, 8$ for $t = 0, \dots, 7$, and $(1 + j)^{8} = 16$, so that for $|r| + 1 \ge 8$ the value is $16^{m}$ times the tabulated one, the same table follows. For $n$ even the polar form is nondegenerate by (iii) and the definition of the Arf invariant applies directly; comparing the sign of the Gauss sum with the classification (Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}: $p - q \equiv 0, 2$ real, $4, 6$ quaternionic, $1$ two real, $5$ two quaternionic, $3, 7$ complex matrix algebras) gives the even statement. For $n$ odd with $q(\{1, \dots, n\}) = 1$, $S \mapsto S \triangle \{1, \dots, n\}$ changes $q$ by $1$ (since $b(S, \{1, \dots, n\}) = 0$), so the Gauss sum is $0$ and by (iii) the pseudoscalar squares to $-1$, the complex case $p - q \equiv 3, 7$. Otherwise $q$ is constant on the cosets of the radical, the quotient form on $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n-1}$ has nondegenerate polar form, and the Gauss sum is twice the quotient's, $\pm 2 \cdot 2^{(n-1)/2}$, with the sign $+$ for $p - q \equiv 1$ and $-$ for $p - q \equiv 5$. The check computes $q$ from the GA squares, the radical, the Gauss sum and the scalar part of $(1 - j)(1 + j)^{p}(1 - j)^{q}$ with $j = e_{1}e_{2}$ in $\Cl(2,0)$ for all $44$ signatures with $1 \le n \le 8$, and compares each with the type of the classification.

\emph{(v)} By Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} with one plane, the twisted generators $x_{i}\omega$ satisfy the ground relations, $(x_{i}\omega)^{2} = x_{i}^{2}$ because the even element $\omega$ commutes with the ground generators and $\omega^{2} = 1$, and they commute with $e$ and $f$. So the square of the product $y_{A,B}$ of the $x_{i}\omega$, $i \in A$, with $e_{B}$ is $(-1)^{q_{(p,q)}(A)}(-1)^{q_{(1,1)}(B)}$. As $\omega^{|A|}$ is $1$ or $\pm ef$, $y_{A,B}$ is $\pm$ the blade with index set $A \triangle (\{e, f\}$ if $|A|$ is odd$) \triangle B$, which is linear in $(A, B)$ and injective; so it is an isometry $q_{(p,q)} \perp q_{(1,1)} \to q_{(p+1,q+1)}$. The Gauss sum is multiplicative on orthogonal sums, and $q_{(1,1)}$ takes the values $0, 0, 1, 0$ on $\emptyset, \{e\}, \{f\}, \{e,f\}$, Gauss sum $2 = 2^{1}$, Arf invariant $0$; so the sign of the Gauss sum, and with it the type, is unchanged, which is the division-ring clause of Theorem \claimref{tower.rigidity-clock-frozen}. For $(0,2)$, $e_{1}^{2} = e_{2}^{2} = (e_{1}e_{2})^{2} = -1$, Gauss sum $-2$, Arf invariant $1$. The check builds the twisted products in $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ for five ground signatures and verifies the squares, the commutation and the bijection. For an anisotropic plane $e', f'$ with $Q(e') = Q(f') = -1$, $\omega' = e'f'$ has $\omega'^{2} = -1$, so $(x_{i}\omega')^{2} = -x_{i}^{2}$: the twisted ground generators have the opposite squares, and the same argument gives an isometry $q_{(q,p)} \perp q_{(0,2)} \to q_{(p,q+2)}$, not $q_{(p,q)} \perp q_{(0,2)}$; so $\Cl(2,2)$, real, comes from $\Cl(2,0)$, real, and $\Cl(0,4)$, quaternionic, from $\Cl(0,2)$, quaternionic. The check verifies this isometry for four ground signatures and the two examples.

synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or any ordered field, and $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ the Clifford algebra of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} with coefficients in $k$, with blades $e_{S}$, the blade inverse $x \mapsto x^{\dagger}$ and the scalar part $\langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$ as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}; by clause (iii) of that theorem $\langle x^{\dagger}x\rangle_{0}$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$. Everything below is relative to the fixed split of the generators that defines $\dagger$. Premise (P), positivity of values (Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}), is assumed, not derived: values are given by a \emph{state}, a $k$-linear $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$ (normalisation), $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ (positivity) and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ (reality).

\emph{Definitions.} A \emph{projector} is an element $E$ with $E^{\dagger} = E = E^{2}$. The \emph{corner} of a projector $\Pi$ is $\Pi\Cl_{k}(p,q)\Pi$. An \emph{atom} is a nonzero projector $\Pi$ whose corner has no self-adjoint elements other than the multiples of $\Pi$. A nonzero projector $\Pi$ with $\Pi x\Pi = \langle\Pi x\rangle_{0}\Pi/\langle\Pi\rangle_{0}$ for all $x$ (corner $k\Pi$) is an atom; in $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the vacuum projector of (i) and every atom of its orbit (ii) are of this form, and results on the mode algebras that define an atom by this identity use a special case of the present definition. A functional $\omega$ is \emph{sharp} on a projector $\Pi$ if $\omega(\Pi) = 1$. For a nonzero projector $\Pi$ put $\omega_{\Pi}(x) = \langle\Pi x\rangle_{0}/\langle\Pi\rangle_{0}$; it is a state sharp on $\Pi$ (clause (iii) of the theorem above, with $\rho = \Pi = \Pi\Pi^{\dagger}$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Atoms exist in every signature; proved, with a table computed for $p + q \le 5$ and for $(2,4)$, $(3,3)$.)} Let $b_{1}, \dots, b_{m}$ be commuting blades of square $1$, independent (no product of a nonempty subset is $\pm 1$) and maximal (every blade of square $1$ that commutes with all of them is, up to sign, a product of some of them); such a set exists in every signature, and $m = 0$ is allowed. For signs $\chi \in \{\pm 1\}^{m}$ put $\Pi_{\chi} = \prod_{i}\tfrac12(1 + \chi_{i}b_{i})$. Then every $\Pi_{\chi}$ is an atom with $\langle\Pi_{\chi}\rangle_{0} = 2^{-m}$, the $2^{m}$ atoms $\Pi_{\chi}$ are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, and the corner of $\Pi_{\chi}$ is spanned by $\Pi_{\chi}$ and by elements $b\Pi_{\chi}$, $b$ a blade of square $-1$ commuting with every $b_{i}$, each of which is anti-self-adjoint with square $-\Pi_{\chi}$. In $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ with the modes of Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors} ($Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$, $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j})$, $p_{j} = f_{j}e_{j}$) the parities $p_{1}, \dots, p_{\ell}$ are such a set, the atom $\Pi_{0} = \prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 + p_{j})$ satisfies $v_{j}\Pi_{0} = 0$ for all $j$ (the vacuum projector), and its corner is $k\Pi_{0}$. The proof of this clause is an argument on blades valid in every signature and does not use the table that follows, which is a sample confirming it. Computed: in every signature with $p + q \le 5$ and in $(2,4)$ and $(3,3)$ the corner of $\Pi_{\chi}$ has dimension $1$, $2$ or $4$ (for example $1$ in $(1,1)$, $(2,0)$, $(2,2)$, $(3,3)$; $2$ in $(3,0)$; $4$ in $(0,2)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,4)$), with $m = 1, 1, 2, 3, 1, 0, 1, 2$ in these eight.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The orbit of an atom, and hermitian squares; proved.)} Let $\Pi$ be an atom and $y$ an element with $y\Pi \ne 0$. Then $\Pi y^{\dagger}y\Pi = n_{y}\Pi$ with $n_{y} = \langle\Pi y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0}/\langle\Pi\rangle_{0} > 0$, and $\Pi_{y} = y\Pi y^{\dagger}/n_{y}$ is an atom with $\langle\Pi_{y}\rangle_{0} = \langle\Pi\rangle_{0}$. With the atoms $\Pi_{\chi}$ of (i), every $y$ satisfies $yy^{\dagger} = \sum_{\chi}n_{y,\chi}(\Pi_{\chi})_{y}$, the sum over the $\chi$ with $y\Pi_{\chi} \ne 0$ and $n_{y,\chi} > 0$ the number $n_{y}$ for $\Pi_{\chi}$: every element $yy^{\dagger}$ is a combination of atoms with positive coefficients. Consequently a $k$-linear functional that is non-negative on every atom is non-negative on every $yy^{\dagger}$: given linearity, the positivity clause of (P) is equivalent to non-negative values on all atoms.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The weights, under (P); proved.)} Let $\omega$ be a state and $\Pi$ an atom. If $\omega$ is sharp on $\Pi$ then $\omega = \omega_{\Pi}$:
\[
\omega(x) = \frac{\langle\Pi x\rangle_{0}}{\langle\Pi\rangle_{0}} \quad\text{for all } x, \qquad\text{and for every projector } E:\quad \omega(E) = \frac{\langle\Pi E\rangle_{0}}{\langle\Pi\rangle_{0}} = \frac{\langle(E\Pi)^{\dagger}(E\Pi)\rangle_{0}}{\langle\Pi^{\dagger}\Pi\rangle_{0}} \in [0,1] .
\]
The weight of the outcome $E$ in the state sharp on $\Pi$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $E\Pi$ divided by that of $\Pi$; for projectors $E_{1}, \dots, E_{r}$ with $E_{i}E_{j} = 0$ ($i \ne j$) and sum $1$ the weights sum to $1$. For two atoms $\Pi_{x}$, $\Pi_{y}$ of the orbit of $\Pi$, with overlap $z = \Pi x^{\dagger}y\Pi$,
\[
\omega_{\Pi_{x}}(\Pi_{y}) = \omega_{\Pi_{y}}(\Pi_{x}) = \frac{\langle zz^{\dagger}\rangle_{0}}{n_{x}\,n_{y}\,\langle\Pi\rangle_{0}} ,
\]
and when the corner of $\Pi$ is $k\Pi$, $z = c\Pi$ and the weight is $c^{2}/(n_{x}n_{y})$: the square of the overlap over the product of the squared norms. All weights lie in $k$: no square root is taken, because the atom $\Pi_{y}$ depends only on the ray of $y\Pi$ and $y$ is not normalised.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Each hypothesis is needed; proved by examples, and the atom condition is necessary and sufficient.)} (a) Without the reality clause the conclusion of (iii) holds on self-adjoint elements only: on one mode, $\Cl_{k}(1,1)$ with $\Pi = \tfrac12(1 + p_{1})$, the functional $\mu(x) = \omega_{\Pi}(x) + \langle f_{1}x\rangle_{0}$ is linear, normalised, non-negative on every $xx^{\dagger}$ and sharp on $\Pi$, with $\mu(f_{1}) = -1 \ne 0 = \omega_{\Pi}(f_{1})$. (b) Without the positivity clause: $\nu(x) = \langle(1 + p_{1} + \tfrac13 e_{1})x\rangle_{0}$ is linear, normalised, real and sharp on $\Pi$, with $\nu(e_{1}) = \tfrac13 \ne 0 = \omega_{\Pi}(e_{1})$; it has the value $-\tfrac43$ on $yy^{\dagger}$ for $y = -3 + 3e_{1} - 2f_{1} + 2p_{1}$. (c) If a nonzero projector $\Pi'$ is not an atom, the states sharp on $\Pi'$ are not unique: for a self-adjoint $s$ in its corner with $\langle s\rangle_{0} = 0$, $s \ne 0$, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ in $k$ such that $x \mapsto \langle(\Pi' + ts)x\rangle_{0}/\langle\Pi'\rangle_{0}$ is a state sharp on $\Pi'$ for every $t \in k$ with $|t| \le \varepsilon$; in $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$, $\Pi' = \tfrac12(1 + p_{1})$ and $s = \Pi'p_{2}$ give the states with $\omega(p_{2}) = t$, $|t| \le 1$. So sharpness on a projector fixes the state exactly when the projector is an atom.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Scope.} The theorem is conditional on (P). Atoms and projectors are self-adjoint for the split that defines $\dagger$, the same split for which $\omega$ is a state, and the weights are numbers in $[0,1]$ only for such projectors: an idempotent that is self-adjoint for another split can receive a value outside $[0,1]$ (in $\Cl_{k}(1,1)$ the state $x \mapsto \langle(1 + e_{1})x\rangle_{0}$ gives the idempotent $\tfrac12(1 + \tfrac54 e_{1} + \tfrac34 f_{1})$ of a boosted frame the value $\tfrac98$), and sharpness on such an idempotent does not fix a state. It says what a state sharp on an atom is; it does not say that physical states are sharp on atoms, which elements are outcomes of measurements, or why values should be linear on elements that do not commute. The last is assumed in (P), and it is the assumption that theorems of Gleason's type derive from weaker ones for projectors; so the result does not derive the Born rule from the stored measurement premises. Under (P), and given sharpness on an atom, which is itself assumed, it makes the envariance argument (Zurek 2005, prior art; versions 1 to 3 of the stored Born account, Proposition \claimref{one-relation.measure-indifference-borns-rule-located}, rested on it through an imported Fact, now retired, and version 4 rests on clause (iii) here) unnecessary for the weights of a sharp state: no indifference premise, environment, fine-graining or continuity step is used. The saturating state of clause (viii) of the theorem above is the case of one atom over $k \ni \sqrt{2}$.
synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-.technical:
Under Premise (P), positivity of values (values are given by a linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$, the adjoint being the blade inverse for a fixed split of the generators; assumed, not derived), the weights of a sharp state are the Born weights, in every Clifford algebra $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ over an ordered field $k$, the rationals included. The statement needs the right notion of a sharp state. A projector is a self-adjoint idempotent; an atom is a projector $\Pi$ whose corner $\Pi\Cl_{k}(p,q)\Pi$ has only the multiples of $\Pi$ as self-adjoint elements. Atoms exist in every signature: the product of the idempotents $\tfrac12(1 + b_{i})$ over a maximal set of commuting blades of square one is an atom, and for the mode algebra $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the blades can be taken to be the mode parities, which gives the vacuum projector. The corner of an atom can be larger than the multiples of the atom (it has dimension $2$ in $\Cl(3,0)$ and $4$ in $\Cl(1,3)$ and $\Cl(2,4)$), but the extra elements are anti-self-adjoint.

The theorem, under (P): a state with value $1$ on an atom $\Pi$ is $x \mapsto \langle\Pi x\rangle_{0}/\langle\Pi\rangle_{0}$, and nothing else. The weight it gives an outcome projector $E$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $E\Pi$ divided by that of $\Pi$, a squared norm; between two atoms of one orbit it is the squared overlap divided by the two squared norms. All weights are in the field: no square root and no completion is needed. Each clause of (P) is needed (without reality the functional is fixed on self-adjoint elements only; without positivity a real normalised functional sharp on the atom gives other values), and a projector that is not an atom carries several sharp states. Given linearity, positivity itself is the same as non-negative values on all atoms, because every $yy^{\dagger}$ is a positive combination of atoms.

What this does and does not do, given (P): the weights follow with no indifference premise, no environment, no fine-graining and no continuity, so under (P), and given sharpness on an atom, which is itself assumed (physical states are not shown to be sharp), the envariance argument (Zurek), on which the stored Born account rested up to its version 3, is not needed for them. But the assumption that argument isolates, that weights exist and add, is not removed; it sits inside (P), whose linearity on elements that do not commute is the non-contextuality assumption of Gleason-type theorems. Stated plainly: the derivation relocates the content of the imported argument into the linearity of (P) across elements that do not commute, and does not reduce it. The mathematics is classical (the support-projection argument and the trace form of the Born rule); the placement over the rationals with the blade inverse, and the atom condition stated without the classification of the algebras, are what is recorded.
synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-.lay:
Quantum theory says the chance of an outcome is a squared size, the Born rule. The series has an assumption, called (P), about averages: the rule giving averages adds up over sums, gives the trivial quantity the average 1, never gives a quantity times its mirror image a negative average, and gives a quantity and its mirror image the same average. This result shows that, assuming (P), a state that answers yes with certainty to one of the finest yes-or-no questions the algebra contains (an atom) is fixed completely, and the chances it gives are the squared-size rule. It does not show that physical states are of this kind, nor which questions are measurements. Under (P) there is exactly one such state for each atom; the chance it gives any other yes-or-no question is a ratio of two sums of squares, the squared size of the overlap. With whole-number or fractional ingredients the chances are fractions: no square roots and no limits are needed.

This is not a derivation of the Born rule from nothing. The assumption (P) already contains the idea that averages add up even for quantities that cannot be measured together, and that idea is what the well-known theorems in this area work hardest to justify. So the assumption that chances do not depend on which other questions are asked alongside is moved into (P), not removed. What the result does is show that, once (P) is assumed and the state is certain on an atom, which is itself assumed, the separate argument the series had borrowed for the Born rule is no longer needed for these chances. The mathematics is long known; what is new here is only its statement inside the series' algebra with fractions.

e 0$ for some $y$, take $t = - eta(N,y)/( eta(y,y) + 1) \in k$: then $ eta(N + ty, N + ty) = 2t eta(N,y) + t^{2} eta(y,y) = - eta(N,y)^{2}\,( eta(y,y) + 2)/( eta(y,y) + 1)^{2} < 0$, a contradiction; this uses only that $k$ is ordered. synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or any ordered field, and $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ the Clifford algebra of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} with coefficients in $k$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.division-gives-the-rationals}), with blades $e_{S}$, the images of the group $G$ of signed directions. Let $x \mapsto x^{\dagger}$ be the linear extension of the inverse of $G$, $e_{S}^{\dagger} = e_{S}^{-1}$. The adjoint is defined by the chosen generators. In definite signature it does not depend on the orthonormal frame; in indefinite signature it depends on the split into generators of square $1$ and of square $-1$, so observables, states and (P) are relative to that split, and each statement holds for every fixed split. An \emph{observable} is an $x$ with $x^{\dagger} = x$ and $x^{2} = 1$.

\emph{Hypothesis (P), positivity of values:} values are given by a \emph{state}, a $k$-linear $\omega : \Cl_{k}(p,q) \to k$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$; (P) is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}, assumed, not derived.

The functionals $\omega_{\rho}(x) = \langle\rho x\rangle_{0}/\langle\rho\rangle_{0}$, $\rho = \sum_{r}y_{r}y_{r}^{\dagger} \ne 0$, are states; (P) extends the stored definition of a state as an element $\rho = \sum_{r}x_{r}x_{r}^{\dagger}$ of unit trace from elements to functionals. Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{1}, B_{2}$ be observables with $A_{i}B_{j} = B_{j}A_{i}$ for all $i, j$ (a \emph{configuration}; any signature, and no subsystem structure is assumed in (i) to (v)), and
\[
C = A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2}) + A_{2}(B_{1} - B_{2}), \qquad X = [A_{1},A_{2}], \quad Y = [B_{1},B_{2}], \quad S_{A} = A_{1}A_{2} + A_{2}A_{1}, \quad S_{B} = B_{1}B_{2} + B_{2}B_{1} .
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The identity; proved, classical.)} $C^{\dagger} = C$ and $C^{2} = 4 - XY$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The certificate; proved.)} With $Z = X - Y$,
\[
8 - C^{2} = \tfrac12\bigl(Z^{\dagger}Z + S_{A}^{2} + S_{B}^{2}\bigr), \qquad X^{\dagger}X = 4 - S_{A}^{2}, \quad Y^{\dagger}Y = 4 - S_{B}^{2},
\]
identities with rational coefficients in which $S_{A}$, $S_{B}$ are self-adjoint.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The bound, under (P); proved; the check samples the two inequalities and not the strictness.)} $\langle x^{\dagger}x\rangle_{0}$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$, so $\omega_{\rho}$ is a state. For every state
\[
\omega(C)^{2} \le \omega(C^{2}) = 8 - \tfrac12\omega(Z^{\dagger}Z) - \tfrac12\omega(S_{A}^{2}) - \tfrac12\omega(S_{B}^{2}) \le 8, \qquad \bigl(\omega(C^{2}) - 4\bigr)^{2} \le \omega(4 - S_{A}^{2})\,\omega(4 - S_{B}^{2}) .
\]
If $2$ is not a square in $k$ (as for $k = \Q$) then $\omega(C)^{2} < 8$. If $\omega(C)^{2} = 8$ then $\omega(S_{A}^{2}) = \omega(S_{B}^{2}) = \omega(Z^{\dagger}Z) = 0$. If $A_{1}A_{2} = A_{2}A_{1}$ or $B_{1}B_{2} = B_{2}B_{1}$ then $C^{2} = 4$ and $\omega(C)^{2} \le 4$. The bound $8$ is an upper bound in every signature; whether it is approached depends on whether configurations with $XY \ne 0$ exist, which depends on the signature. This clause uses of (P) only $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(1) = 1$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Blade lemma; proved.)} Let the four observables be blades up to sign with $A_{1}A_{2} = -A_{2}A_{1}$ and $B_{1}B_{2} = -B_{2}B_{1}$ (any signature in which such a configuration exists). Then with $K = -A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2}$,
\[
C^{2} = 4 + 4K, \qquad K^{\dagger} = K, \quad K^{2} = 1, \quad KC = CK = C, \qquad C^{3} = 8C, \qquad \langle C\rangle_{0} = \langle K\rangle_{0} = 0 ,
\]
and $K$ is a blade up to sign and not a scalar. For $r \in k$ the functional $\omega_{r}(x) = \langle(1 + K)(1 + rC)x\rangle_{0}$ satisfies (P) exactly when $8r^{2} \le 1$, and then $\omega_{r}(C) = 8r$, $\omega_{r}(C^{2}) = 8$. So over $\Q$ every rational $v$ with $v^{2} < 8$ is a value $\omega_{r}(C)$, the supremum of the values is $2\sqrt{2}$ and is not attained, and over an ordered field containing $\sqrt{2}$ the value $2\sqrt{2}$ is attained at $r = \sqrt{2}/4$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Without positivity the value $4$ occurs; proved.)} In the situation of (iv), $\lambda(x) = \langle(1 + C)x\rangle_{0}$ is linear with $\lambda(1) = 1$ and $\lambda(x^{\dagger}) = \lambda(x)$, and $\lambda(C) = 4$; $\lambda((C - t)(C - t)^{\dagger}) = t^{2} - 8t + 4$, which is negative at $t = 1$. So $\lambda$ satisfies every part of (P) except $\lambda(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$, and the bound of (iii) fails for it.
\item[(vi)] \emph{(Self-adjointness for one fixed frame is needed; proved by an example.)} In $\Cl_{\Q}(2,2)$ with the notation of (vii), $A = \tfrac{17}{8}e_{1} + \tfrac{15}{8}f_{1}$ has $A^{2} = 1$ and $A^{\dagger} \ne A$, it commutes with the observable $p_{2}$, and for $A_{1} = A_{2} = A$, $B_{1} = B_{2} = p_{2}$ the state $\omega_{\rho}$, $\rho = \tfrac14(1 + e_{1})(1 + p_{2})$, has $\omega_{\rho}(C) = \tfrac{17}{4} > 4$, while $C^{2} = 4$. So square one and commutation alone give no bound on values, not even the bound $4$. $A$ is a unit vector of square $1$, the first generator of the boosted frame $A$, $\tfrac{15}{8}e_{1} + \tfrac{17}{8}f_{1}$ (anticommuting, of squares $1$ and $-1$); it is an observable for the adjoint of that frame, for which $\omega_{\rho}$ is not a state (its value on $(1 - A)^{2}$, which is $(1 - A)(1 - A)^{\dagger'}$ for that adjoint, is $-\tfrac94$). So the clause shows that the bound is relative to one split into positive and negative generators, not that such elements are unphysical.
\item[(vii)] \emph{(Realisation: one mode against the Klein-twisted other mode of $\Cl(2,2)$, with parity-odd directions, under (P); proved.)} Let $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$ have generators $e_{1}, f_{1}, e_{2}, f_{2}$ with $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$ and mode parities $p_{j} = f_{j}e_{j}$. The adjoint fixes $e_{j}$ and negates $f_{j}$; the self-adjoint elements of the sub-Clifford algebra of mode $j$ are spanned by $1, e_{j}, p_{j}$, and its observables are $\pm 1$ and the \emph{directions} $xe_{j} + zp_{j}$, $x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$. The directions of mode $1$ and of mode $2$ do not commute ($e_{1}e_{2} = -e_{2}e_{1}$, and $e_{1}e_{2}$ is not self-adjoint), so the two sub-Clifford algebras are not two parties. The parties are mode $1$ and the copy of mode $2$ twisted by $p_{1}$ as in Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} (generators $e_{2}p_{1}$, $f_{2}p_{1}$, which keep their squares, anticommute, and commute with mode $1$): party $A$ has the directions $a = xe_{1} + zp_{1}$ and party $B$ the directions $b = x\,e_{2}p_{1} + z\,p_{2}$. These commute, and for directions $a_{1}, a_{2}$ of $A$ and $b_{1}, b_{2}$ of $B$, with $a_{1} \cdot a_{2} = x_{1}x_{2} + z_{1}z_{2}$ and $a_{1} \wedge a_{2} = x_{1}z_{2} - z_{1}x_{2}$ (so $(a_{1} \cdot a_{2})^{2} + (a_{1} \wedge a_{2})^{2} = 1$),
\[
S_{A} = 2\,a_{1} \cdot a_{2}, \qquad C^{2} = 4 + 4\,(a_{1} \wedge a_{2})(b_{1} \wedge b_{2})\,K, \qquad K = e_{1}f_{2}, \quad K^{\dagger} = K, \quad K^{2} = 1, \quad KC = CK .
\]
Hence $\omega(C)^{2} \le 4 + 4\,|a_{1} \wedge a_{2}|\,|b_{1} \wedge b_{2}|$ for every state, and the value $8$ of $\omega(C^{2})$ requires $a_{1} \cdot a_{2} = b_{1} \cdot b_{2} = 0$: each party's two directions anticommute. For directions this is forced as an identity of elements; for general observables it is not (clause (ix)). \emph{Parity.} The directions $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}p_{1}$ anticommute with the total parity $\Gamma = p_{1}p_{2}$, so the parity average $x \mapsto \tfrac12(x + \Gamma x\Gamma)$ (Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average}, in its total-parity form) sends $xe_{1} + zp_{1}$ to $zp_{1}$ and $x\,e_{2}p_{1} + z\,p_{2}$ to $z\,p_{2}$: the averaged directions commute, and the CHSH combination of the averaged directions is $\bigl(z_{1}(z'_{1} + z'_{2}) + z_{2}(z'_{1} - z'_{2})\bigr)p_{1}p_{2}$ with coefficient of absolute value at most $2$ ($z_{i}$, $z'_{j}$ the $p$-components of $a_{i}$, $b_{j}$). This realisation is therefore the setting in which parity-odd elements are observables; in the other setting, parity-even observables only, it gives nothing above $2$, each party needs two modes, no twist is needed, and clauses (i) to (iv) apply unchanged. Neither setting is singled out here.
\item[(viii)] \emph{(The saturating state of the realisation (vii); proved.)} At $A_{1} = e_{1}$, $A_{2} = p_{1}$, $B_{1} = e_{2}p_{1}$, $B_{2} = p_{2}$, a configuration of blades as in (iv): $C = e_{2}f_{1} + e_{1}p_{2} + e_{2} - p_{1}p_{2}$ and $K = e_{1}f_{2}$. If $k$ contains $\sqrt{2}$,
\[
P = \tfrac14(1 + K) + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{8}\,C
\]
satisfies $P^{\dagger} = P = P^{2}$, $CP = 2\sqrt{2}\,P$, $\langle P\rangle_{0} = \tfrac14$ and $PxP = 4\langle Px\rangle_{0}P$ for every $x$; $\omega_{P}(x) = 4\langle Px\rangle_{0}$ is the functional $\omega_{r}$ of (iv) at $r = \sqrt{2}/4$, a state with $\omega_{P}(C) = 2\sqrt{2}$, and at these settings it is the only state with that value: any functional with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(C) = 2\sqrt{2}$ agrees with $\omega_{P}$ on all self-adjoint elements, and the reality clause of (P) then gives equality on all elements. Its projection onto the blades of mode $1$ is $\tfrac14$. At these blade directions $P$ does not commute with the total parity $p_{1}p_{2}$ (this depends on the directions: with party $B$'s pair turned by an eighth of a turn, which puts $\sqrt{2}$ in the directions, the saturating state can be even), and its projection onto the blades of mode $2$ is $\tfrac14 + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{8}e_{2}$. Only $\sqrt{2}$ is adjoined.
\item[(ix)] \emph{(For general observables anticommutation holds only on the state; proved.)} In $\Cl_{k}(3,3)$ with a third mode $e_{3}, f_{3}$, $p_{3} = f_{3}e_{3}$, let $P_{\pm} = \tfrac12(1 \pm p_{3})$ and
\[
A_{1} = p_{1}, \qquad A_{2} = e_{1}P_{+} + p_{1}P_{-}, \qquad B_{1} = p_{2}, \qquad B_{2} = e_{2}p_{1} .
\]
These are observables commuting across the pairs, $S_{A} = 1 - p_{3} \ne 0$, and $C^{2} = 4 + 4K'P_{+}$ with $K' = -p_{1}e_{1}\,p_{2}\,e_{2}p_{1}$, a self-adjoint blade of square $1$. For $8r^{2} \le 1$ the functional $\omega'_{r}(x) = \langle(1 + K')(1 + p_{3})(1 + rC)x\rangle_{0}$ satisfies (P), with $\omega'_{r}(C^{2}) = 8$, $\omega'_{r}(C) = 8r$ and $\omega'_{r}(S_{A}^{2}) = 0$. So the value $8$ of $\omega(C^{2})$ does not force $S_{A} = 0$ as an identity of elements, only $\omega(S_{A}^{2}) = 0$ as in (iii).
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-.technical:
The Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt combination of four two-valued quantities, two for each of two parties, is bounded by $2\sqrt{2}$ in quantum theory (Tsirelson's bound), by $2$ for quantities that commute, and by $4$ on general grounds. This result places the first of these inside the Clifford algebra that the foundation postulates of the series produce, with rational coefficients. The quantities are self-adjoint elements of square one, where the adjoint is the inverse on the group of signed directions extended linearly, and a party's quantities commute with the other party's. The square of the combination is $4$ minus the product of the two commutators (Landau's identity), and $8$ minus that square is one half of a sum of three squares with rational coefficients. Everything about values rests on Hypothesis (P), positivity of values: values are given by a state, a linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$; (P) is assumed, not derived. Under (P) the combination has a squared value of at most $8$, and over the rationals strictly less. Positivity of the scalar part is a theorem of the blade basis, so states exist, and no step uses real coefficients; but (P) itself does not follow from the algebra: the functional $\langle(1 + C)\,\cdot\,\rangle_{0}$ is linear, normalised and real, has the value $4$ on the combination, and fails only the positivity clause. The adjoint, and with it observables, states and (P), is relative to the chosen split of the generators into those of square $1$ and those of square $-1$: a unit vector of a boosted frame has square one, is not self-adjoint for the original split, and gives the combination the value $17/4$ on a state of the original split. The bound holds in every signature; whether it is approached depends on the signature.

When the four quantities are blades that anticommute within each pair, the squared combination is $4 + 4K$ with $K$ a self-adjoint blade of square one, its cube is $8$ times itself, and the functionals $\langle(1 + K)(1 + rC)\,\cdot\,\rangle_{0}$ are states exactly for $8r^{2} \le 1$, with values $8r$: over the rationals every rational value of square below $8$ occurs and $2\sqrt{2}$ does not. Two settings are recorded side by side. In the first, parity-odd elements count as observables: for two modes of the split-signature algebra $\Cl(2,2)$ the parties are one mode and the Klein-twisted copy of the other, since the untwisted sub-Clifford algebras anticommute on odd elements; each party's quantities are the unit directions of a plane, the squared combination is $4 + 4(a_{1} \wedge a_{2})(b_{1} \wedge b_{2})K$, and the value $8$ needs both parties' directions to anticommute. At anticommuting blade directions the state reaching $2\sqrt{2}$ is a single element of the algebra with coefficients in the rationals extended by $\sqrt{2}$, a primitive idempotent, the only such state at these settings, and not invariant under the total parity. In the second setting only parity-even elements are observables; the parity average removes the odd directions of the one-mode realisation, which then gives at most $2$, and each party needs two modes, to which the identity, the certificate, the bound and the blade lemma apply unchanged. For observables that are not directions the anticommutation at the bound holds only on the state: a three-mode example has anticommutator $1 - p_{3}$ and states with squared-combination value $8$.
synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-.lay: Two experimenters each choose between two yes-or-no measurements on their half of a shared system, and a particular combination of the four possible correlations is formed. If the world were made of pre-existing answers the combination could not exceed 2; quantum theory allows up to about 2.83 (2 times the square root of 2) and no more. That limit is a known theorem from 1980. What is done here is to place it inside the algebra of directions that the series builds from its simplest assumptions (a yes-no bit, the least possible dependence on order, and whole-number addition), using only fractions. The limit comes out as a single algebraic identity: 8 minus the square of the combination is a sum of squares. The limit rests on one assumption that is not part of the algebra and is assumed, not derived, called (P), positivity of values: averages of measurements are given by a rule that is linear, gives the trivial measurement the value 1, never gives a quantity times its mirror image (its adjoint) a negative average, and gives a quantity and its mirror image the same average. Without the positivity part the combination can reach 4, and an example is given. The example in which the quantum limit is reached uses the algebra of two paired directions of opposite kind for each experimenter, and measurements that change the count of particles between even and odd; if such measurements are not allowed, each experimenter needs a larger system, and both cases are recorded without choosing between them. The result also shows that for simple directions the limit is reached only when each experimenter's two measurements are as incompatible as possible; that which quantities count as measurements depends on a chosen division of the directions into two kinds, and a quantity that is a legitimate measurement for another division breaks the limit for this one; and it writes down the shared state that reaches the limit, the only one at these settings, which needs the square root of 2 and nothing more.

proofs.main:
\emph{Premise.} Hypothesis (P) of the statement is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}; every statement below about the values of states is under it, relative to the fixed split of the generators.

\emph{Preliminaries.} By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} the algebra over $\Z$ is free on the blades $e_{S}$, the images of the group $G$ of signed directions, with $e_{S}e_{T} = \pm e_{S \triangle T}$; by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.division-gives-the-rationals} the same holds with coefficients in $\Q$, and by base change in any field $k$ of characteristic $0$. Inversion is an anti-automorphism of $G$ fixing the sign bit, so its linear extension $\dagger$ is an anti-automorphism with $x^{\dagger\dagger} = x$. The product $e_{S}^{\dagger}e_{T} = \pm e_{S \triangle T}$ is a scalar only for $S = T$, where it is $1$; hence for $x = \sum x_{S}e_{S}$, $y = \sum y_{S}e_{S}$,
\[
\langle x^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0} = \sum_{S}x_{S}y_{S}, \qquad \langle x^{\dagger}x\rangle_{0} = \sum_{S}x_{S}^{2} \ge 0, \qquad \langle xy\rangle_{0} = \langle yx\rangle_{0},
\]
the last because $e_{S}e_{T}$ and $e_{T}e_{S}$ are scalars only for $S = T$, where they agree. In an ordered field a sum of squares is non-negative and vanishes only if every term does. For a state $\omega$ and a self-adjoint $h$, $0 \le \omega((h - t)(h - t)^{\dagger}) = \omega(h^{2}) - 2t\omega(h) + t^{2}$ for every scalar $t$; at $t = \omega(h)$ this gives $\omega(h)^{2} \le \omega(h^{2})$. For any $u, v$ and scalar $t$, $0 \le \omega((u + tv)^{\dagger}(u + tv))$ is a quadratic polynomial in $t$, so
\[
\bigl(\omega(u^{\dagger}v) + \omega(v^{\dagger}u)\bigr)^{2} \le 4\,\omega(u^{\dagger}u)\,\omega(v^{\dagger}v). \tag{CS}
\]
(Here and below $\omega(x^{\dagger}x) \ge 0$ is used in place of $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$; the two are the same condition, applied to $x^{\dagger}$.) For self-adjoint $\rho$, $\langle\rho x^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \langle(x\rho)^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \langle x\rho\rangle_{0} = \langle\rho x\rangle_{0}$, since $\langle y^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \langle y\rangle_{0}$; so every functional $x \mapsto \langle\rho x\rangle_{0}$ with $\rho^{\dagger} = \rho$ has the reality property of (P). The frame remark of the statement: in signature $(p,0)$ the adjoint is the reverse and in $(0,q)$ the Clifford conjugate, both defined without reference to a frame; in indefinite signature clause (vi) gives two orthonormal frames with different adjoints.

\emph{(i).} $(A_{i}B_{j})^{\dagger} = B_{j}A_{i} = A_{i}B_{j}$, so $C^{\dagger} = C$. Put $S = B_{1} + B_{2}$, $D = B_{1} - B_{2}$; they commute with $A_{1}, A_{2}$, and $S^{2} + D^{2} = 4$, $SD = -Y$, $DS = Y$. So $C^{2} = (A_{1}S + A_{2}D)^{2} = S^{2} + D^{2} + A_{1}A_{2}SD + A_{2}A_{1}DS = 4 - (A_{1}A_{2} - A_{2}A_{1})Y = 4 - XY$.

\emph{(ii).} $X^{\dagger} = A_{2}A_{1} - A_{1}A_{2} = -X$ and likewise $Y^{\dagger} = -Y$, while $S_{A}^{\dagger} = S_{A}$, $S_{B}^{\dagger} = S_{B}$. Since $A_{1}^{2} = A_{2}^{2} = 1$, $X^{2} = A_{1}A_{2}A_{1}A_{2} + A_{2}A_{1}A_{2}A_{1} - 2$ and $S_{A}^{2} = A_{1}A_{2}A_{1}A_{2} + A_{2}A_{1}A_{2}A_{1} + 2$, so
\[
X^{\dagger}X = -X^{2} = 4 - S_{A}^{2}, \qquad Y^{\dagger}Y = 4 - S_{B}^{2}.
\]
$X$ and $Y$ commute, so $Z^{\dagger}Z = (Y - X)(X - Y) = -X^{2} - Y^{2} + 2XY = 8 - S_{A}^{2} - S_{B}^{2} + 2XY$. Therefore $\tfrac12(Z^{\dagger}Z + S_{A}^{2} + S_{B}^{2}) = 4 + XY = 8 - C^{2}$.

\emph{(iii).} Positivity of $\langle x^{\dagger}x\rangle_{0}$ is in the preliminaries. For $\rho = \sum_{r}y_{r}y_{r}^{\dagger}$, $\langle\rho\rangle_{0} = \sum_{r}\langle y_{r}^{\dagger}y_{r}\rangle_{0} > 0$ unless every $y_{r} = 0$, and $\langle\rho\,xx^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \sum_{r}\langle y_{r}^{\dagger}xx^{\dagger}y_{r}\rangle_{0} = \sum_{r}\langle(x^{\dagger}y_{r})^{\dagger}(x^{\dagger}y_{r})\rangle_{0} \ge 0$ by cyclicity; so $\omega_{\rho}$ is non-negative on every $xx^{\dagger}$; $\rho$ is self-adjoint, so $\omega_{\rho}$ is real, and it is a state. For any state, $\omega(C)^{2} \le \omega(C^{2})$ since $C$ is self-adjoint, and applying $\omega$ to the certificate of (ii) gives the displayed equality; the three terms are values of $Z^{\dagger}Z$, $S_{A}S_{A}^{\dagger}$, $S_{B}S_{B}^{\dagger}$, hence non-negative, which gives $\omega(C^{2}) \le 8$. If $\omega(C)^{2} = 8$ then $\omega(C^{2}) = 8$ and the three non-negative terms sum to zero, so each is zero; and $2\,(\omega(C)/2)^{2} = 4$ shows that $2$ is a square in $k$, which excludes $k = \Q$. For the second inequality take $u = X$, $v = Y$ in (CS): $u^{\dagger}v = -XY = v^{\dagger}u$, so $4\,\omega(XY)^{2} \le 4\,\omega(X^{\dagger}X)\,\omega(Y^{\dagger}Y) = 4\,\omega(4 - S_{A}^{2})\,\omega(4 - S_{B}^{2})$, and $\omega(C^{2}) - 4 = -\omega(XY)$. If $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ commute then $X = 0$ and $C^{2} = 4$; likewise for $B$.

\emph{(iv).} A blade is invertible with inverse $\pm$ itself, so a self-adjoint blade has square $1$, and two blades commute or anticommute. $X = 2A_{1}A_{2}$ and $Y = 2B_{1}B_{2}$, so by (i) $C^{2} = 4 - 4A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2} = 4 + 4K$. $K$ is a blade up to sign; $K^{\dagger} = -B_{2}B_{1}A_{2}A_{1} = -A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2} = K$ (two sign changes), so $K^{2} = KK^{\dagger} = 1$. $A_{1}$ anticommutes with $A_{1}A_{2}$ and commutes with $B_{1}B_{2}$, and likewise for the other three, so each $A_{i}B_{j}$ commutes with $K$ and $KC = CK$. $K$ is not a scalar: otherwise $A_{1}A_{2} = \pm B_{1}B_{2}$ would commute with $A_{1}$. Since the $A$'s commute with the $B$'s, $KA_{1}B_{1} = -(A_{1}A_{2}A_{1})(B_{1}B_{2}B_{1}) = -(-A_{2})(-B_{2}) = -A_{2}B_{2}$, and in the same way $KA_{2}B_{2} = -A_{1}B_{1}$, $KA_{1}B_{2} = A_{2}B_{1}$, $KA_{2}B_{1} = A_{1}B_{2}$; so $KC = C$ and $C^{3} = 4C + 4KC = 8C$. Each $A_{i}B_{j}$ is a blade that is not a scalar ($A_{i} = \pm B_{j}$ is excluded because $B_{j}$ commutes with both $A$'s), so $\langle C\rangle_{0} = \langle KC\rangle_{0} = 0$, and $\langle K\rangle_{0} = 0$. \emph{The functionals.} $\rho_{r} = (1 + K)(1 + rC)$ is self-adjoint, so $\omega_{r}$ is real. $\omega_{r}(1) = \langle 1 + K + rC + rKC\rangle_{0} = 1$; $\omega_{r}(C) = \langle(1 + K)C\rangle_{0} + r\langle(1 + K)(4 + 4K)\rangle_{0} = 8r$; $\omega_{r}(C^{2}) = \langle(1 + K)(4 + 4K)\rangle_{0} + r\langle(1 + K)C^{3}\rangle_{0} = 8 + 8r\langle(1 + K)C\rangle_{0} = 8$. Positivity: put $\Pi = \tfrac12(1 + K)$, a self-adjoint idempotent commuting with $C$, and $y = \Pi x$. By cyclicity, $\tfrac12\omega_{r}(xx^{\dagger}) = \langle x^{\dagger}\Pi(1 + rC)\Pi x\rangle_{0}$, which is $\langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0} + r\langle y^{\dagger}Cy\rangle_{0}$. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the positive symmetric form $\langle a^{\dagger}b\rangle_{0}$ (an inequality between squares, valid in any ordered field), $\langle y^{\dagger}Cy\rangle_{0}^{2} \le \langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0}\langle y^{\dagger}C^{2}y\rangle_{0} = 8\langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0}^{2}$, because $C^{2}\Pi = 8\Pi$. So $(r\langle y^{\dagger}Cy\rangle_{0})^{2} \le 8r^{2}\langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0}^{2} \le \langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0}^{2}$ when $8r^{2} \le 1$, and $\omega_{r}(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$. Conversely if $\omega_{r}$ satisfies (P) then by (iii) $64r^{2} = \omega_{r}(C)^{2} \le \omega_{r}(C^{2}) = 8$. For rational $v$ with $v^{2} < 8$, $r = v/8$ has $8r^{2} < 1$. The rational $r$ with $8r^{2} \le 1$ have supremum $\sqrt{2}/4$, which is not rational, and by (iii) no state has $\omega(C)^{2} = 8$ over $\Q$; a field containing $\sqrt{2}$ contains $r = \sqrt{2}/4$.

\emph{(v).} $1 + C$ is self-adjoint, so $\lambda$ is real; $\lambda(1) = 1 + \langle C\rangle_{0} = 1$ and $\lambda(C) = \langle C\rangle_{0} + \langle C^{2}\rangle_{0} = \langle 4 + 4K\rangle_{0} = 4$ by (iv). $\lambda((C - t)^{2}) = \langle(1 + C)(C^{2} - 2tC + t^{2})\rangle_{0} = \langle C^{2}\rangle_{0} + t^{2} + \langle C^{3}\rangle_{0} - 2t\langle C^{2}\rangle_{0} = 4 + t^{2} - 8t$, using $\langle C\rangle_{0} = 0$ and $\langle C^{3}\rangle_{0} = 8\langle C\rangle_{0} = 0$; at $t = 1$ it is $-3$. $C - t$ is self-adjoint, so this is a value on an element $xx^{\dagger}$.

\emph{(vi).} $e_{1}$ and $f_{1}$ anticommute, so $A^{2} = (\tfrac{17}{8})^{2} - (\tfrac{15}{8})^{2} = \tfrac{289 - 225}{64} = 1$, and $A^{\dagger} = \tfrac{17}{8}e_{1} - \tfrac{15}{8}f_{1} \ne A$. $p_{2} = f_{2}e_{2}$ is an even element of the other mode, so it commutes with $e_{1}$, $f_{1}$; it is self-adjoint with square $1$. $e_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ are commuting observables, so $\rho = \tfrac12(1 + e_{1})\,\tfrac12(1 + p_{2})$ is a self-adjoint idempotent, $\rho = \rho\rho^{\dagger}$, and $\omega_{\rho}$ is a state with $\langle\rho\rangle_{0} = \tfrac14$. $C = 2Ap_{2}$, and $\langle\rho\,e_{1}p_{2}\rangle_{0} = \tfrac14$ (the term $e_{1}p_{2}$ of $\rho$), $\langle\rho\,f_{1}p_{2}\rangle_{0} = 0$; so $\omega_{\rho}(C) = 2 \cdot \tfrac{17}{8} = \tfrac{17}{4}$. $C^{2} = 4A^{2}p_{2}^{2} = 4$. The step $\omega(C)^{2} \le \omega(C^{2})$ fails because $C$ is not self-adjoint. \emph{The boosted frame.} $F = \tfrac{15}{8}e_{1} + \tfrac{17}{8}f_{1}$ has $F^{2} = \tfrac{225 - 289}{64} = -1$ and $AF + FA = 2 \cdot \tfrac{17 \cdot 15}{64}(e_{1}^{2} + f_{1}^{2}) = 0$, so $A, F, e_{2}, f_{2}$ are orthonormal generators of the same algebra with the same signs, and the adjoint $\dagger'$ defined from them fixes $A$. Then $(1 - A)(1 - A)^{\dagger'} = (1 - A)^{2} = 2 - 2A$, and $\omega_{\rho}(2 - 2A) = 2 - 2 \cdot \tfrac{17}{8} = -\tfrac94$.

\emph{(vii).} The adjoint fixes $e_{j}$ (square $1$) and negates $f_{j}$ (square $-1$), and $p_{j}^{\dagger} = e_{j}^{\dagger}f_{j}^{\dagger} = -e_{j}f_{j} = f_{j}e_{j} = p_{j}$, with $p_{j}^{2} = -f_{j}^{2}e_{j}^{2} = 1$ and $e_{j}p_{j} = -p_{j}e_{j}$. The sub-Clifford algebra of mode $j$ has basis $1, e_{j}, f_{j}, p_{j}$, so its self-adjoint part is spanned by $1, e_{j}, p_{j}$, and $(s + xe_{j} + zp_{j})^{2} = s^{2} + x^{2} + z^{2} + 2s(xe_{j} + zp_{j})$ equals $1$ exactly when $s = 0$, $x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$ or $x = z = 0$, $s = \pm 1$. $e_{1}e_{2} = -e_{2}e_{1}$ has square $-1$ and adjoint $e_{2}e_{1} = -e_{1}e_{2}$. The twist is that of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} with one plane (mode $1$) and ground algebra mode $2$; the lines needed are proved here. $p_{1}$ is an even element of mode $1$, so it commutes with $e_{2}$, $f_{2}$, and it anticommutes with $e_{1}$, $f_{1}$, with $p_{1}^{2} = 1$. Hence for $y, y' \in \{e_{2}, f_{2}\}$: $(yp_{1})^{2} = y^{2}p_{1}^{2} = y^{2}$; $(yp_{1})(y'p_{1}) = yy'$, so $e_{2}p_{1}$ and $f_{2}p_{1}$ anticommute; and for $g \in \{e_{1}, f_{1}\}$, $g\,yp_{1} = -y\,gp_{1} = y\,p_{1}g$, so $yp_{1}$ commutes with mode $1$. The twisted generators generate a copy $B'$ of $\Cl(1,1)$; its parity is $(f_{2}p_{1})(e_{2}p_{1}) = p_{2}$ and $(e_{2}p_{1})^{\dagger} = p_{1}e_{2} = e_{2}p_{1}$, so the self-adjoint part of $B'$ is spanned by $1$, $e_{2}p_{1}$, $p_{2}$ and its directions are $x\,e_{2}p_{1} + z\,p_{2}$. For directions $a_{1}, a_{2}$ of $A$: $a_{1}a_{2} = a_{1} \cdot a_{2} + (a_{1} \wedge a_{2})\,e_{1}p_{1}$, so $S_{A} = 2a_{1} \cdot a_{2}$ and $X = 2(a_{1} \wedge a_{2})e_{1}p_{1} = -2(a_{1} \wedge a_{2})f_{1}$; likewise $Y = 2(b_{1} \wedge b_{2})\,e_{2}p_{1}p_{2} = -2(b_{1} \wedge b_{2})f_{2}p_{1}$. Then $f_{1}f_{2}p_{1} = f_{1}f_{2}f_{1}e_{1} = f_{2}e_{1} = -e_{1}f_{2}$, so $XY = -4(a_{1} \wedge a_{2})(b_{1} \wedge b_{2})K$ and $C^{2} = 4 - XY$ is as stated. $K^{\dagger} = f_{2}^{\dagger}e_{1}^{\dagger} = -f_{2}e_{1} = K$ and $K^{2} = -e_{1}^{2}f_{2}^{2} = 1$. $K = e_{1}f_{2}$ anticommutes with $e_{1}$, $p_{1}$, $e_{2}p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$, so it commutes with every product of a direction of $A$ and a direction of $B$, whatever the wedges. Since $K$ is self-adjoint with square $1$, $\omega(K)^{2} \le 1$, so $\omega(C)^{2} \le \omega(C^{2}) = 4 + 4(a_{1} \wedge a_{2})(b_{1} \wedge b_{2})\omega(K) \le 4 + 4|a_{1} \wedge a_{2}||b_{1} \wedge b_{2}|$. With $(a_{1} \wedge a_{2})^{2} = 1 - (a_{1} \cdot a_{2})^{2} \le 1$, the value $8$ requires both wedges to have square $1$, that is $a_{1} \cdot a_{2} = b_{1} \cdot b_{2} = 0$, which is $S_{A} = S_{B} = 0$. \emph{Parity.} $\Gamma = p_{1}p_{2}$ anticommutes with $e_{1}$ and with $e_{2}p_{1}$ and commutes with $p_{1}$, $p_{2}$; so $\tfrac12(x + \Gamma x\Gamma)$ removes the $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}p_{1}$ components of the directions, the averaged directions are $z_{i}p_{1}$ and $z'_{j}p_{2}$, and their CHSH combination is the stated multiple of $p_{1}p_{2}$, with $|z_{1}(z'_{1} + z'_{2}) + z_{2}(z'_{1} - z'_{2})| \le |z'_{1} + z'_{2}| + |z'_{1} - z'_{2}| \le 2$ since all $|z| \le 1$. Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} is stated for one mode; its total-parity form, used here, is a definition.

\emph{(viii).} Expanding with $p_{1}e_{2}p_{1} = e_{2}$ and $e_{1}e_{2}p_{1} = e_{1}e_{2}f_{1}e_{1} = e_{2}f_{1}$ gives $C$; the wedges are $1$, so $C^{2} = 4(1 + K)$. $K$ anticommutes with each of the four directions, so $KA_{1}B_{1} = -(A_{1}A_{2}A_{1})(B_{1}B_{2}B_{1})$ with $K = -A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2}$ (from $XY = 4A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2}$), which is $-A_{2}B_{2}$; in the same way $KA_{2}B_{2} = -A_{1}B_{1}$, $KA_{1}B_{2} = A_{2}B_{1}$, $KA_{2}B_{1} = A_{1}B_{2}$. So $KC = C$ and $C^{3} = 4C + 4KC = 8C$. Then $P^{2} = \tfrac{1}{16}(1 + K)^{2} + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{16}(1 + K)C + \tfrac{2}{64}C^{2} = \tfrac18(1 + K) + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{8}C + \tfrac18(1 + K) = P$, $P^{\dagger} = P$, and $CP = \tfrac14(C + KC) + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{8}C^{2} = \tfrac12C + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(1 + K) = 2\sqrt{2}\,P$. The four terms of $C$ and $K$ are blades other than $1$, so $\langle P\rangle_{0} = \tfrac14$. The identity $PxP = 4\langle Px\rangle_{0}P$ is linear in $x$ and is verified on the sixteen blades by the check (with coefficients $a + b\sqrt{2}$, $a, b \in \Q$, as exact pairs). $\omega_{P}$ is a state because $P = PP^{\dagger}$ is self-adjoint; $4P = (1 + K)(1 + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}C)$ because $KC = C$, so $\omega_{P}$ is the $\omega_{r}$ of (iv) at $r = \sqrt{2}/4$; and $\omega_{P}(C) = 4\langle PC\rangle_{0} = 4 \cdot 2\sqrt{2}\langle P\rangle_{0} = 2\sqrt{2}$. The blades of $P$ in mode $1$ alone are $\tfrac14$; those in mode $2$ alone are $\tfrac14$ and the term $e_{2}$ of $C$. $p_{1}p_{2}$ commutes with $K$, $e_{2}f_{1}$ and $p_{1}p_{2}$ and anticommutes with the odd terms $e_{1}p_{2}$ and $e_{2}$ of $C$.

\emph{Uniqueness on self-adjoint elements.} Let $\omega$ be linear with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(C) = 2\sqrt{2}$ (reality is not used until the last line) and $D = C - 2\sqrt{2}$. By (iii), $\omega(D^{2}) = \omega(C^{2}) - 8 \le 0$, so $\omega(D^{2}) = 0$. \emph{Bounded elements.} For $y = \sum_{S}y_{S}e_{S}$ and $c = (\sum_{S}|y_{S}|)^{2}$,
\[
c - y^{\dagger}y = \tfrac12\sum_{S,T}|y_{S}y_{T}|\,(e_{S} - \epsilon_{ST}e_{T})^{\dagger}(e_{S} - \epsilon_{ST}e_{T}), \qquad \epsilon_{ST} = \sgn(y_{S}y_{T}),
\]
since $(e_{S} - \epsilon e_{T})^{\dagger}(e_{S} - \epsilon e_{T}) = 2 - \epsilon(e_{S}^{\dagger}e_{T} + e_{T}^{\dagger}e_{S})$; so $D(c - y^{\dagger}y)D$ is a sum of terms $t\,w^{\dagger}w$ with $t \ge 0$, and $\omega((yD)^{\dagger}(yD)) \le c\,\omega(D^{2}) = 0$. By (CS) with $u = x$, $v = yD$: $\omega(x^{\dagger}yD) + \omega(Dy^{\dagger}x) = 0$ for all $x, y$. Now $1 - P = -\tfrac{1}{16}(C - 2\sqrt{2})(C + 4\sqrt{2}) = gD = Dg$ with $g = -\tfrac{1}{16}(C + 4\sqrt{2})$ self-adjoint (the product is $-\tfrac{1}{16}(C^{2} + 2\sqrt{2}C - 16)$, and $C^{2} = 4(1 + K)$). For self-adjoint $h$, $h - PhP = (1 - P)h + Ph(1 - P) = Dgh + PhgD$. With $x = 1$, $y = hg$: $\omega(hgD) + \omega(Dgh) = 0$. So $\omega(h - PhP) = -\omega(hgD) + \omega(PhgD) = -\omega((1 - P)hgD) = -\omega(DmD)$ with $m = ghg$ self-adjoint. Finally $DmD = \tfrac14\bigl(((1 + m)D)^{\dagger}(1 + m)D - ((1 - m)D)^{\dagger}(1 - m)D\bigr)$, and both terms have value $0$ by the bound just proved. Hence $\omega(h) = \omega(PhP) = 4\langle Ph\rangle_{0}\,\omega(P)$, and $h = 1$ gives $\omega(P) = 1$: $\omega(h) = \omega_{P}(h)$. A state with $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ is determined by its values on self-adjoint elements. So under (P) it equals $\omega_{P}$.

\emph{(ix).} $p_{3}$ is self-adjoint of square $1$ and commutes with the generators of modes $1$ and $2$, so $P_{\pm}$ are self-adjoint idempotents with $P_{+}P_{-} = 0$, commuting with $A_{1}$, $e_{1}$, $B_{1}$, $B_{2}$. Then $A_{2}$ is self-adjoint, $A_{2}^{2} = e_{1}^{2}P_{+} + p_{1}^{2}P_{-} = 1$, it commutes with $B_{1}, B_{2}$ (as $e_{1}$ and $p_{1}$ do, by (vii)), and $S_{A} = (p_{1}e_{1} + e_{1}p_{1})P_{+} + 2P_{-} = 1 - p_{3}$, while $X = [A_{1},A_{2}] = 2p_{1}e_{1}P_{+}$. By (i), $C^{2} = 4 - 2p_{1}e_{1}P_{+} \cdot 2B_{1}B_{2} = 4 + 4K'P_{+}$. Let $C_{0}$ be the CHSH element of the blade configuration $(p_{1}, e_{1}; p_{2}, e_{2}p_{1})$; $K'$ is its element $K$ of (iv), so $K'^{\dagger} = K'$, $K'^{2} = 1$, $K'C_{0} = C_{0}K' = C_{0}$ and $C_{0}^{2} = 4 + 4K'$. Since $A_{2}P_{+} = e_{1}P_{+}$, $CP_{+} = C_{0}P_{+}$. Put $\Pi = \tfrac14(1 + K')(1 + p_{3})$, a self-adjoint idempotent (a product of commuting ones) with $\Pi = \Pi P_{+}$ and $\Pi K' = \Pi$. Then $C\Pi = C_{0}\Pi = \Pi C_{0} = \Pi C$, $C^{2}\Pi = (4 + 4K')\Pi = 8\Pi$ and $S_{A}\Pi = (1 - p_{3})\Pi = 0$. The functional is $\omega'_{r}(x) = 4\langle\Pi(1 + rC)x\rangle_{0}$, real because $\Pi(1 + rC)$ is self-adjoint. The blades of $C_{0}$, $K'$ and $K'C_{0} = C_{0}$ are not scalars and do not contain the generators of mode $3$, so they stay non-scalar after multiplication by $p_{3}$: $4\langle\Pi\rangle_{0} = 1$ and $4\langle\Pi C\rangle_{0} = 4\langle\Pi C_{0}\rangle_{0} = 0$. Hence $\omega'_{r}(1) = 1$, $\omega'_{r}(C) = 4r\langle\Pi C^{2}\rangle_{0} = 8r$, $\omega'_{r}(C^{2}) = 8 + 8r \cdot 4\langle\Pi C\rangle_{0} = 8$, and $\omega'_{r}(S_{A}^{2}) = 4\langle(1 + rC)S_{A}^{2}\Pi\rangle_{0} = 0$. Positivity is as in (iv): with $y = \Pi x$, $\tfrac14\omega'_{r}(xx^{\dagger}) = \langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0} + r\langle y^{\dagger}Cy\rangle_{0}$ and $\langle y^{\dagger}Cy\rangle_{0}^{2} \le \langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0}\langle y^{\dagger}C^{2}y\rangle_{0} = 8\langle y^{\dagger}y\rangle_{0}^{2}$, so $8r^{2} \le 1$ gives $\omega'_{r}(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$.

synthesis.chsh-bound-needs-positivity-ac.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or an ordered field, and $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$ the algebra of two modes: generators $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$ with $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$, $p_{j} = f_{j}e_{j}$, the integer algebra $\Cl_{\Z}(2,2)$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} inside it. As in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, $\dagger$ is the linear extension of the inverse on blades, observables are self-adjoint elements of square $1$, and $C = A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2}) + A_{2}(B_{1} - B_{2})$ for a configuration. The adjoint is defined by the chosen generators. In definite signature it does not depend on the orthonormal frame; in indefinite signature it depends on the split into generators of square $1$ and of square $-1$, so observables, states and (P) are relative to that split, and each statement holds for every fixed split.

\emph{Hypothesis (P), positivity of values:} values are given by a \emph{state}, a $k$-linear $\omega : \Cl_{k}(2,2) \to k$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$; (P) is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}, assumed, not derived.

(P) extends the stored definition of a state as an element $\rho = \sum_{r}x_{r}x_{r}^{\dagger}$ of unit trace from elements to functionals. Throughout, the configuration is the blade configuration $A_{1} = p_{1}$, $A_{2} = e_{1}$, $B_{1} = p_{2}$, $B_{2} = e_{2}p_{1}$ (mode $1$ against the copy of mode $2$ twisted as in Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}; integer blades, commuting across the pairs, anticommuting within), with $C^{2} = 4 + 4K$, $K = -A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2}$, by clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}. Let $\lambda(x) = \langle(1 + C)x\rangle_{0}$, the functional of clause (v) of that theorem: integer-valued on $\Cl_{\Z}(2,2)$, extended $\Q$-linearly, with $\lambda(1) = 1$, $\lambda(x^{\dagger}) = \lambda(x)$, $\lambda(C) = 4$. The element $1 + C$ is self-adjoint of unit scalar part and is not a stored state: it is not a sum of elements $xx^{\dagger}$, by (ii).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The box: a probability table at every setting pair; proved.)} $\lambda(A_{i}) = \lambda(B_{j}) = 0$, $\lambda(A_{1}B_{1}) = \lambda(A_{1}B_{2}) = \lambda(A_{2}B_{1}) = 1$, $\lambda(A_{2}B_{2}) = -1$. For each setting pair $(i,j)$ and outcomes $a, b = \pm 1$ the values $\lambda\bigl(\tfrac12(1 + aA_{i})\,\tfrac12(1 + bB_{j})\bigr) = \tfrac14(1 + ab\,\lambda(A_{i}B_{j}))$ on the four idempotents (elements of the algebra over $\Q$, not of the integer algebra) are $0$ or $\tfrac12$, they sum to $1$, and each party's marginal is $\tfrac12$ whatever the other party's setting. Moreover $\lambda(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ for every $x$ in the algebra generated by one setting pair $A_{i}, B_{j}$: inside one setting pair $\lambda$ is a probability measure.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Where the box is negative; proved.)} The symmetric form $(x, y) \mapsto \lambda(xy^{\dagger})$ on the $16$-dimensional algebra has inertia $(12, 4, 0)$: it is negative definite on a subspace of dimension $4$ and no larger. $\lambda((C - t)(C - t)^{\dagger}) = t^{2} - 8t + 4$, negative exactly for $4 - 2\sqrt{3} < t < 4 + 2\sqrt{3}$ (so for $t = 1, \dots, 7$; value $-12$ at $t = 4$). Negative values occur also on elements using only two setting pairs with a shared setting: $h = A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2})$ has $\lambda((h - 2)^{2}) = -2$. All such elements combine different setting pairs; by (i) none lies in the algebra of one setting pair.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(A sufficient pair of positivity conditions, for this blade configuration; proved.)} Let $\varphi$ be $k$-linear with $\varphi(1) = 1$. If $\varphi((C - \varphi(C))^{2}) \ge 0$ and $\varphi((1 - K)^{2}) \ge 0$, then $\varphi(C)^{2} \le \varphi(C^{2}) = 4 + 4\varphi(K) \le 8$. Both elements combine different setting pairs. $\lambda$ satisfies the second condition ($\lambda((1 - K)^{2}) = 2$) and fails the first. The two conditions are sufficient; nothing here shows they are necessary, and other sufficient sets exist. Consequence: the stored identity for $C^{2}$, which $\lambda$ satisfies as an identity of elements, together with linearity, normalisation, reality and a probability table at every setting pair, does not imply the bound; the bound follows under (P), and (P) is not implied by the algebra.
\end{enumerate}

\emph{Scope (version 2).} A ``setting pair'' in (i) to (iii) is one of the four configured pairs $(A_{i}, B_{j})$. The functional is not non-negative at every pair of observables the two parties can measure together: $b = \tfrac35 B_{1} + \tfrac45 B_{2}$ is self-adjoint of square $1$ and commutes with $A_{1}$, and by linearity from (i) $\lambda(A_{1}b) = \tfrac75$, so the joint outcome idempotent $\tfrac14(1 + A_{1})(1 - b)$ has $\lambda = \tfrac14(1 - \tfrac75) = -\tfrac{1}{10}$. This element combines the two configured pairs $(A_{1},B_{1})$ and $(A_{1},B_{2})$, in agreement with (ii). By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.local-weights-give-the-chsh-bound-and-do-not-fix-positivity-of-values}, clause (ii), with one twisted mode per party non-negative weights at all pairs of local directions already give $\varphi(C)^{2} \le 8$. So what the counter-model shows is that non-negative weights at the four configured pairs do not give the bound; it does not show that the bound needs positivity on elements combining quantities that are never measured together. The bound follows under (P), and (P) is more than non-negative local weights (clause (iv) of that theorem).
synthesis.chsh-bound-needs-positivity-ac.technical: The identity $C^{2} = 4 - [A_{1},A_{2}][B_{1},B_{2}]$ holds already in the integer Clifford algebra, but it bounds no value by itself; the bound is a statement under Hypothesis (P), positivity of values (values are given by a state, a linear $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$, $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$; assumed, not derived). On $\Cl_{\Z}(2,2)$, extended $\Q$-linearly, the stored functional $\lambda(x) = \langle(1 + C)x\rangle_{0}$ is normalised, real on self-adjoint elements, assigns to each of the four configured pairs of settings a non-negative no-signalling probability table, and has CHSH value $4$: the Popescu-Rohrlich box as a functional on the algebra. It is non-negative on $xx^{\dagger}$ for every $x$ in the algebra of one setting pair. It is negative on $(C - t)^{2}$ for $4 - 2\sqrt{3} < t < 4 + 2\sqrt{3}$ (about $0.54 < t < 7.46$) and on other elements that combine different setting pairs, for example $(A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2}) - 2)^{2}$ with value $-2$, never inside one setting pair; the form $\lambda(xy^{\dagger})$ has inertia $(12, 4, 0)$. For this blade configuration the bound $\varphi(C)^{2} \le 8$ follows from positivity on $(C - \varphi(C))^{2}$ and $(1 - K)^{2}$; these two conditions are sufficient and are not claimed necessary. So the bound on values holds under (P), which the algebra does not supply. The setting pairs meant are the four configured ones: at the pair of $A_{1}$ with the direction $\tfrac35 B_{1} + \tfrac45 B_{2}$ the functional has a weight $-\tfrac{1}{10}$, and with one twisted mode per party non-negative weights at all pairs of local directions already give the bound (the stored result on local weights), so positivity across settings is what the box violates and is not shown to be what the bound needs. The stored definition of a state as an element $\sum x_{r}x_{r}^{\dagger}$ has positivity built in, and $1 + C$ is not such an element; the gap is between functionals and stored states. The adjoint, and with it (P), is relative to the split into generators of square $1$ and $-1$. Classical mathematics throughout.
synthesis.chsh-bound-needs-positivity-ac.lay: The quantum limit $2\sqrt{2}$ on correlations between two parties is often derived from an algebraic identity. This result shows that the identity is not enough. Inside the same whole-number algebra there is a rule for assigning average values that gives sensible, non-negative probabilities for each of the four experiments of the standard test (each party choosing one of two settings), lets neither party signal to the other, and still reaches $4$, the largest value arithmetic allows. What rules it out is an extra requirement, Hypothesis (P): that a quantity multiplied by its mirror image never has a negative average. That requirement is an assumption about how values are assigned (assumed, not derived), not a consequence of the algebra. Inside each of the four experiments the rule that reaches $4$ respects it. It breaks it on combinations of them, and one such combination is itself a single experiment the two parties could perform, with a setting in between the two configured ones: there the rule gives a negative probability. So the rule is excluded already by asking for sensible probabilities at all settings, not only at the four; (P) asks for more than that.

proofs.main:
\emph{Premise.} Hypothesis (P) of the statement is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}; every statement below about the values of states is under it, relative to the fixed split of the generators.

\emph{Preliminaries.} By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} the integer algebra is free on the blades; the adjoint, observables and (P) are those of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, whose preliminaries give $\langle x^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \langle x\rangle_{0}$, $\langle ab\rangle_{0} = \langle ba\rangle_{0}$, that a self-adjoint blade has square $1$, and that the scalar part of a product of two blades is zero unless they are equal up to sign. \emph{The configuration.} $p_{1} = f_{1}e_{1}$ is self-adjoint of square $1$, anticommutes with $e_{1}$, $f_{1}$ and commutes with $e_{2}$, $f_{2}$; hence $e_{2}p_{1}$ has square $e_{2}^{2}p_{1}^{2} = 1$, is self-adjoint, commutes with $e_{1}$ ($e_{1}e_{2}p_{1} = -e_{2}e_{1}p_{1} = e_{2}p_{1}e_{1}$) and with $p_{1}$, and anticommutes with $p_{2}$ as $e_{2}$ does; this is the twisted generator of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}. So the four blades are a configuration with anticommuting pairs, and clauses (iv), (v) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate} give $C^{2} = 4 + 4K$, $K^{\dagger} = K$, $K^{2} = 1$, $\langle K\rangle_{0} = 0$, and for $\lambda$: $\lambda(1) = 1$, $\lambda(x^{\dagger}) = \lambda(x)$, $\lambda(C) = 4$, $\lambda((C - t)(C - t)^{\dagger}) = t^{2} - 8t + 4$.

\emph{(i).} The four products $A_{i}B_{j}$ are, up to sign, the blades $p_{1}p_{2}$, $p_{1}e_{2}p_{1} = e_{2}$, $e_{1}p_{2}$, $e_{1}e_{2}p_{1}$: distinct, not scalars, self-adjoint of square $1$, and none equals $\pm$ an $A_{i}$, a $B_{j}$ or $K$ (the check lists them). For a blade $b$ of square $1$, $\lambda(b)$ is the coefficient of $b$ in $1 + C$: this gives the values $1, 1, 1, -1$ on the products and $0$ on the $A_{i}$, the $B_{j}$ and $K$. Expanding, $\lambda(\tfrac14(1 + aA_{i})(1 + bB_{j})) = \tfrac14(1 + ab\,\lambda(A_{i}B_{j}))$, which is $\tfrac12$ or $0$; summing over $b$ gives $\tfrac12$, independent of $j$, and likewise over $a$. \emph{One setting pair.} $A_{i}$ and $B_{j}$ are commuting self-adjoint elements of square $1$, so the algebra they generate is spanned by $1, A_{i}, B_{j}, A_{i}B_{j}$, equivalently by the four idempotents $E_{ab} = \tfrac14(1 + aA_{i})(1 + bB_{j})$, which are self-adjoint, mutually orthogonal and sum to $1$. For $x = \sum x_{ab}E_{ab}$, $xx^{\dagger} = \sum x_{ab}^{2}E_{ab}$ and $\lambda(xx^{\dagger}) = \sum x_{ab}^{2}\lambda(E_{ab}) \ge 0$.

\emph{(ii).} The Gram matrix $\lambda(e_{S}e_{T}^{\dagger})$ on the sixteen blades is a rational symmetric matrix (symmetric because $\lambda(x^{\dagger}) = \lambda(x)$); exact congruence diagonalisation gives $12$ positive, $4$ negative and no zero diagonal entries (the check), and by the law of inertia this is the largest dimension of a subspace on which the form is negative definite. The quadratic $t^{2} - 8t + 4$ has roots $4 \pm 2\sqrt{3}$. For $h = A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2})$: $h^{\dagger} = h$, $h^{2} = (B_{1} + B_{2})^{2} = 2 + B_{1}B_{2} + B_{2}B_{1} = 2$, $\lambda(h) = 2$, so $\lambda((h - 2)^{2}) = 2 - 8 + 4 = -2$. An element $x$ with $\lambda(xx^{\dagger}) < 0$ cannot lie in the algebra of one setting pair, by (i).

\emph{(iii).} $\varphi((C - t)^{2}) = \varphi(C^{2}) - 2t\varphi(C) + t^{2}$, which at $t = \varphi(C)$ is $\varphi(C^{2}) - \varphi(C)^{2}$; so the first condition is $\varphi(C)^{2} \le \varphi(C^{2})$. $(1 - K)^{2} = 2 - 2K$, so the second gives $\varphi(K) \le 1$ and $\varphi(C^{2}) = 4 + 4\varphi(K) \le 8$. $C$ contains all four products $A_{i}B_{j}$, and $K$ is, up to sign, $A_{1}B_{1} \cdot A_{2}B_{2}$. For $\lambda$: $\lambda((1 - K)^{2}) = 2 - 2\lambda(K) = 2$, and $\lambda((C - 4)^{2}) = -12$. Since $\lambda$ is a normalised linear functional on the algebra with $\lambda(x^{\dagger}) = \lambda(x)$, satisfies every identity of elements, and has $\lambda(C)^{2} = 16 > 8$, no argument from the algebra, linearity, normalisation and reality alone gives the bound; and since a sum of elements $xx^{\dagger}$ would make $\langle(1 + C)\,\cdot\,\rangle_{0}$ non-negative on every $yy^{\dagger}$ (as $\langle xx^{\dagger}yy^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \langle (y^{\dagger}x)^{\dagger}(y^{\dagger}x)\rangle_{0} \ge 0$), $1 + C$ is not such a sum.
