synthesis.positivity-of-values-is-additi.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or an ordered field, and $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$, the blade inverse $\dagger$ and the scalar part $\langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$ as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, for a fixed split of the generators. Premise (P), positivity of values (Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}), is assumed, not derived, wherever states are spoken of: a \emph{state} is a $k$-linear $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$.

\emph{Definitions.} The \emph{cone} $\mathcal{K}$ is the set of sums $\sum_{r}c_{r}x_{r}x_{r}^{\dagger}$ with $c_{r} \ge 0$ in $k$. An \emph{effect} is an element $E$ with $E \in \mathcal{K}$ and $1 - E \in \mathcal{K}$; projectors (elements $E = E^{\dagger} = E^{2}$) are effects. A \emph{weight} is a map $\mu$ from effects to $k$ with $\mu(E) \ge 0$, $\mu(1) = 1$, and $\mu(E + F) = \mu(E) + \mu(F)$ whenever $E$, $F$ and $E + F$ are effects.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The unit bounds every self-adjoint element; proved.)} The self-adjoint elements are the span of the blades of square $1$. For such a blade $b$, $1 \pm b = \tfrac12(1 \pm b)(1 \pm b)^{\dagger}$. Hence for self-adjoint $s = \sum_{b}c_{b}b$ and $n_{s} = \sum_{b}|c_{b}|$ both $n_{s} - s$ and $n_{s} + s$ lie in $\mathcal{K}$; every self-adjoint element is a difference of two elements of $\mathcal{K}$, and the effects span the self-adjoint elements.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Weights on effects are the states of (P); proved for $k = \Q$ and for every Archimedean ordered $k$.)} The restriction of a state to the effects is a weight, and every weight is the restriction of exactly one state. For $k = \Q$ the non-negativity of $\mu$ is not used in showing that $\mu$ extends to a linear functional: every map on effects with values in $\Q$ that is additive in the sense above extends uniquely to a $\Q$-linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$, and it is non-negative on effects exactly when $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ for all $x$. So (P) is equivalent to: values of effects are non-negative, normalised and additive.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(An effect relation at work; proved, one instance.)} On one mode, $\Cl_{k}(1,1)$ with $p_{1} = f_{1}e_{1}$, let $\Pi_{e} = \tfrac12(1 + e_{1})$, $\Pi_{p} = \tfrac12(1 + p_{1})$, $E_{a} = \tfrac12(1 + \tfrac35 e_{1} + \tfrac45 p_{1})$, three projectors. Then $\tfrac12E_{a} + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{3}{10}\Pi_{e} + \tfrac{4}{10}\Pi_{p}$, with every term and both sides effects. A weight with $\mu(\Pi_{p}) = 1$ and $\mu(\Pi_{e}) = \tfrac12$ therefore has $\mu(E_{a}) = \tfrac{9}{10}$. By (ii) and clause (iii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, every weight with $\mu(\Pi_{p}) = 1$ is the restriction of the one state sharp on the atom $\Pi_{p}$, $x \mapsto 2\langle\Pi_{p}x\rangle_{0}$, so both values hold for it; the relation shows how additivity on effects carries the second value to the third. The function $\tfrac12(1 + xe_{1} + zp_{1}) \mapsto \tfrac12(1 + z^{3})$ on the projectors other than $0$ and $1$ is non-negative, takes those two values, and is additive on every pair of projectors with sum $1$, the only families of orthogonal projectors of one mode; it gives $E_{a}$ the value $\tfrac{189}{250}$ and so is not the restriction of a weight on effects.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The parity average keeps the cone and adds no positivity; proved.)} Let $\Gamma$ be self-adjoint with $\Gamma^{2} = 1$ and $E_{\Gamma}(x) = \tfrac12(x + \Gamma x\Gamma)$, the average of Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} (there for one mode; for the total parity as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.mode-split-of-the-clifford-algebra-and-its-klein-twist-to-the-tensor-product}). Then $E_{\Gamma}(x^{\dagger}) = E_{\Gamma}(x)^{\dagger}$, $E_{\Gamma}(yy^{\dagger}) = \tfrac12\bigl(yy^{\dagger} + (\Gamma y)(\Gamma y)^{\dagger}\bigr)$, and $E_{\Gamma}(\mathcal{K})$ is the set of elements of $\mathcal{K}$ fixed by $E_{\Gamma}$. So for a linear functional $\varphi$, $\varphi \circ E_{\Gamma}$ is non-negative on $\mathcal{K}$ exactly when $\varphi$ is non-negative on the fixed elements of $\mathcal{K}$: a functional invariant under the average satisfies the positivity clause only if it is already non-negative on the fixed positive elements, and the average does not make it so. Example: on $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$, $\varphi(x) = \langle(1 + 2p_{1})x\rangle_{0}$ is linear, normalised, real and invariant under the total parity average, with $\varphi(\tfrac12(1 - p_{1})) = -\tfrac12$. Rider: averaging over more involutions leaves fewer fixed elements. In $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the composition of the averages over the mode parities $p_{1}, \dots, p_{\ell}$ has as fixed elements the span of the $2^{\ell}$ orthogonal projectors $\prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 \pm p_{j})$, and a normalised functional invariant under it satisfies the positivity clause exactly when its $2^{\ell}$ values on these projectors are non-negative: for the mode-wise average (P) reduces to finitely many non-negative weights, while for the total parity alone it does not. For the grading automorphism $\alpha$ of $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$, $p + q \ge 1$ (the map that fixes even and negates odd elements; in a general signature it need not be conjugation by a self-adjoint element of square $1$), and $E = \tfrac12(\mathrm{id} + \alpha)$, the same statements hold, and the fixed elements of $\mathcal{K}$ are the sums $\sum_{r}c_{r}y_{r}y_{r}^{\dagger}$ with every $y_{r}$ even: for a functional that vanishes on odd elements, (P) on the algebra is equivalent to (P) for its restriction to the even subalgebra. This, and the statement that $\omega \circ E$ is a state when $\omega$ is, is clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.univalence-even-extension-split} (for the completed mode algebra: $\omega \circ E$ is the one even state agreeing with $\omega$ on the even part), here over $k$ with the blade inverse; what is added is that the hermitian squares of odd elements are hermitian squares of even ones.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Even states see the products of odd directions; proved, under (P) for the inequality.)} In $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$ let $\Gamma = p_{1}p_{2}$ and take the directions of clause (vii) of the theorem cited first, $a_{i} = x_{i}e_{1} + z_{i}p_{1}$ and $b_{j} = x'_{j}e_{2}p_{1} + z'_{j}p_{2}$ ($x_{i}^{2} + z_{i}^{2} = x'^{2}_{j} + z'^{2}_{j} = 1$), with CHSH element $C = a_{1}(b_{1} + b_{2}) + a_{2}(b_{1} - b_{2})$. Put $X = x_{1}(x'_{1} + x'_{2}) + x_{2}(x'_{1} - x'_{2})$, $Z = z_{1}(z'_{1} + z'_{2}) + z_{2}(z'_{1} - z'_{2})$ and $u = e_{2}f_{1}$. Then
\[
E_{\Gamma}(C) = Xu + Z\Gamma, \qquad u^{\dagger} = u, \quad u^{2} = 1, \quad u\Gamma = \Gamma u ,
\]
while the CHSH element of the averaged directions $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}) = z_{i}p_{1}$, $E_{\Gamma}(b_{j}) = z'_{j}p_{2}$ is $Z\Gamma$: the average is not multiplicative, $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}b_{j}) \ne E_{\Gamma}(a_{i})E_{\Gamma}(b_{j})$ when $x_{i}x'_{j} \ne 0$. For every state $\omega$ with $\omega \circ E_{\Gamma} = \omega$ (an even state): $\omega(C) = X\omega(u) + Z\omega(\Gamma)$ and $|\omega(C)| \le |X| + |Z|$, with equality on the four even projectors $\tfrac14(1 \pm u)(1 \pm \Gamma)$ for suitable signs (atoms in the sense of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, clause (i), the blades $u$, $\Gamma$ being a maximal independent commuting set), and $(|X| + |Z|)^{2} \le 8$. At $a_{1} = e_{1}$, $a_{2} = p_{1}$, $b_{1} = \tfrac35 e_{2}p_{1} + \tfrac45 p_{2}$, $b_{2} = \tfrac45 e_{2}p_{1} - \tfrac35 p_{2}$: $X = Z = \tfrac75$, the even state of $\tfrac14(1 + u)(1 + \Gamma)$ has $\omega(C) = \tfrac{14}{5} > 2$, and the averaged directions give at most $\tfrac75$. The value above $2$ uses directions of mixed parity ($b_{1}$, $b_{2}$ have an odd and an even part); when every direction is even or odd ($x_{i}z_{i} = 0$ and $x'_{j}z'_{j} = 0$) one checks from the formula that $|X| + |Z| \le 2$. So a restriction to even states (Premise \claimref{singularity.p-univalence}, which is not assumed here) together with the parity average does not reduce the setting with parity-odd directions to the setting with parity-even observables; only a restriction on which elements are observables would.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Scope.} Clause (ii) does not derive (P); it says what (P) is equivalent to, and over $\Q$ it is close to a restatement: non-negativity on effects is the positivity clause and additivity is linearity. Its content is the reading of the stored residual postulate (weights exist and add) as additivity over all effects; that reading is argued, effects that are not projectors are not outcomes of the stored record account, and additivity over effects that do not commute is the non-contextuality assumption again. So the content of the envariance argument (Zurek; prior art of the stored Born account) is relocated into (P), not reduced. The equivalent statement is strong: additivity is asked of all effects, including sums of effects that do not commute, which no single measurement realises. Clause (iv) is about one algebra and the positivity clause; it does not show that (P) is independent of the series' other premises.
synthesis.positivity-of-values-is-additi.technical:
Premise (P), positivity of values, is assumed in the series and not derived. This result says what it is equivalent to and what the descent does for it, in every Clifford algebra $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ over the rationals or an Archimedean ordered field, with the blade inverse as adjoint. Call an element an effect if it and its complement to $1$ are combinations, with non-negative coefficients, of elements $xx^{\dagger}$; projectors are effects, and so are their multiples by numbers between $0$ and $1$. Then the states of (P) are exactly the assignments of non-negative numbers to effects that give $1$ the value $1$ and add whenever a sum of two effects is an effect. Over the rationals additivity alone already gives linearity, with no continuity argument; non-negativity then is the positivity clause. So, given this reading, (P) is the statement that weights exist on all effects, are non-negative and add; it is a strong form of the residual postulate that the stored Born account isolates, and it is strong because it asks additivity also of effects that do not commute. A relation among effects of one mode shows the mechanism: it forces the weight $\tfrac{9}{10}$ where a function that is additive only on complementary projectors can give $\tfrac{189}{250}$.

The parity average of the descent, $x \mapsto \tfrac12(x + \Gamma x\Gamma)$, commutes with the adjoint and maps positive elements to positive elements, so it preserves states (for the completed mode algebra this is clause (i) of the stored even-extension theorem); but it creates no positivity. A functional invariant under the average satisfies the positivity clause only if it is already non-negative on the positive even elements, and a normalised real invariant functional can give a projector the value $-\tfrac12$. For functionals that vanish on odd elements, (P) is a statement about the even subalgebra alone. Finally, under (P), the average is not multiplicative: for the stored one-mode directions of mixed parity against the Klein-twisted other mode, the average of the CHSH element is $Xu + Z\Gamma$ with $u = e_{2}f_{1}$ even, and an even state gives it values up to $|X| + |Z|$, for example $\tfrac{14}{5}$, where the CHSH element of the averaged directions gives at most $\tfrac75$. So restricting states to even ones and applying the average does not turn the setting with parity-odd directions into the setting with even observables; that would take a restriction on observables.
synthesis.positivity-of-values-is-additi.lay:
The series assumes a rule, called (P), for the averages of measurable quantities: averages add up, the trivial quantity has average 1, and a quantity times its mirror image never has a negative average. This result shows, under that reading of the terms, what the assumption amounts to. Think of every yes-or-no question, sharp or blurred, as having a chance. Then (P) holds exactly when those chances are never negative, the certain question has chance 1, and the chances add up whenever two questions combine into one. Over fractions nothing more is needed, not even an argument about limits. So (P) is the assumption that chances exist and add, in a strong form: the adding is required even for questions that cannot be asked in the same experiment.

Two further points, both given the series' stated definitions. The series has an averaging step, part of what it calls the descent, that erases quantities which change the count of particles from even to odd. Assuming nothing beyond its definition, that step keeps non-negative averages non-negative, but it cannot produce the property where it is absent, so (P) cannot be obtained from it. And although the step erases each such quantity on its own, it does not erase the product of two of them, which is of the even kind. Under (P), a state that respects the even-odd rule can still show correlations of 2.8 between two parties who use such quantities, above the limit of 2 that holds, with one mode for each party, when they do not; this needs quantities that mix the even and the odd kind. So the even-odd rule for states does not settle whether such quantities count as measurements.

proofs.main:
\emph{Preliminaries.} Write $\tau = \langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$. By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} the blades are a basis and each blade $b$ has $b^{-1} = \pm b$, so $b^{\dagger} = b$ exactly when $b^{2} = 1$ and $b^{\dagger} = -b$ otherwise; $\dagger$ is an anti-automorphism, and $\tau(x^{\dagger}x)$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$ (clause (iii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}). The cone $\mathcal{K}$ is closed under sums and under multiplication by non-negative elements of $k$, and contains $1 = 1 \cdot 1^{\dagger}$ and every projector $E = EE^{\dagger}$; if $E$ is a projector so is $1 - E$, so projectors are effects. Two remarks used below. (A) If $E$ is an effect and $0 \le t \le 1$ in $k$, then $tE$ is an effect, since $1 - tE = t(1 - E) + (1 - t)$. (B) If $c, c' \in \mathcal{K}$ and $c + c'$ is an effect, then $c$ and $c'$ are effects, since $1 - c = (1 - c - c') + c'$.

\emph{(i).} The self-adjoint elements are the span of the self-adjoint blades because $\dagger$ multiplies each blade by $\pm 1$. For a blade $b$ of square $1$, $(1 \pm b)^{\dagger} = 1 \pm b$ and $(1 \pm b)^{2} = 2(1 \pm b)$. For $s = \sum_{b}c_{b}b$ (the scalar blade included), $n_{s} - s = \sum_{b}|c_{b}|\,(1 - \operatorname{sgn}(c_{b})\,b)$, and each term is $|c_{b}|$ times an element $\tfrac12(1 \mp b)(1 \mp b)^{\dagger}$ (for the scalar blade the term is $0$ or $2|c_{b}|$); likewise $n_{s} + s$. So $s = \tfrac12(n_{s} + s) - \tfrac12(n_{s} - s)$ is a difference of elements of $\mathcal{K}$, and for $s \ne 0$ the element $(n_{s} + s)/(2n_{s})$ is an effect, with complement $(n_{s} - s)/(2n_{s})$, so $s$ is a combination of that effect and of the effect $1$.

\emph{(ii).} A state restricts to a weight: non-negativity on $\mathcal{K}$ is the positivity clause with linearity, and additivity is linearity. Conversely let $\mu$ be a weight. Step 1: for an effect $E$ and integers $0 \le j \le n$, $n \ge 1$, the elements $jE/n$ are effects by (A), so additivity gives $\mu(jE/n) = j\mu(E/n)$ and $\mu(E) = n\mu(E/n)$: $\mu(rE) = r\mu(E)$ for rational $r \in [0,1]$. Step 2, used only when $k \ne \Q$: for $t \in k$ with $0 \le t \le 1$ and rationals $r \le t \le r'$ in $[0,1]$, $\mu(tE) = \mu(rE) + \mu((t - r)E) \ge r\mu(E)$ and $\mu(r'E) = \mu(tE) + \mu((r' - t)E) \ge \mu(tE)$, by additivity and non-negativity; so $\mu(tE)$ and $t\mu(E)$ both lie between $r\mu(E)$ and $r'\mu(E)$, and since $k$ is Archimedean $r' - r$ can be made smaller than any positive element, whence $\mu(tE) = t\mu(E)$. Step 3: for $c \in \mathcal{K}$ there is an integer $n \ge 1$ with $c/n$ an effect: by (i) $n_{c} - c \in \mathcal{K}$, and any integer $n \ge n_{c}$ (which exists as $k$ is Archimedean) has $1 - c/n = \bigl((n_{c} - c) + (n - n_{c})\bigr)/n \in \mathcal{K}$. Put $\omega(c) = n\mu(c/n)$; by Step 1 this does not depend on $n$ (compare $n$ and $n'$ through $nn'$). For $c, c' \in \mathcal{K}$ choose $n$ with $(c + c')/n$ an effect; by (B) $c/n$ and $c'/n$ are effects and additivity of $\mu$ gives $\omega(c + c') = \omega(c) + \omega(c')$. By Steps 1 and 2, $\omega(tc) = t\omega(c)$ for $t \ge 0$ in $k$, and $\omega \ge 0$ on $\mathcal{K}$. Step 4: by (i) every self-adjoint $s$ is $c - c'$ with $c, c' \in \mathcal{K}$; put $\omega(s) = \omega(c) - \omega(c')$, well defined because $c - c' = d - d'$ gives $c + d' = d + c'$ and additivity on $\mathcal{K}$ applies. This $\omega$ is $k$-linear on the self-adjoint elements. Step 5: put $\omega(x) = \omega(\tfrac12(x + x^{\dagger}))$ for all $x$. Then $\omega$ is $k$-linear, $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ because $xx^{\dagger} \in \mathcal{K}$, $\omega(1) = \mu(1) = 1$, and $\omega = \mu$ on effects (take $n = 1$): $\omega$ is a state in the sense of Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}. Uniqueness: two states that agree on effects agree on their span, the self-adjoint elements, and the reality clause gives $\omega(x) = \omega(\tfrac12(x + x^{\dagger}))$. For $k = \Q$ Step 2 is not needed, and Steps 1, 3, 4, 5 use only additivity: they give a $\Q$-linear real $\omega$ for any additive map on effects with values in $\Q$; then $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ for all $x$ exactly when $\mu \ge 0$ on effects, because every element of $\mathcal{K}$ is a positive integer multiple of an effect.

\emph{(iii).} $\tfrac{3}{10}\Pi_{e} + \tfrac{4}{10}\Pi_{p} = \tfrac{7}{20} + \tfrac{3}{20}e_{1} + \tfrac{4}{20}p_{1} = \tfrac12E_{a} + \tfrac{1}{10}$. Each term is a multiple of a projector or of $1$ by a number in $[0,1]$, hence an effect by (A), and the common value is an effect because its complement is $\tfrac12(1 - E_{a}) + \tfrac{4}{10} \in \mathcal{K}$; so by (B) the partial sums are effects and additivity applies to both sides: $\tfrac12\mu(E_{a}) + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{3}{10}\mu(\Pi_{e}) + \tfrac{4}{10}\mu(\Pi_{p})$, using Step 1 of (ii) for the rational multiples. With the two given values, $\mu(E_{a}) = \tfrac{9}{10}$. $\Pi_{p}$ is the vacuum projector of one mode, an atom by clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}; a weight with $\mu(\Pi_{p}) = 1$ extends by (ii) to a state sharp on it, which by clause (iii) of that theorem is $x \mapsto 2\tau(\Pi_{p}x)$, with values $\tfrac12$ on $\Pi_{e}$ and $\tfrac{9}{10}$ on $E_{a}$. Here $\Cl_{k}(1,1)$ is one mode in the sense of Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}, with generators $e_{1}$, $f_{1}$ of squares $1$, $-1$. Its self-adjoint elements are the span of $1$, $e_{1}$, $p_{1}$ (by (i): $f_{1}^{2} = -1$), and $\tfrac12(1 + n)$ with $n = xe_{1} + zp_{1}$ is idempotent exactly when $n^{2} = x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$ (the elements $e_{1}$, $p_{1}$ anticommute), while an idempotent $c + \tfrac12 n'$ with $c \ne \tfrac12$ forces $n' = 0$ and $c \in \{0, 1\}$; two such projectors $\tfrac12(1 + n)$, $\tfrac12(1 + n')$ have product zero only if $n' = -n$. So the families of orthogonal nonzero projectors are the pairs $\{E, 1 - E\}$, and a function $g$ on these projectors is additive on them exactly when $g(\tfrac12(1 - n)) = 1 - g(\tfrac12(1 + n))$, which holds for $\tfrac12(1 + z^{3})$ since $z \mapsto z^{3}$ is odd; it is non-negative because $|z| \le 1$. Its values $1$, $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac{189}{250}$ are the script's, and $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{189}{250} + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{239}{500} \ne \tfrac{275}{500}$.

\emph{(iv).} $\Gamma^{\dagger} = \Gamma$ gives $(\Gamma x\Gamma)^{\dagger} = \Gamma x^{\dagger}\Gamma$, so $E_{\Gamma}$ commutes with $\dagger$; and $\Gamma yy^{\dagger}\Gamma = (\Gamma y)(\Gamma y)^{\dagger}$. Hence $E_{\Gamma}(\mathcal{K}) \subset \mathcal{K}$, every element of $E_{\Gamma}(\mathcal{K})$ is fixed because $E_{\Gamma}$ is idempotent (Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} for one mode; in general $\Gamma^{2} = 1$ gives $E_{\Gamma}E_{\Gamma} = E_{\Gamma}$), and a fixed element $c$ of $\mathcal{K}$ is $E_{\Gamma}(c)$. The statement about $\varphi \circ E_{\Gamma}$ follows. In the example $1 + 2p_{1}$ is self-adjoint and commutes with the total parity $p_{1}p_{2}$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.mode-split-of-the-clifford-algebra-and-its-klein-twist-to-the-tensor-product}, so $\varphi$ is real and invariant; $\varphi(\tfrac12(1 - p_{1})) = \tfrac12(1 - 2) = -\tfrac12$, and $\tfrac12(1 - p_{1})$ is a projector. Rider: the averages over the commuting self-adjoint $p_{j}$ commute, and their composition $E$ annihilates every blade that anticommutes with some $p_{j}$ and fixes the others, which are, up to sign, the products of the $p_{j}$; their span is the span of the $2^{\ell}$ orthogonal projectors $\Pi_{\chi} = \prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 + \chi_{j}p_{j})$. A fixed element of $\mathcal{K}$ is $c = \sum_{\chi}c_{\chi}\Pi_{\chi}$ with $c_{\chi}\tau(\Pi_{\chi}) = \tau(\Pi_{\chi}c) \ge 0$, because $\tau(\Pi_{\chi}yy^{\dagger}) = \tau((\Pi_{\chi}y)(\Pi_{\chi}y)^{\dagger}) \ge 0$; so an invariant functional is non-negative on $\mathcal{K}$ exactly when it is non-negative on the $\Pi_{\chi}$. For the grading: the grading automorphism $\alpha$ fixes even and negates odd elements and commutes with $\dagger$ (both act on each blade by a sign), so $E = \tfrac12(\mathrm{id} + \alpha)$ is idempotent and commutes with $\dagger$; that $\omega \circ E$ is then the even state agreeing with $\omega$ on even elements is clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.univalence-even-extension-split}, whose argument uses only this. Moreover, so for $y = y_{0} + y_{1}$ split into even and odd parts $E_{\Gamma}(yy^{\dagger}) = y_{0}y_{0}^{\dagger} + y_{1}y_{1}^{\dagger}$, the cross terms being odd. For a generator $g$, $gg^{\dagger} = gg^{-1} = 1$, so $y_{1}y_{1}^{\dagger} = (y_{1}g)(y_{1}g)^{\dagger}$ with $y_{1}g$ even. So the fixed elements of $\mathcal{K}$ are combinations, with non-negative coefficients, of hermitian squares of even elements, and conversely such combinations are fixed. A functional vanishing on odd elements is invariant, so it is non-negative on $\mathcal{K}$ exactly when it is non-negative on hermitian squares of even elements; normalisation and reality restrict in the obvious way.

\emph{(v).} With $p_{1} = f_{1}e_{1}$: $e_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1} = e_{1}e_{2}f_{1}e_{1} = e_{2}f_{1} = u$ (moving the last $e_{1}$ to the front costs two transpositions), $p_{1}p_{2} = \Gamma$, and the two mixed products $e_{1}p_{2}$ and $p_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1} = e_{2}$ are odd. So $a_{i}b_{j} = x_{i}x'_{j}u + z_{i}z'_{j}\Gamma + (\text{odd})$ and $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}b_{j}) = x_{i}x'_{j}u + z_{i}z'_{j}\Gamma$; summing with the CHSH signs gives $E_{\Gamma}(C) = Xu + Z\Gamma$. $u^{2} = e_{2}f_{1}e_{2}f_{1} = -e_{2}^{2}f_{1}^{2} = 1$, so $u$ is a blade of square $1$, self-adjoint, and it commutes with $\Gamma$ because it is even. $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}) = z_{i}p_{1}$ and $E_{\Gamma}(b_{j}) = z'_{j}p_{2}$ ($e_{1}$ and $e_{2}p_{1}$ are odd), whose CHSH element is $Z\Gamma$. For an even state, $\omega(C) = \omega(E_{\Gamma}(C)) = X\omega(u) + Z\omega(\Gamma)$. For self-adjoint $w$ with $w^{2} = 1$, $1 \pm w = \tfrac12(1 \pm w)(1 \pm w)^{\dagger}$ and positivity give $|\omega(w)| \le 1$; hence $|\omega(C)| \le |X| + |Z|$. The four elements $\tfrac14(1 + \epsilon u)(1 + \epsilon'\Gamma)$, $\epsilon, \epsilon' = \pm 1$, are projectors (products of commuting projectors; atoms by clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, since the blades commuting with $\Gamma$ are the even ones, and among the bivectors only $e_{2}f_{1} = u$ and $e_{1}f_{2} = \pm u\Gamma$ have square $1$ and commute with $u$: $e_{1}f_{1}$ and $e_{2}f_{2}$ anticommute with $u$, $e_{1}e_{2}$ and $f_{1}f_{2}$ have square $-1$), even, of scalar part $\tfrac14$ because $u$, $\Gamma$ and $u\Gamma$ are non-scalar blades; the state $x \mapsto 4\langle\tfrac14(1 + \epsilon u)(1 + \epsilon'\Gamma)x\rangle_{0}$ is even and has $\omega(u) = \epsilon$, $\omega(\Gamma) = \epsilon'$, so $\omega(C) = \epsilon X + \epsilon'Z$, which is $|X| + |Z|$ for suitable signs. The bound: with the plane vectors $\alpha_{i} = (x_{i}, z_{i})$, $\beta_{j} = (x'_{j}, z'_{j})$ of unit length, $X + Z = \alpha_{1} \cdot (\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}) + \alpha_{2} \cdot (\beta_{1} - \beta_{2})$, so $(X + Z)^{2} \le 2\bigl(|\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}|^{2} + |\beta_{1} - \beta_{2}|^{2}\bigr) = 8$ by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $k^{2}$; replacing $z'_{j}$ by $-z'_{j}$ gives the same for $X - Z$, and $|X| + |Z|$ is $|X + Z|$ or $|X - Z|$. The numbers at the stated directions, $X = 1 \cdot (\tfrac35 + \tfrac45) = \tfrac75$ and $Z = 1 \cdot (\tfrac45 + \tfrac35) = \tfrac75$, and the value $\tfrac{14}{5}$, are confirmed by the script.

synthesis.premise-minimal-non-commutativ.technical: The second primitive lets independent distinctions depend on order by the least possible amount. The directions together with one central bit $c$ generate a group that, once the bit is divided out, is the configuration space $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ of the bit premise, and any two distinct directions commute only up to that bit: $e_{i}e_{j} = c\,e_{j}e_{i}$ with $c \ne 1$. The bit has order two; for two or more directions this follows from reading the relation both ways, and it is stated so that the single-direction case is covered. Each direction then squares to $1$ or to $c$, and which ones square to $c$ is the signature, left free. Everything about signs and squares follows from this premise as theorems; it is a mathematical choice, not a physical hypothesis.
synthesis.premise-minimal-non-commutativ.lay: This assumption, again a choice about mathematics rather than a claim about nature, lets the order of two different distinctions matter, but only by the smallest possible amount: swapping them flips one extra on-off bit. That one bit is where the minus sign comes from (read later, in the series, as the sign behind rotation), and with it the possibility of different kinds of directions, some squaring to plus one and some to minus one. Which directions are of which kind is left open.

synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values.formal:
\emph{Premise (P), positivity of values.} Let $k$ be $\Q$ or any ordered field, and $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ the Clifford algebra of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} with coefficients in $k$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.division-gives-the-rationals}), with blades $e_{S}$, the images of the group $G$ of signed directions. Let $x \mapsto x^{\dagger}$ be the linear extension of the inverse of $G$, $e_{S}^{\dagger} = e_{S}^{-1}$ (the blade inverse): the anti-automorphism that fixes each generator of square $1$ and negates each generator of square $-1$. The premise is: values are given by a \emph{state}, a $k$-linear $\omega : \Cl_{k}(p,q) \to k$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$. The three clauses are called normalisation, positivity and reality. The value of an element $x$ is $\omega(x)$.

\emph{The split.} The adjoint is defined by the chosen generators, so (P) is stated relative to a split of the generators into those of square $+1$ and those of square $-1$. The split meant is the one that defines the modes: in $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the generators $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$ with $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$ of the null pairs $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j})$, $w_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} - f_{j})$ (Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}); the adjoint fixes $e_{j}$, negates $f_{j}$ and exchanges $v_{j}$ with $w_{j}$. In definite signature the adjoint does not depend on the orthonormal frame (it is the reverse in signature $(p,0)$ and the Clifford conjugate in signature $(0,q)$). In indefinite signature another split gives another adjoint, and with it other self-adjoint elements and other states: by clause (vi) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, in $\Cl_{\Q}(2,2)$ the unit vector $\tfrac{17}{8}e_{1} + \tfrac{15}{8}f_{1}$ of a boosted frame has square $1$ and is not self-adjoint for the split $e_{j}, f_{j}$, the functional of $\rho = \tfrac14(1 + e_{1})(1 + p_{2})$, $p_{2} = f_{2}e_{2}$, which satisfies (P) for that split, is not a state for the boosted one, and it gives a CHSH element built with that vector, an element of square $4$, the value $\tfrac{17}{4}$, where (P) bounds the value of an element of square $4$ that is self-adjoint for the split $e_{j}, f_{j}$ by $2$. So every statement made under (P) is relative to one fixed split and holds for each fixed split. In the mode algebras $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the split is fixed by the stored null pairs as vectors, $e_{j} = v_{j} + w_{j}$, $f_{j} = v_{j} - w_{j}$; the two isotropic subspaces they span fix it only up to a positive definite form on one of them, and the states of (P) that are states for every split adapted to those subspaces are the mixtures of the sector projectors of the number element (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.splits-adapted-to-the-null-pairs-and-the-states-common-to-all-of-them}). So the datum that supplies the split there is the choice of the pairs within their subspaces, which the relations the pairs satisfy do not force. For other indefinite signatures the premise does not say which stored datum supplies the split.

\emph{Status and cost.} A premise of the series about values, adopted by decision (10 November 2026): assumed, not derived. It is not one of the foundation postulates F1 to F4 and is not part of the foundation layer. The foundation gives the algebra, its blades and, once the generators are chosen, the adjoint; (P) is a further premise, about the functionals that give values, and the results that use it hold given it. It is not the univalence premise of the singularity results, which carries the same letter (Premise \claimref{singularity.p-univalence}).

What it does. It is what turns an identity of elements into a bound on values. For two commuting pairs of self-adjoint elements of square one, the identity for the square of the CHSH element $C$ and the certificate that writes $8 - C^{2}$ as one half of a sum of three squares (clauses (i) and (ii) of the theorem above) hold in the algebra with no premise about values; they need only the foundation postulates F1 to F3. With (P) they give Tsirelson's bound, $\omega(C)^{2} \le \omega(C^{2}) \le 8$ (clause (iii)), which uses the normalisation and positivity clauses only. Without the positivity clause the value $4$ occurs: at a configuration of blades the functional $\lambda(x) = \langle(1 + C)x\rangle_{0}$ is linear, normalised and real, has $\lambda(C) = 4$, and is negative on some $xx^{\dagger}$ (clause (v)); it gives a probability table with no signalling at each of its four configured pairs of settings and is negative only on elements that combine different pairs among those four (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-needs-positivity-across-settings-and-anticommutation-holds-only-on-the-state}); among such elements is the joint outcome idempotent of a single pair of local directions outside the four (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.local-weights-give-the-chsh-bound-and-do-not-fix-positivity-of-values}, clause (iii)). So (P) is not implied by the algebra together with linearity, normalisation and reality. The reality clause is used where a functional has to be fixed on all elements by its values on self-adjoint ones (the uniqueness statement of clause (viii)). The completion postulate F4 is not needed for the bound; the bound is attained only when $2$ is a square in $k$, that is, over the rationals, only after $\sqrt{2}$ is adjoined (clauses (iii), (iv) and (viii)).

What it extends. The stored definition of a state is an element $\rho = \sum_{r}x_{r}x_{r}^{\dagger}$ of unit trace (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.mode-split-of-the-clifford-algebra-and-its-klein-twist-to-the-tensor-product}). For such an element the functional $x \mapsto \langle\rho x\rangle_{0}/\langle\rho\rangle_{0}$ satisfies (P), because $\langle x^{\dagger}x\rangle_{0}$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$ (clause (iii)). (P) extends that definition from elements to functionals: it says that every assignment of values is of the positive kind, which the definition of the elements $\rho$ does not say.

What it costs, and what it leaves open. Positivity is asked on every element $xx^{\dagger}$, including those that combine quantities which the two parties never measure together, and it is assumed. What the counter-model shows is narrower than version 1 of this premise said: in the one-mode realisation, local weights already give the bound, that is, non-negative weights at every pair of local directions give $\omega(C)^{2} \le 8$ with no positivity on any other element, and the box has a negative weight at such a pair outside its four (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.local-weights-give-the-chsh-bound-and-do-not-fix-positivity-of-values}, clauses (ii) and (iii)); positivity across settings is what the box violates, and it is not shown to be what the bound needs. What positivity on all elements adds to non-negative local weights is not visible in the values of products of local observables: a family of functionals with the same values on all of them satisfies (P) at one parameter only (clause (iv) of the same theorem). In terms of weights, (P) is equivalent to: the values of effects are non-negative, normalised and additive, additivity being asked also across effects that do not commute (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positivity-of-values-is-additivity-of-non-negative-weights-on-effects}, clause (ii), for $k = \Q$ and Archimedean ordered $k$); that is the non-contextuality assumption, and it is inside the premise. Under (P) a state sharp on an atom is fixed and its weights are squared norms (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}); that theorem does not derive (P) or sharpness. No derivation of (P) from the series' account of measurement is stored (the store's Born account, Proposition \claimref{one-relation.measure-indifference-borns-rule-located}, rests on (P) from its version 4 and does not derive it; the envariance argument of Zurek is prior art there), and (P) has not been shown independent of the store's other premises: the counter-model is a functional on one algebra, not a model of the whole store. The premise does not say which self-adjoint elements are observables. In particular it does not decide whether elements odd under the total parity are observables: both settings are recorded side by side (clause (vii) of the theorem above; Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-with-parity-even-observables-needs-two-modes-per-party-and-no-klein-twist}). These questions are the open problem op.positivity-of-values.
synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values.technical:
The series' results on correlations between two or three parties speak of the values of elements of a Clifford algebra with rational coefficients (or coefficients in any ordered field). This premise says what a value is: values are given by a state, a linear functional $\omega$ on the algebra with $\omega(1) = 1$ (normalisation), $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ for every $x$ (positivity) and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ (reality), where the adjoint $\dagger$ is the inverse on blades extended linearly. It is assumed, not derived, and it is not one of the four foundation postulates: those give the algebra, and this is a separate premise about values, which the results using it hold given.

The adjoint is fixed by the choice of generators, so the premise is relative to a split of the generators into those of square $+1$ and those of square $-1$. The split meant is the one that defines the modes, the pairs $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$ of the null pairs. In definite signature the adjoint does not depend on the frame. In indefinite signature another split gives another adjoint, other self-adjoint elements and other states, and a bound that holds under (P) for one split can fail for elements that are self-adjoint for another: a stored example gives the CHSH combination the value $17/4$, above $2\sqrt{2}$ and above $4$. For the mode algebras the stored null pairs, as vectors, fix the split; the two isotropic subspaces alone do not, and what fixes the pairs within them is open.

Under the premise the identity for the square of the CHSH combination, which holds in the algebra without it and needs only the first three foundation postulates, becomes Tsirelson's bound: the squared value is at most $8$. Without the positivity clause the bound fails: a linear, normalised, real functional gives the combination the value $4$, with a legitimate probability table at each of its four pairs of settings, and is negative only on elements that combine different pairs among those four. That does not make positivity across settings the part the bound needs: with one mode per party, non-negative weights at every pair of local directions already give the bound, and the functional has a negative weight at a pair outside its four. In terms of weights the premise says that the values of effects are non-negative, normalised and additive, also across effects that do not commute. The premise extends the stored definition of a state, an element that is a sum of terms $xx^{\dagger}$ of unit trace, from elements to functionals. It does not say which self-adjoint elements are observables, and in particular not whether parity-odd elements are; a derivation of the premise from the series' structure, or a proof that it is independent of the other premises, is an open problem.
synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values.lay:
This is an assumption about what the average result of a measurement is. The series builds an algebra of directions from very simple starting points, and its results on correlations between distant experimenters need to say what number an average takes. The assumption, called (P), is that averages are given by a rule with three properties: the average of a sum is the sum of the averages; the trivial quantity 1 has average 1; and a quantity multiplied by its mirror image (its adjoint) never has a negative average, with a quantity and its mirror image having the same average. It is assumed, not proved, and it is not one of the four basic assumptions the algebra itself is built from.

It matters because the algebra alone does not limit correlations to the quantum limit. With this assumption the well-known limit of about 2.83 on a standard combination of correlations follows; if the "never negative" part is dropped, a rule exists that reaches 4, the largest value the combination could have, while still giving sensible probabilities for every single experiment.

Two things are left open. The mirror image depends on a division of the directions into two kinds, those squaring to plus one and those squaring to minus one; the assumption is stated for the division that defines the series' modes, and a different division gives a different mirror image and different allowed averages (for the series' modes the stored pairs of light-like directions fix the division; the two families of such directions alone would not). And the assumption does not say which quantities count as measurements. Whether it can be derived from the series' own account of measurement is an open problem.

synthesis.premise-superposition-over-the.formal:
\emph{Premise (F3), superposition over the integers.} Grant Premise (F2), with its group $G$ and central bit $c$. Signed configurations (the elements of $G$) can be added, with integer coefficients, and the sign bit acts as $-1$: the algebra of the foundation is
\[
A = \Z[G]/(c + 1),
\]
the integral group ring of $G$ modulo the two-sided ideal generated by $c + 1$.

\emph{Status and cost.} A chosen primitive of the foundation, mathematical and not physical. The coefficient ring is the integers, the ring the unit generates under addition; the rationals and the reals are not assumed here (the first is reached by dividing by the squares of directions, the second needs the premise of completion). Identifying $c$ with $-1$ is part of the choice: in the group ring $c$ is a central element with $c^{2} = 1$, and the other possibility, $c$ acting as $+1$ (the only other integer of square $1$), gives the commutative group ring of the configurations, in which order is forgotten. What it does not say: that the coefficients are a field, or anything about limits. No observation bears on it directly; that quantum superposition is this addition is a reading, argued and not proved.
synthesis.premise-superposition-over-the.technical: The third primitive lets configurations be superposed: the group of directions acts linearly, with integer coefficients, and its sign bit acts as minus one. Formally the algebra is the integral group ring of the group of directions divided by the ideal generated by $c + 1$. The integers are chosen because they are the ring the unit generates; nothing finer is assumed. The choice of $-1$ for the bit is what keeps the order of directions visible, since sending the bit to $+1$ instead collapses the algebra to the commutative group ring of the configurations. From this premise the rule that a vector squares to its quadratic form, and the identification with the Clifford algebra over the integers, are theorems.
synthesis.premise-superposition-over-the.lay: The third starting assumption, like the first two a choice about mathematics and not a claim about nature, is that the on-off patterns can be added together and counted with whole numbers, with the special swap bit counting as minus one. Nothing beyond whole numbers is assumed: fractions come later from division, and the continuum of real numbers needs a separate assumption. With this step the whole-number form of the algebra of directions used throughout the series appears.

history.text: Version 1 -> 2. Leon's decision of 8 November 2026: the foundation layer. Marked as a foundation postulate, founded on synthesis.premise-minimal-non-commutativity. Foundation postulates are reported as what a result rests on, separately from the premises it holds given (store/conventions.md, "The foundation").

synthesis.premise-the-bit.formal:
\emph{Premise (F1), the bit.} The foundation takes as primitive a single distinction with two states, written $0$ (nothing) and $1$ (something), combined by comparison: making a distinction and making it again returns to nothing, $1 + 1 = 0$. With the product $1 \cdot 1 = 1$ (both made) and $0$ otherwise, the states form the two-element field $\mathbb{F}_{2}$. Distinctions are independent: for $n \ge 0$ distinctions a configuration is the set $S \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$ of those made, and configurations combine by comparison, the symmetric difference $S \triangle T$. So the configurations form the vector space $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$, with $2^{n}$ elements, $\binom{n}{k}$ of them containing $k$ distinctions.

\emph{Status and cost.} A chosen primitive of the foundation, mathematical and not physical: it posits a structure, the two-element field and its finite powers, and asserts nothing about the world. Nothing beneath it is available to derive it from. What it does not contain: a sign ($1 = -1$ in $\mathbb{F}_{2}$, so a distinction cannot be told from its reversal), an order between distinctions (comparison is commutative), and any magnitude or geometry; the sign and the order enter with the premise of minimal non-commutativity, superposition with the premise of superposition over the integers. No observation bears on it; what can fail is the reading that the algebra of physics is built on it, which is argued and not proved.
synthesis.premise-the-bit.technical: The root of the series' algebra is a single distinction: two states, $0$ and $1$, combined by comparison, so that $1 + 1 = 0$; with the product it is the field $\mathbb{F}_{2}$. Repeating it independently $n$ times, a configuration is the set of distinctions made, and configurations combine by symmetric difference, giving $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$: $2^{n}$ configurations, graded by how many distinctions they contain, which is the counting of the blades of a geometric algebra before any geometry. The premise is mathematical, a choice of starting structure. It carries no sign, since $1 = -1$ in $\mathbb{F}_{2}$, no order and no geometry; those come from the later premises.
synthesis.premise-the-bit.lay: This is the starting assumption of the whole construction, and it is a choice about mathematics, not a claim about nature: the simplest possible difference, something versus nothing, where doing the same thing twice undoes it. Many such differences, independent of one another, give a collection of on-off patterns. These patterns already have the shape of the algebra of directions used throughout the series, but none of its geometry yet: no sign, no order and no lengths.

synthesis.records-keep-even-states-even-.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or any ordered field and $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the algebra of $\ell$ modes: generators $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$ with $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$, mode parities $p_{j} = f_{j}e_{j}$, adjoint $\dagger$ the linear extension of the inverse on blades (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra}), scalar part $\langle x\rangle_{0}$. Let $\Gamma = p_{1}\cdots p_{\ell}$ be the total parity, $\alpha(x) = \Gamma x\Gamma$ (the grade involution: it fixes even blades and negates odd ones) and $E = \tfrac12(\mathrm{id} + \alpha)$ the total-parity average (Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} in its total-parity form). A functional $\omega$ is \emph{even} if $\omega \circ \alpha = \omega$. An \emph{observable} is an $a$ with $a^{\dagger} = a$, $a^{2} = 1$; it is \emph{homogeneous} if $\alpha(a) = a$ or $\alpha(a) = -a$. \emph{(P)} is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}; a \emph{state} is a functional satisfying it. The \emph{sector average} of an observable $a$, called its \emph{record map} below (that it describes a record is a reading, stated after the clauses and not part of the theorem), is
\[
E_{a}(x) = \tfrac12(x + axa) = P_{+}xP_{+} + P_{-}xP_{-}, \qquad P_{\pm} = \tfrac12(1 \pm a) .
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The sector average, under (P) for its statements about states; proved.)} $E_{a}$ is linear and idempotent, $E_{a}(1) = 1$, $E_{a}(x^{\dagger}) = E_{a}(x)^{\dagger}$, $E_{a}(xx^{\dagger}) = (P_{+}x)(P_{+}x)^{\dagger} + (P_{-}x)(P_{-}x)^{\dagger}$, and $E_{a}(P_{+}xP_{-}) = 0$. So if $\omega$ satisfies (P) then so does $\omega \circ E_{a}$, and $\omega \circ E_{a}$ vanishes on the elements $P_{+}xP_{-}$ and $P_{-}xP_{+}$ that connect the two sectors of $a$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Sector averages and parity; proved.)} For an observable $a$ the following are equivalent: (1) under (P), $\omega \circ E_{a}$ is even for every even state $\omega$; (2) $E_{a}\alpha = \alpha E_{a}$; (3) $a$ is homogeneous.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(One mode per party, under (P); proved.)} In $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$ with the parties of clause (vii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate} (mode $1$, and mode $2$ twisted by $p_{1}$ as in Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}), the homogeneous observables other than $\pm 1$ are $\pm X_{1}$, $\pm Z_{1}$ for party $1$ and $\pm X_{2}$, $\pm Z_{2}$ for party $2$, where $X_{1} = e_{1}$, $X_{2} = e_{2}p_{1}$ (odd) and $Z_{1} = p_{1}$, $Z_{2} = p_{2}$ (even). For every choice $A_{1}, A_{2}$ among the first four and $B_{1}, B_{2}$ among the second four, with $C = A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2}) + A_{2}(B_{1} - B_{2})$, $U = X_{1}X_{2}$ and $V = Z_{1}Z_{2}$: $E(C) = \mu U + \nu V$ with $|\mu| + |\nu| \le 2$, and every even state has $|\omega(C)| = |\omega(E(C))| \le 2$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The settings above $2$ are of mixed parity, under (P); proved by an example.)} At $A_{1} = X_{1}$, $A_{2} = Z_{1}$, $B_{1} = \tfrac35X_{2} + \tfrac45Z_{2}$, $B_{2} = \tfrac45X_{2} - \tfrac35Z_{2}$, clause (v) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positivity-of-values-is-additivity-of-non-negative-weights-on-effects} gives an even state $\omega$, that of the atom $\tfrac14(1 + U)(1 + V)$, with $\omega(C) = \tfrac{14}{5} > 2$ (there $u = U$ and $\Gamma = V$), and notes that the value above $2$ uses directions of mixed parity; clause (viii) of the stored CHSH theorem notes the same possibility. What is added here is the record: $B_{1}$ is not homogeneous, and $\omega \circ E_{B_{1}}$ is not even, its value on the odd element $X_{1}Z_{2}$ being $\tfrac{12}{25}$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Odd observables with two modes per party, under (P); proved.)} In $\Cl_{k}(4,4)$ let $A_{1} = e_{1}$, $A_{2} = e_{2}$, $B_{1} = e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}$, $B_{2} = e_{4}p_{1}p_{2}$. All four are odd observables, blades up to sign; $A_{i}$ commutes with $B_{j}$; $C$ and $K = -A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2}$ are even, and the functional $\omega(x) = \langle(1 + K)(1 + \tfrac13C)x\rangle_{0}$ is an even state with $\omega(C) = \tfrac83 > 2$. The record maps of the four observables commute with $\alpha$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Reading (argued, not part of the theorem).} Premise \claimref{one-relation.recorded-sectors-superselected-premise} says that after a record the recorded sectors do not interfere; for a two-valued observable $a$ and values given by a functional $\omega$, the functional with no interference between the sectors of $a$ and the same values on what commutes with $a$ is $\omega \circ E_{a}$. Premise \claimref{singularity.p-univalence} says that physical states are even. If both hold, before and after a record, then by (ii) an observable that can be recorded is even or odd, never a sum of the two. Odd observables are then allowed, one mode per party gives at most $2$ in both settings, and a value above $2$ needs two modes per party whether the observables are even (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-with-parity-even-observables-needs-two-modes-per-party-and-no-klein-twist}) or odd (clause (v)). Sufficient conditions for the value at most $2$ with one mode per party that are recorded and consistent: homogeneous settings and even states (clause (iii)); averaged directions (clause (vii) of the stored CHSH theorem); and, as a formula, $|X| + |Z| \le 2$ in clause (v) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positivity-of-values-is-additivity-of-non-negative-weights-on-effects} when every direction is even or odd, of which clause (iii) is the statement for all signed choices with its certificate.

\emph{Remark (another route, argued).} Theorem \claimref{synthesis.univalence-from-even-stationary-dynamics}, clause 3, says that every density stationary under the flow of an even generator is even exactly when no odd signed sum of weights vanishes. If ``recorded'' is read as ``never unwritten, hence stationary'', that theorem gives that a recorded observable is even, without the map $E_{a}$ and without asking that univalence hold after a record. The comparison: that route also needs a reading (recorded implies stationary); it is stored for the complex Fock realisation, not for $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ under (P); and its conclusion, even, is stronger than even or odd and would exclude the odd observables of clause (v). It does not replace clause (ii), which is about an arbitrary observable and the map $E_{a}$. Which reading of a record is meant is not decided here.
synthesis.records-keep-even-states-even-.technical: The univalence premise restricts states to those that vanish on parity-odd elements; it says nothing directly about observables. This result supplies the link through records, under (P), positivity of values, for the statements about states. The theorem is about the sector average $E_{a}(x) = \tfrac12(x + axa)$ of a two-valued observable $a$, which removes the interference between the two sectors of $a$ and sends states to states; that it describes a record of $a$ is a reading. The theorem: $E_{a}$ sends every even state to an even state exactly when $a$ is even or odd under the total parity. An observable that is a sum of an even and an odd part, such as the direction $\tfrac35e_{1} + \tfrac45p_{1}$ of one mode, turns an even state into one that is not even. In the realisation of the CHSH bound with one mode per party and a Klein twist, the only homogeneous observables are $\pm e_{1}$, $\pm p_{1}$ and their twisted partners, and at these settings every even state gives the CHSH combination a value of at most $2$; the settings that reach $14/5$ on an even state use a direction of mixed parity. Parity-odd observables as such are not excluded: with two modes per party, four odd blades give $8/3$ on an even state. So, under the reading that records act by $E_{a}$ and that states stay even after a record, the two settings recorded side by side (even observables, or odd ones with a twist) both need two modes per party, and the one-mode violation is not available. The reading is argued; the algebra is proved. A different reading (recorded means stationary) with the stored theorem on even stationary dynamics would give that recorded observables are even, excluding the odd ones; the two readings are not decided between here.
synthesis.records-keep-even-states-even-.lay: The series has a rule that physical states must look the same when every fermion-like mode changes sign ("even" states), but it had no rule about which quantities can be measured. This result connects the two, assuming (P), the series' assumption that averages are never negative on a quantity times its mirror image. When a two-valued quantity is measured and the result recorded, the state changes in a definite way. The theorem says that this change keeps every even state even exactly when the measured quantity is itself purely even or purely odd; a quantity that mixes the two kinds spoils the rule. For two experimenters with one mode each, the only quantities that pass this test are too few to beat the classical limit of 2 on the standard combination of correlations. Quantities of the odd kind are still allowed, but each experimenter needs two modes to exceed 2. This holds if recording works as described and the rule on states holds after a recording too; those two points are a reading of the series' premises, not something proved here.

proofs.main:
\emph{Premise.} (P) of the statement is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}, assumed and not derived; every statement below about states is under it, relative to the fixed split of the generators.

\emph{Preliminaries.} The properties of the adjoint and of the scalar part used are those of the preliminaries of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}: $\langle xy\rangle_{0} = \langle yx\rangle_{0}$, $\langle x^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \langle x\rangle_{0}$, $\langle xx^{\dagger}\rangle_{0}$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$ (so it vanishes only for $x = 0$), and the scalar part of a product of two blades is zero unless they are equal up to sign; the blades are a basis (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra}). The $p_{j}$ are commuting self-adjoint elements of square $1$; $p_{j}$ anticommutes with $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$ and commutes with the other generators, so $\Gamma$ is self-adjoint of square $1$ and anticommutes with every generator: $\alpha$ is the grade involution, an automorphism commuting with $\dagger$, and $E$ is the projection onto the even part, the group average of Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} for the group $\{\mathrm{id}, \alpha\}$. Write $x_{+} = E(x)$ and $x_{-} = x - E(x)$. For a self-adjoint blade $s$, $s^{2} = 1$ and $1 \pm s = \tfrac12(1 \pm s)(1 \pm s)^{\dagger}$, so $x \mapsto \langle(1 \pm s)x\rangle_{0}$ satisfies (P) (as does $\langle x\rangle_{0}$), and it is even when $s$ is even.

\emph{(i).} $P_{\pm}$ are self-adjoint idempotents with $P_{+}P_{-} = 0$, $P_{+} + P_{-} = 1$, $a = P_{+} - P_{-}$; expanding gives $P_{+}xP_{+} + P_{-}xP_{-} = \tfrac12(x + axa)$. The listed properties follow: idempotence from $P_{\pm}P_{\mp} = 0$; $E_{a}(xx^{\dagger}) = \sum_{\pm}P_{\pm}xx^{\dagger}P_{\pm} = \sum_{\pm}(P_{\pm}x)(P_{\pm}x)^{\dagger}$. If $\omega$ satisfies (P) then $\omega(E_{a}(xx^{\dagger})) \ge 0$, $\omega(E_{a}(1)) = 1$ and $\omega(E_{a}(x^{\dagger})) = \omega(E_{a}(x)^{\dagger}) = \omega(E_{a}(x))$.

\emph{(ii).} (3) implies (2): $\alpha(E_{a}(x)) = \tfrac12(\alpha(x) + \alpha(a)\alpha(x)\alpha(a)) = E_{a}(\alpha(x))$ when $\alpha(a) = \pm a$. (2) implies (1): $\omega \circ E_{a} \circ \alpha = \omega \circ \alpha \circ E_{a} = \omega \circ E_{a}$, and $\omega \circ E_{a}$ is a state by (i). (1) implies (3): write $a = a_{+} + a_{-}$; both parts are self-adjoint, and $a^{2} = 1$ gives $a_{+}^{2} + a_{-}^{2} = 1$ and $a_{+}a_{-} + a_{-}a_{+} = 0$. \emph{Step 1.} Let $y$ be odd and self-adjoint and $w = E(E_{a}(y))$, even and self-adjoint. For every even state $\omega$, $\omega(E_{a}(y)) = 0$ by (1), and $\omega(E_{a}(y)) = \omega(w)$ since $\omega$ is even. Taking $\omega = \langle\,\cdot\,\rangle_{0}$ and $\omega = \langle(1 \pm s)\,\cdot\,\rangle_{0}$ for the even self-adjoint blades $s$ gives $\langle w\rangle_{0} = 0$ and $\langle sw\rangle_{0} = 0$; a self-adjoint even element is a combination of the scalar and of even self-adjoint blades (a blade is self-adjoint or anti-self-adjoint), so $w = 0$. \emph{Step 2.} Let $x$ be even and self-adjoint and $z = (E_{a}(x))_{-} = \tfrac12(a_{+}xa_{-} + a_{-}xa_{+})$, odd and self-adjoint. For odd self-adjoint $y$, $\langle zy\rangle_{0} = \langle E_{a}(x)y\rangle_{0} = \langle xE_{a}(y)\rangle_{0} = \langle xw\rangle_{0} = 0$ (the scalar part of an even times an odd element is zero; $\langle E_{a}(x)y\rangle_{0} = \langle xE_{a}(y)\rangle_{0}$ by cyclicity; Step 1). For odd anti-self-adjoint $y$, $\langle zy\rangle_{0} = \langle(zy)^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = -\langle yz\rangle_{0} = -\langle zy\rangle_{0}$, so it is zero. Hence $\langle zz^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = 0$ and $z = 0$:
\[
a_{+}xa_{-} + a_{-}xa_{+} = 0 \qquad \text{for every even self-adjoint } x . \tag{$*$}
\]
\emph{Step 3.} Put $x = a_{+}$ in $(*)$: $a_{+}^{2}a_{-} + a_{-}a_{+}^{2} = 2a_{-} - 2a_{-}^{3} = 0$, so $a_{-}^{3} = a_{-}$ and $q = a_{-}^{2}$ is a self-adjoint even idempotent commuting with $a_{-}$; it commutes with $a_{+}$ (two anticommutations), and $(a_{+}q)(a_{+}q)^{\dagger} = a_{+}^{2}q = (1 - q)q = 0$, so $a_{+}q = 0$. Thus $a_{+} = a_{+}(1 - q)$, $a_{-} = a_{-}q$, $a_{+}^{2} = 1 - q$, $a_{-}^{2} = q$. \emph{Step 4.} For even $x'$ the element $x = qx'(1 - q) + (1 - q)x'^{\dagger}q$ is even and self-adjoint, and $(*)$ reads $a_{+}(1 - q)x'^{\dagger}q\,a_{-} + a_{-}q\,x'(1 - q)a_{+} = 0$. The first term lies in $(1 - q)\mathcal{A}q$ and the second in $q\mathcal{A}(1 - q)$ (with $\mathcal{A}$ the algebra), so each is zero; multiplying $a_{-}qx'(1 - q)a_{+} = 0$ by $a_{-}$ on the left and $a_{+}$ on the right gives $qx'(1 - q) = 0$, and the adjoint statement gives $(1 - q)x'q = 0$. So $q$ commutes with every even element. \emph{Step 5.} An even element commuting with every even element commutes with every product $g_{i}g_{j}$ of two distinct generators; conjugation by $g_{i}g_{j}$ multiplies a blade by $-1$ exactly when the blade contains one of the two generators and not the other, so only the scalar blade and the top blade survive: $q = c_{0} + c_{1}\Gamma$, and $q^{2} = q$ gives $q \in \{0, 1, \tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma)\}$. If $q = \tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma)$ then $a_{-}q = (1 - q)a_{-}$ because $a_{-}$ anticommutes with $\Gamma$, while $a_{-}q = qa_{-}$; multiplying by $q$ gives $qa_{-} = 0$, so $a_{-} = a_{-}^{3} = a_{-}q = qa_{-} = 0$ and then $q = a_{-}^{2} = 0$, a contradiction. So $q = 0$, and $a_{-}a_{-}^{\dagger} = q = 0$ gives $a = a_{+}$; or $q = 1$, and $a_{+}a_{+}^{\dagger} = 1 - q = 0$ gives $a = a_{-}$.

\emph{(iii).} The self-adjoint blades of the algebra of mode $1$ are $1$, $e_{1}$, $e_{1}f_{1} = -p_{1}$ ($f_{1}$ is anti-self-adjoint), so its self-adjoint elements are $t + xe_{1} + zp_{1}$; the square is $t^{2} + x^{2} + z^{2} + 2t(xe_{1} + zp_{1})$, which is $1$ only for $\pm 1$ or $t = 0$, $x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$. The even part is $zp_{1}$ and the odd part $xe_{1}$, so the homogeneous ones are $\pm e_{1}$, $\pm p_{1}$. The twisted mode is the image of mode $2$ under the isomorphism $e_{2} \mapsto e_{2}p_{1}$, $f_{2} \mapsto f_{2}p_{1}$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}, which preserves $\dagger$, parity and $p_{2}$; so its homogeneous observables are $\pm e_{2}p_{1}$, $\pm p_{2}$. A product $A_{i}B_{j}$ is even exactly when both factors are odd (the product is $\pm U$) or both even ($\pm V$), so $E(C) = \mu U + \nu V$; the check enumerates the $256$ choices and finds $|\mu| + |\nu| \le 2$ in each. $U$, $V$ are commuting self-adjoint elements of square $1$, and for signs $\sigma, \tau$
\[
2 - \sigma U - \tau V = \tfrac12(1 - \sigma U)(1 - \sigma U)^{\dagger} + \tfrac12(1 - \tau V)(1 - \tau V)^{\dagger} ,
\]
so a state has $\omega(\sigma U) \le 1$, $\omega(\tau V) \le 1$ for all signs and $|\omega(\mu U + \nu V)| \le |\mu| + |\nu| \le 2$. For an even $\omega$, $\omega(C) = \omega(E(C))$.

\emph{(iv).} The state, the average $E(C) = \tfrac75(U + V)$ and the value $\tfrac{14}{5}$ are those of clause (v) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positivity-of-values-is-additivity-of-non-negative-weights-on-effects} at these directions, with $u = e_{2}f_{1} = U$ and $\Gamma = V$ (the check recomputes the value). $B_{1}$ has the odd part $\tfrac35X_{2}$ and the even part $\tfrac45Z_{2}$, so by (ii) some even state is sent to a functional that is not even; for this $\omega$ the value $\tfrac{12}{25}$ of $\omega \circ E_{B_{1}}$ on $X_{1}Z_{2}$ is computed by the check.

\emph{(v).} $p_{1}p_{2}$ is even, self-adjoint, of square $1$, anticommutes with $e_{1}$, $e_{2}$ and commutes with $e_{3}$, $e_{4}$; so $e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}$ and $e_{4}p_{1}p_{2}$ are odd, self-adjoint, of square $1$, anticommute with each other and commute with $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ (two anticommutations each), by the twist of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} applied to the two modes of party $1$ together. The configuration is one of blades with $A_{1}A_{2} = -A_{2}A_{1}$, $B_{1}B_{2} = -B_{2}B_{1}$, so clause (iv) of the CHSH theorem applies: $C^{2} = 4 + 4K$, $KC = C$, and $\langle(1 + K)(1 + rC)x\rangle_{0}$ satisfies (P) for $8r^{2} \le 1$ with value $8r$ on $C$; at $r = \tfrac13$ the check also verifies $(1 + K)(1 + \tfrac13C) = \tfrac34R^{2}$ with $R = (1 + K)(\tfrac23 + \tfrac16C)$ self-adjoint. $C$ and $K$ are products of an even number of odd elements, so the functional is even. The observables are odd, so their record maps commute with $\alpha$ by (ii).

synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generat.formal:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A \emph{bit over $R$} is the free module $M = R\,s_{\mathrm{off}} \oplus R\,s_{\mathrm{on}}$ on two states; \emph{set} is the $R$-linear map $v$ with $v\,s_{\mathrm{off}} = s_{\mathrm{on}}$, $v\,s_{\mathrm{on}} = 0$, and \emph{clear} the $R$-linear map $w$ with $w\,s_{\mathrm{on}} = s_{\mathrm{off}}$, $w\,s_{\mathrm{off}} = 0$. A \emph{switch} in an associative unital ring is a pair $(a, b)$ with $a^{2} = b^{2} = 0$ and $ab + ba = 1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $(v, w)$ is a switch. The products $vw$ and $wv$ are idempotents with $vw + wv = 1$ and $vw \cdot wv = wv \cdot vw = 0$; $vw$ fixes $s_{\mathrm{on}}$ and annihilates $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ (the test ``is on''), and $wv$ the reverse.
\item[(ii)] The $R$-algebra generated by $v$ and $w$ is $\mathrm{End}_{R}(M)$, free with basis $1, v, w, vw$.
\item[(iii)] For $x = \alpha v + \beta w$ with $\alpha, \beta \in R$, $x^{2} = \alpha\beta$. With $L = Rv \oplus Rw$ and $Q(x) = \alpha\beta$ (the hyperbolic quadratic module): for every associative unital $R$-algebra $B$ and $R$-linear $\phi : L \to B$ with $\phi(x)^{2} = Q(x)\,1$ there is exactly one unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $\Phi : \mathrm{End}_{R}(M) \to B$ extending $\phi$. So $\mathrm{End}_{R}(M)$ is the Clifford algebra of the hyperbolic plane over every $R$, with no hypothesis on $2$.
\item[(iv)] $e_{+} = v + w$ and $e_{-} = v - w$ satisfy $e_{+}^{2} = 1$, $e_{-}^{2} = -1$, $e_{+}e_{-} = -e_{-}e_{+} = wv - vw$; $e_{+}$ exchanges the two states and $e_{+}e_{-}$ is $+1$ on $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ and $-1$ on $s_{\mathrm{on}}$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generat.technical: Take a two-state system and only the two operations of setting it and clearing it. They square to zero, their anticommutator is the identity, and their two products are the tests for on and for off: the relations of one fermionic mode, with no sign and no fraction put in. They generate every linear operation on the two states, over any commutative ring of coefficients, and the square of a combination $\alpha v + \beta w$ is $\alpha\beta$, the hyperbolic form; the algebra has the universal property of the Clifford algebra of that form. The sum and difference of set and clear are two anticommuting directions of squares $+1$ and $-1$, so the orthonormal description of the hyperbolic plane is obtained from the switch, where the usual construction obtains the switch from the orthonormal pair with a factor one half.
synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generat.lay: Think of a light switch with two operations: switch on and switch off. Switching on something that is already on does nothing useful, and at any moment the light is either on or off. Written as algebra, those two facts are exactly the rules physicists use for a single particle of matter. From the two operations alone, by adding and subtracting them, one gets two directions, one that squares to plus one and one that squares to minus one, which is the pair of directions the series adds at each step. No halves are needed along the way.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} $v^{2}$ sends $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ to $v\,s_{\mathrm{on}} = 0$ and $s_{\mathrm{on}}$ to $0$; likewise $w^{2} = 0$. $vw$ sends $s_{\mathrm{on}}$ to $v\,s_{\mathrm{off}} = s_{\mathrm{on}}$ and $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ to $0$; $wv$ sends $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ to $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ and $s_{\mathrm{on}}$ to $0$. So $vw$ and $wv$ are the two coordinate projections: idempotent, with sum $1$ and products $0$.

\emph{(ii)} In the basis $(s_{\mathrm{off}}, s_{\mathrm{on}})$ the maps $wv$, $w$, $v$, $vw$ are the four matrices with a single entry $1$, a basis of the $2 \times 2$ matrices over $R$, and $wv = 1 - vw$; so $1, v, w, vw$ is a basis as well (the change of basis has determinant $\pm 1$).

\emph{(iii)} $x^{2} = \alpha^{2}v^{2} + \beta^{2}w^{2} + \alpha\beta\,(vw + wv) = \alpha\beta$. Let $\phi : L \to B$ be $R$-linear with $\phi(x)^{2} = Q(x)\,1$, and put $a = \phi(v)$, $b = \phi(w)$. Then $a^{2} = Q(v) = 0$, $b^{2} = Q(w) = 0$ and $ab + ba = (a + b)^{2} - a^{2} - b^{2} = Q(v + w) = 1$: $(a, b)$ is a switch in $B$. Define the $R$-linear map $\Phi$ on the basis of (ii) by $1 \mapsto 1$, $v \mapsto a$, $w \mapsto b$, $vw \mapsto ab$. The sixteen products of basis elements are reduced to the basis using only $v^{2} = w^{2} = 0$ and $wv = 1 - vw$: $v \cdot w = vw$, $w \cdot v = 1 - vw$, $v \cdot vw = 0$, $vw \cdot v = v(1 - vw) = v$, $w \cdot vw = (1 - vw)w = w$, $vw \cdot w = 0$, $vw \cdot vw = v(1 - vw)w = vw$, and the rest are $0$ or involve $1$. The same reductions hold for $a$, $b$, which satisfy the same relations, so $\Phi$ is multiplicative on the basis and hence a homomorphism. It is unique because $v$ and $w$ generate $\mathrm{End}_{R}(M)$ by (ii).

\emph{(iv)} $(v \pm w)^{2} = v^{2} + w^{2} \pm (vw + wv) = \pm 1$, and $(v + w)(v - w) = v^{2} - vw + wv - w^{2} = wv - vw = -(v - w)(v + w)$. By (i), $v + w$ sends $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ to $s_{\mathrm{on}}$ and back, and $wv - vw$ is $+1$ on $s_{\mathrm{off}}$ and $-1$ on $s_{\mathrm{on}}$.
