synthesis.signatures-in-which-commuting-.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or any ordered field and $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$, $n = p + q \ge 1$, the Clifford algebra of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} with coefficients in $k$: generators $e_{1}, \dots, e_{n}$, the first $p$ of square $1$ and the rest of square $-1$ (the label $(p,q)$ follows the stored convention, $p$ generators of square $1$), blades $e_{S}$ a basis. As in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, $x \mapsto x^{\dagger}$ is the linear extension of the inverse on blades, an \emph{observable} is an $x$ with $x^{\dagger} = x$ and $x^{2} = 1$, a \emph{configuration} is four observables $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{1}, B_{2}$ with $A_{i}B_{j} = B_{j}A_{i}$ for all $i, j$, and $C = A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2}) + A_{2}(B_{1} - B_{2})$. No subsystem structure is assumed: the two parties are any two commuting pairs inside the one algebra. The adjoint is defined by the chosen generators. In definite signature it does not depend on the orthonormal frame; in indefinite signature it depends on the split into generators of square $1$ and of square $-1$, so observables, states and (P) are relative to that split, and each statement holds for every fixed split. The list below does not depend on the frame: a change of frame is an automorphism carrying the configurations for one adjoint to the configurations for the other.

\emph{Hypothesis (P), positivity of values:} values are given by a \emph{state}, a $k$-linear $\omega : \Cl_{k}(p,q) \to k$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$; (P) is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}, assumed, not derived.

(P) extends the stored definition of a state as an element $\rho = \sum_{r}x_{r}x_{r}^{\dagger}$ of unit trace from elements to functionals.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Excluded signatures; proved; the value bound under (P).)} Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the following fourteen signatures: the nine with $1 \le n \le 3$, and $(4,0)$, $(1,3)$, $(0,4)$, $(5,0)$, $(1,4)$. For $(p,q) \in \mathcal{E}$ every configuration has $[A_{1},A_{2}][B_{1},B_{2}] = 0$, so $C^{2} = 4$ and, under (P), $\omega(C)^{2} \le 4$ for every state (clauses (i) and (iii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}). The reason: the self-adjoint elements are $s + v$ ($s$ a scalar, $v$ in the span $V$ of a set of at most five anticommuting blades of square $1$), or two such blocks cut out by a central self-adjoint pseudoscalar $J$ with $J^{2} = 1$ (signatures $(1,0)$, $(2,1)$, $(0,3)$, $(5,0)$, $(1,4)$); in each block the observables are $\pm 1$ and the unit vectors of $V$, and two unit vectors of $V$ commute only if they are equal or opposite. In $\Cl(4,0)$ the frame is $e_{1}, \dots, e_{4}$ and the pseudoscalar; in $\Cl(1,3)$ it is $e_{1}$, $e_{1}e_{2}$, $e_{1}e_{3}$, $e_{1}e_{4}$ and $e_{2}e_{3}e_{4}$; in $\Cl(3,0)$ it is $e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(All other signatures; proved; values under (P).)} For $n \ge 1$ and $(p,q) \notin \mathcal{E}$ there is a configuration of blades with $A_{1}A_{2} = -A_{2}A_{1}$ and $B_{1}B_{2} = -B_{2}B_{1}$. By the blade lemma, clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, $C^{2} = 4 + 4K$ with $K = -A_{1}A_{2}B_{1}B_{2}$ a non-scalar blade of square $1$, and the functionals $\omega_{r}(x) = \langle(1 + K)(1 + rC)x\rangle_{0}$, $8r^{2} \le 1$, satisfy (P) with $\omega_{r}(C) = 8r$: over $\Q$ every rational $v$ with $v^{2} < 8$ is a value, with supremum $2\sqrt{2}$ not attained, and $2\sqrt{2}$ is attained over an ordered field containing $\sqrt{2}$. In signature $(3,1)$: $A_{1} = e_{1}$, $A_{2} = e_{2}$, $B_{1} = e_{3}e_{4}$, $B_{2} = e_{1}e_{2}e_{4}$; in $(2,2)$: $A_{1} = e_{1}$, $A_{2} = e_{2}$, $B_{1} = e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}$, $B_{2} = e_{1}e_{2}e_{4}$; the thirteen signatures with $4 \le n \le 6$ are tabulated in the check, and $n \ge 7$ follows by restriction to six generators.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(Reading; proved from Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}.)} $\mathcal{E}$ is exactly the set of signatures with $n \ge 1$ in which the real Clifford algebra is a matrix algebra of size at most $2$ over $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$, or a sum of two such ($(0,0)$ is left out only by $n \ge 1$). In particular one copy of the algebra of space $\Cl(3,0)$, or of the spacetime algebra in signature $(1,3)$, carries no configuration with value above $2$, while signature $(3,1)$ and the split signature $(2,2)$ do; with four directions these two are the only ones. This concerns two commuting pairs inside ONE copy of the algebra with real or rational coefficients. It says nothing against Bell violations for two systems each described by the spacetime algebra: two such systems live in a larger algebra (two commuting copies, or more generators), which is outside $\mathcal{E}$. It also depends on the coefficients: adjoining a unit that commutes with $\Cl(1,3)$ gives $\Cl(4,1)$, of matrix size $4$, which is outside $\mathcal{E}$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.signatures-in-which-commuting-.technical: Whether two commuting pairs of observables inside one Clifford algebra can have a CHSH value above $2$ depends on the signature, which the premise of minimal non-commutativity leaves free. Observables are self-adjoint elements of square one for the adjoint that sends a blade to its inverse; values are taken under Hypothesis (P), positivity of values (values are given by a state, a linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$; (P) is assumed, not derived). In fourteen signatures (the nine with one to three directions, and $(4,0)$, $(1,3)$, $(0,4)$, $(5,0)$, $(1,4)$) the observables are, block by block, the unit vectors of one anticommuting frame, two of them commute only when parallel, so one of the two commutators in the stored identity for $C^{2}$ always vanishes: $C^{2} = 4$, and under (P) the value never exceeds $2$. In every other signature there is a blade configuration to which the stored blade lemma applies, giving under (P) every rational value of square below $8$. The excluded signatures are those of matrix size at most two in the stored classification. The adjoint depends, in indefinite signature, on the split into positive and negative generators; the list does not. The statement is about two commuting pairs inside ONE copy of the algebra with real or rational coefficients: it says nothing against Bell violations for two systems each described by the spacetime algebra, which live in a larger algebra outside the list, and adjoining a unit that commutes with $\Cl(1,3)$ gives $\Cl(4,1)$, of matrix size $4$, also outside the list. Classical mathematics; the complete list and the elementary proof by blades are what is recorded.
synthesis.signatures-in-which-commuting-.lay: The quantum limit on correlations between two parties, $2\sqrt{2}$ where everyday reasoning allows only $2$, needs room: each party must have two measurements that do not commute with each other but do commute with the other party's. This result asks in which single algebras of directions that room exists, when the numbers used are ordinary real or rational numbers, and when average values are assumed to be non-negative on squares (Hypothesis (P), an assumption, not something derived). The answer depends on how many directions square to plus one and how many to minus one. With three or fewer directions there is never room, and with four directions there is room in only two of the five cases. For the spacetime algebra with one plus and three minus signs: inside a single copy of that algebra there are not two independent pairs of such measurements; this is a statement about the size of one algebra, not about experiments in spacetime. Two systems, each described by such an algebra, live in a larger algebra, where there is room. The mathematics is classical; what is recorded is the exact list and a short proof inside the algebra.

proofs.main:
\emph{Premise.} Hypothesis (P) of the statement is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}; every statement below about the values of states is under it, relative to the fixed split of the generators.

\emph{Preliminaries.} By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} the algebra is free on the blades $e_{S}$, the images of the elements of the group $G$ of signed directions, and each blade is invertible with $e_{S}^{-1} = \pm e_{S}$. Inversion is an anti-automorphism of $G$ fixing the sign bit, so its linear extension $\dagger$ is an anti-automorphism of the algebra with $x^{\dagger\dagger} = x$. Since $e_{S}e_{T}^{\dagger} = \pm e_{S \triangle T}$ is a scalar only for $S = T$, where it is $1$, $\langle xy^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \sum_{S}x_{S}y_{S}$; this form is symmetric and $\langle xx^{\dagger}\rangle_{0} = \sum x_{S}^{2} \ge 0$. A self-adjoint blade satisfies $e_{S} = e_{S}^{\dagger} = e_{S}^{-1}$, so it has square $1$. Two blades commute or anticommute (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}(ii)). The adjoint, observables, configurations and (P) are those of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}.

\emph{(i).} \emph{The frame.} For each $(p,q) \in \mathcal{E}$ the self-adjoint blades are enumerated (the check does this for all fourteen): they are $1$, a set $F$ of pairwise anticommuting blades, and, in the five signatures named, the pseudoscalar $J$ (central, $J^{\dagger} = J$, $J^{2} = 1$) and the blades $Jh$, $h \in F$. Moreover the products $hk$ ($h \ne k$ in $F$, one for each unordered pair) are blades distinct from each other and from $1$ and the elements of $F$, also after multiplication by $J$. The sizes of $F$ are $0, 0$; $2, 2, 0$; $3, 2, 3, 0$; $5, 5, 5$; $5, 5$ in the order $(1,0), (0,1)$; $(2,0), (1,1), (0,2)$; $(3,0), (2,1), (1,2), (0,3)$; $(4,0), (1,3), (0,4)$; $(5,0), (1,4)$.

\emph{Blocks.} Without $J$ put $P = 1$. With $J$, the elements $P_{\pm} = \tfrac12(1 \pm J)$ are central self-adjoint idempotents with $P_{+} + P_{-} = 1$, $P_{+}P_{-} = 0$, and every statement below is made in the algebra $P_{\pm}\Cl(p,q)$ with unit $P_{\pm}$, where $Jh = \pm h$. In a block $P$, a self-adjoint element is $P(s + v)$ with $s$ a scalar and $v = \sum_{h \in F}v_{h}h$, uniquely; and since the $h$ anticommute and have square $1$, $v^{2} = Q(v) := \sum v_{h}^{2}$ and $vv' - v'v = 2\sum_{h < k}(v_{h}v'_{k} - v_{k}v'_{h})hk$.

\emph{Observables of a block.} $(s + v)^{2} = s^{2} + Q(v) + 2sv$. If this is $1$ in the block then $sv = 0$ (the blades of $F$ are independent of $1$ in the block), so either $v = 0$ and $s = \pm 1$, or $s = 0$ and $Q(v) = 1$. If two observables $v, v'$ with $s = s' = 0$ commute, then all $v_{h}v'_{k} - v_{k}v'_{h}$ vanish (the products $hk$ are independent in the block), so $v$ and $v'$ are proportional, and $Q(v) = Q(v') = 1$ gives $v' = \pm v$.

\emph{Conclusion.} Fix a block and suppose the components of $A_{1}, A_{2}$ in it do not commute. Then both have $s = 0$ and their vectors $v_{1}, v_{2}$ are not proportional. The component of $B_{j}$ commutes with both; if it had $s = 0$ its vector would be $\pm v_{1}$ and $\pm v_{2}$, which is impossible, so it is $\pm P$. Hence the components of $B_{1}, B_{2}$ commute. In every block one of the two commutators vanishes, so $[A_{1},A_{2}][B_{1},B_{2}] = 0$; then $C^{2} = 4$ by clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate} and, under (P), $\omega(C)^{2} \le \omega(C^{2}) = 4$ by its clause (iii). \emph{Frames.} If $\alpha$ is an automorphism of the algebra carrying one orthonormal frame to another, the adjoint of the second frame is $\alpha \circ \dagger \circ \alpha^{-1}$, and $\alpha$ carries observables and configurations for the first adjoint to those for the second and preserves $[A_{1},A_{2}][B_{1},B_{2}] = 0$; so the statement holds for every frame.

\emph{(ii).} For the thirteen signatures with $4 \le n \le 6$ outside $\mathcal{E}$ the check lists four self-adjoint blades with $A_{1}A_{2} = -A_{2}A_{1}$, $B_{1}B_{2} = -B_{2}B_{1}$ and $A_{i}B_{j} = B_{j}A_{i}$. For $n \ge 7$ choose six of the generators; the subalgebra they generate is $\Cl(p',q')$ with $p' + q' = 6$, which is not in $\mathcal{E}$, its blades are blades of $\Cl(p,q)$ with the same inverses, and so the configuration is a configuration of blades of $\Cl(p,q)$. Every signature with $n \ge 4$ outside the five listed is covered.

The rest of the clause is the blade lemma, clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, applied to this configuration in $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$: it gives $C^{2} = 4 + 4K$, the functionals $\omega_{r}$, that they satisfy (P) exactly when $8r^{2} \le 1$, and their values $8r$.

\emph{(iii).} By Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras} $\Cl(p,q)$ is $\Mat_{k}(D)$ or a sum of two copies, $D$ one of $\R$, $\C$, $\HH$ according to $p - q \bmod 8$, with $k^{2}\dim D$ (times $2$ for a sum) equal to $2^{n}$. Computing $k$ from the table for each signature gives $k \le 2$ exactly on $\mathcal{E}$ for $n \le 6$ (the check does this up to $n = 8$), and $k \ge 4$ for $n \ge 7$ since $k^{2} \ge 2^{n}/8$. The named cases: $\Cl(3,0) = \Mat_{2}(\C)$, $\Cl(1,3) = \Mat_{2}(\HH)$, $\Cl(3,1) = \Cl(2,2) = \Mat_{4}(\R)$. The label $(p,q)$ is that of the stored theorem ($p$ generators of square $1$). Two commuting copies of $\Cl(1,3)$, or $\Cl(1,3)$ with a further unit commuting with it (which is $\Cl(4,1) = \Mat_{4}(\C)$ by the same table), are algebras outside $\mathcal{E}$, to which (ii) applies.

synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-inte.formal:
Let $n \ge 1$. A \emph{group of signed directions} is a group $G$ with elements $e_{1}, \dots, e_{n}$ and $c$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(F2)] $c$ is central; $G/\langle c\rangle$ is elementary abelian of order $2^{n}$ with basis the images of $e_{1}, \dots, e_{n}$, so that $S \mapsto e_{S}\langle c\rangle$ identifies $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ (subsets of $\{1, \dots, n\}$ under symmetric difference $S \triangle T$) with $G/\langle c\rangle$, where $e_{S}$ is the increasing product of the $e_{i}$, $i \in S$; distinct directions do not commute, $c \ne 1$ and $e_{i}e_{j} = c\,e_{j}e_{i}$ for $i \ne j$; and $c^{2} = 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $e_{i}^{2} \in \langle c\rangle$; write $e_{i}^{2} = c^{s_{i}}$ with $s_{i} \in \{0, 1\}$, $N = \{i : s_{i} = 1\}$, $q = |N|$, $p = n - q$, and $Q(x) = \sum_{i \notin N} x_{i}^{2} - \sum_{i \in N} x_{i}^{2}$. Let
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(F3)] $A = \Z[G]/(c + 1)$, the integral group ring of $G$ modulo the two-sided ideal generated by $c + 1$.
\end{enumerate}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The sign.)} For $n \ge 2$ the clause $c^{2} = 1$ follows from the others; for $n = 1$ it is independent of them: the cyclic group of order $2m$ generated by $e_{1}$, with $c = e_{1}^{2}$, satisfies the other clauses for every $m \ge 2$ and has $c^{2} = 1$ only for $m = 2$. For every sign vector $(s_{1}, \dots, s_{n})$ a group of signed directions exists: $\{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ with $(a, S)(b, T) = (a + b + f(S,T) \bmod 2,\ S \triangle T)$, $f$ as in (ii), $c = (1, \emptyset)$, $e_{i} = (0, \{i\})$; it is unique up to an isomorphism fixing $c$ and the $e_{i}$. Every element of $G$ is $c^{a}e_{S}$ for exactly one $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and $S$, so $|G| = 2^{n+1}$, and $G$ is presented by the generators $e_{1}, \dots, e_{n}, c$ and the relations: $c$ central, $c^{2} = 1$, $e_{i}^{2} = c^{s_{i}}$, $e_{i}e_{j} = c\,e_{j}e_{i}$ ($i \ne j$).
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Squares and commutators.)} $e_{S}e_{T} = c^{f(S,T)}e_{S \triangle T}$ with $f(S,T) = |\{(i, j) \in S \times T : i > j\}| + |S \cap T \cap N|$. Every square and every commutator of $G$ lies in $\{1, c\}$; for $g \in \{e_{S}, c\,e_{S}\}$ and $h \in \{e_{T}, c\,e_{T}\}$, $g^{2} = c^{q(S)}$ and $gh = c^{b(S,T)}hg$ with
\[
q(S) = \binom{|S|}{2} + |S \cap N|, \qquad b(S,T) = |S|\,|T| + |S \cap T| \pmod 2,
\]
a quadratic form over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ and its polar form (the same forms as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}). For $n \ge 2$, $c$ is the only element other than $1$ that is a square or a commutator.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The centre.)} The radical of $b$ is $\{\emptyset\}$ for $n$ even and $\{\emptyset, \{1, \dots, n\}\}$ for $n$ odd, and the centre of $G$ is $\{1, c\}$ for $n$ even and $\{1, c, e_{1 \cdots n}, c\,e_{1 \cdots n}\}$ for $n$ odd, $e_{1 \cdots n} = e_{1}e_{2}\cdots e_{n}$. So for $n$ even the centre, the commutator subgroup and the subgroup generated by the squares coincide and have order $2$: $G$ is an extraspecial $2$-group of order $2^{1+n}$. The element $c$ is the only central element of order $2$ when $n$ is even or $e_{1 \cdots n}^{2} = c$; when $n$ is odd and $e_{1 \cdots n}^{2} = 1$ (exactly when $p - q \equiv 1 \bmod 4$), $e_{1 \cdots n}$ and $c\,e_{1 \cdots n}$ are central of order $2$ as well.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The groups are classified by $q$.)} Two groups of signed directions with the same $n$ are isomorphic by an isomorphism carrying $c$ to $c'$ if and only if their forms are equivalent, $q' \circ \phi = q$ for a linear bijection $\phi$ of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$. For $n \ge 2$ every isomorphism carries $c$ to $c'$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(The integer algebra.)} The ideal $(c + 1)$ is $\bigoplus_{S}\Z\,(1 + c)e_{S}$, and $A$ is a free $\Z$-module with basis the images of the $e_{S}$, written $e_{S}$ again; $c$ maps to $-1$ and $e_{S}e_{T} = (-1)^{f(S,T)}e_{S \triangle T}$, so $A$ has rank $2^{n}$ and integral structure constants.
\item[(vi)] \emph{(The contraction rule as a theorem.)} For $v = \sum_{i} a_{i}e_{i}$ with $a_{i} \in \Z$, $v^{2} = \sum_{i} a_{i}^{2}e_{i}^{2} = Q(v)$.
\item[(vii)] \emph{(The universal property.)} Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $A_{R} = R \otimes_{\Z} A = R[G]/(c + 1)$, free over $R$ with basis the $e_{S}$, and $\iota : R^{n} \to A_{R}$, $x \mapsto \sum_{i} x_{i}e_{i}$. For every associative unital $R$-algebra $B$ and $R$-linear $f : R^{n} \to B$ with $f(x)^{2} = Q(x)\,1$ for all $x$, there is exactly one unital $R$-algebra homomorphism $F : A_{R} \to B$ with $F \circ \iota = f$. So $(A_{R}, \iota)$ is the Clifford algebra $\Cl_{R}(p,q)$ of the quadratic module $(R^{n}, Q)$, isomorphic to the tensor algebra of $R^{n}$ modulo $x \otimes x - Q(x)$, with $\iota$ injective and the blade basis over every $R$; $A = \Cl_{\Z}(p,q)$; and for $R = \R$, $(A_{\R}, \iota)$ is the Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ of Definition \claimref{obj.std-algebra.clifford-algebra}, the $e_{S}$ its blades. If $2 = 0$ in $R$, $A_{R}$ is the commutative group algebra $R[\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}]$ of the configurations.
\item[(viii)] \emph{(Isomorphism classes.)} For signatures $(p,q)$ and $(p',q')$ with $p + q = p' + q' = n$ the following are equivalent: (a) $q_{(p,q)}$ and $q_{(p',q')}$ are equivalent over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$; (b) their groups of signed directions are isomorphic by an isomorphism carrying $c$ to $c'$; (c) $\Cl_{R}(p,q) \cong \Cl_{R}(p',q')$ for every commutative ring $R$; (d) $\Cl_{R}(p,q) \cong \Cl_{R}(p',q')$ as $R$-algebras for one commutative ring $R$ that maps unitally to an ordered field ($\Z$, $\Q$ and $\R$ among them); (e) the Gauss sums $\sum_{S}(-1)^{q(S)}$ agree. With $j = e_{1}$ in $\Cl_{\Z}(0,1)$, $\sum_{S}(-1)^{q(S)} = \langle (1 - j)(1 + j)^{p}(1 - j)^{q}\rangle_{0}$, which is $2^{n/2}$, $-2^{n/2}$, $2^{(n+1)/2}$, $-2^{(n+1)/2}$, $0$ for $p - q$ congruent modulo $8$ to $0$ or $2$, $4$ or $6$, $1$, $5$, $3$ or $7$ (the values of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}); so (e) holds exactly when $p - q$ and $p' - q'$ lie in the same one of these classes. The Gauss sum is the signature of the trace form $(x, y) \mapsto 2^{-n}\Tr(L_{xy}) = \langle xy\rangle_{0}$ ($L_{z}$ left multiplication), which is diagonal on the blades with entries $e_{S}^{2}$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-inte.technical:
Take a group generated by $n$ directions and one central bit $c \ne 1$ such that dividing out the bit leaves the configurations $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$, with any two distinct directions commuting up to $c$. Reading the relation for a pair both ways forces $c^{2} = 1$ once there are two directions; with one direction the order of $c$ is a separate choice. The group then has $2^{n+1}$ elements $\pm e_{S}$, every square and commutator is $1$ or $c$, and the squaring map is the quadratic form over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ already stored for the blades, with polar form the commutator form. For even $n$ the centre is just $\{1, c\}$, which makes the group extraspecial; for odd $n$ the volume element joins the centre, and it is a second central involution when it squares to $1$, so $c$ is singled out as the commutator bit rather than as the only central involution. Groups of this kind are classified by their quadratic forms.

Adding integer superpositions with $c$ acting as $-1$, the ring $\Z[G]/(c + 1)$ is free of rank $2^{n}$ on the blades, and the cross terms of a vector's square cancel because $e_{i}e_{j} + e_{j}e_{i} = (c + 1)e_{j}e_{i}$ maps to $0$: the rule $v^{2} = Q(v)$, usually the defining axiom, is a theorem, and no division by $2$ is needed. The ring has the universal property of the Clifford algebra of the diagonal form $\langle \pm 1, \dots, \pm 1\rangle$ over the integers and, after extending the coefficients, over every commutative ring, so it is $\Cl_{\Z}(p,q)$ and over the reals it is the store's $\Cl(p,q)$; in characteristic $2$ the sign is invisible and the algebra collapses to the commutative group algebra of the configurations. Two signatures of the same dimension give isomorphic algebras, over the integers, the rationals or the reals alike, exactly when their quadratic forms over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ are equivalent, and that happens exactly when the Gauss sums agree, the Gauss sum being the signature of the algebra's trace form.
synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-inte.lay: Start with a handful of independent yes-or-no distinctions and allow them to depend on the order in which they are made, by the smallest possible amount: one extra bit that flips when two distinctions are swapped. That bit has to behave like a minus sign, and every combination of distinctions then squares to plus or minus one. Allowing whole-number combinations of these distinctions produces, with no further assumption, the whole-number form of the algebra of directions used throughout the series, which becomes that algebra once the coefficients are extended, with the rule that a direction times itself gives its squared length coming out as a consequence rather than being assumed. Which version of the algebra one gets is decided entirely by a yes-or-no table of the signs.

proofs.main:
\emph{(i)} For $n \ge 2$ the relation for the pair $(1, 2)$ and the relation for the pair $(2, 1)$ give $e_{1}e_{2} = c\,e_{2}e_{1} = c^{2}e_{1}e_{2}$, so $c^{2} = 1$ by cancellation in $G$ (the same argument as the sign from symmetry, clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}, read in the group). For $n = 1$ there is no pair. In the cyclic group of order $2m$ generated by $e_{1}$, with $m \ge 2$ and $c = e_{1}^{2}$, the element $c$ is central and $\ne 1$, $G/\langle c\rangle = \{\langle c\rangle, e_{1}\langle c\rangle\}$ has order $2$ with basis the image of $e_{1}$, and $c$ has order $m$, so $c^{2} = 1$ exactly when $m = 2$. Existence: $f(S,T) = \sum_{i > j}x_{i}y_{j} + \sum_{i}s_{i}x_{i}y_{i}$, with $x, y \in \mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ the indicator vectors of $S, T$, is $\mathbb{F}_{2}$-bilinear. So on $\{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ the product $(a, S)(b, T) = (a + b + f(S,T), S \triangle T)$ (first entry modulo $2$) is associative, both triple products being $(a + b + d + f(S,T) + f(S,U) + f(T,U), S \triangle T \triangle U)$ for a third factor $(d, U)$; $(0, \emptyset)$ is the identity, as $f$ vanishes when either argument is $\emptyset$; and $(a + f(S,S), S)$ is the inverse of $(a, S)$. Put $c = (1, \emptyset)$, $e_{i} = (0, \{i\})$. Then $c$ is central with $c^{2} = 1 \ne c$; $e_{i}^{2} = (f(\{i\}, \{i\}), \emptyset) = c^{s_{i}}$; for $i \ne j$ the products $e_{i}e_{j}$ and $e_{j}e_{i}$ are $(f(\{i\},\{j\}), \{i, j\})$ and $(f(\{j\},\{i\}), \{i, j\})$, whose first entries add to $1$, so $e_{i}e_{j} = c\,e_{j}e_{i}$; and since $f(S, \{j\}) = 0$ when $j$ exceeds every element of $S$, the increasing product $e_{S}$ is $(0, S)$, so $(a, S) \mapsto S$ identifies the quotient by $\langle c\rangle$ with $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$, the $e_{i}$ mapping to the basis. This is a group of signed directions with the given signs; uniqueness up to an isomorphism fixing $c$ and the $e_{i}$ follows from the presentation below. Granting $c^{2} = 1$ and $c \ne 1$, $\langle c\rangle = \{1, c\}$; each coset of $\langle c\rangle$ is $e_{S}\langle c\rangle$ for exactly one $S$, so each element is $c^{a}e_{S}$ for exactly one $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and one $S$, and $|G| = 2^{n+1}$. The image of $e_{i}^{2}$ in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ is $\{i\} \triangle \{i\} = \emptyset$, so $e_{i}^{2} \in \{1, c\}$. Let $\Gamma$ be the group presented by the generators and relations of the statement. In $\Gamma$, $c^{-1} = c$ and $e_{i}^{-1} = c^{s_{i}}e_{i}$, so every element is a word in $c, e_{1}, \dots, e_{n}$ without inverses, and the rewriting of (ii), which uses only the relations, brings it to the form $c^{a}e_{S}$; hence $|\Gamma| \le 2^{n+1}$. The elements $e_{i}$ and $c$ of $G$ satisfy the relations and generate $G$, so the homomorphism $\Gamma \to G$ sending generators to generators is onto, and since $|G| = 2^{n+1} \ge |\Gamma|$ it is an isomorphism.

\emph{(ii)} In the word $e_{S}e_{T} = e_{i_{1}}\cdots e_{i_{k}}e_{j_{1}}\cdots e_{j_{l}}$ ($i_{1} < \dots < i_{k}$, $j_{1} < \dots < j_{l}$) move $e_{j_{1}}, e_{j_{2}}, \dots$ in turn to the left until they reach their place in increasing order. The letter $e_{j}$ passes exactly the letters $e_{i}$ of $e_{S}$ with $i > j$, each passage costing a factor $c$ (the relation, with $c$ central), and if $j \in S$ it then meets $e_{j}$ and the two merge into $e_{j}^{2} = c^{s_{j}}$; it never meets a letter of $e_{T}$ already placed, those being smaller. Collecting the central factors gives $e_{S}e_{T} = c^{f(S,T)}e_{S \triangle T}$, the sign rule of the blade product of an orthogonal basis, with $c$ in place of $-1$. Since $G/\langle c\rangle$ is elementary abelian, every square $g^{2}$ and every commutator $ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$ maps to $0$ and lies in $\langle c\rangle = \{1, c\}$, which is central. For $g = c^{a}e_{S}$, $g^{2} = c^{2a}e_{S}^{2} = c^{f(S,S)}$, and $f(S,S) = \binom{|S|}{2} + |S \cap N|$, the pairs $(i, j) \in S \times S$ with $i > j$ being the $\binom{|S|}{2}$ two-element subsets of $S$. Also $e_{T}e_{S} = c^{f(T,S)}e_{S \triangle T}$, so, as $c^{-1} = c$, $e_{S}e_{T} = c^{f(S,T) + f(T,S)}e_{T}e_{S}$, and $f(S,T) + f(T,S)$ counts the ordered pairs $(i, j) \in S \times T$ with $i \ne j$, plus $2|S \cap T \cap N|$: it is $|S|\,|T| - |S \cap T| \equiv |S|\,|T| + |S \cap T| = b(S,T) \bmod 2$. The central factors $c^{a}$ do not change squares or commutators. From $hg = c^{b(S,T)}gh$, $(gh)^{2} = g(hg)h = c^{b(S,T)}g^{2}h^{2}$, so $q(S \triangle T) = q(S) + q(T) + b(S,T)$: $q$ is a quadratic form over $\mathbb{F}_{2}$ with polar form $b = f + f^{\top}$, which is bilinear because $f$ is; these are the same forms as in clause (ii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form} (there with the negative directions numbered last; the formulas do not depend on the numbering). For $n \ge 2$, $e_{1}e_{2}e_{1}^{-1}e_{2}^{-1} = c$ is a commutator. It is also a square: if $s_{i} = s_{j}$ for some $i \ne j$, then $(e_{i}e_{j})^{2} = c^{q(\{i, j\})} = c^{1 + s_{i} + s_{j}} = c$; otherwise $n = 2$ and $\{s_{1}, s_{2}\} = \{0, 1\}$, and $e_{i}^{2} = c$ for the $i$ with $s_{i} = 1$.

\emph{(iii)} An element $c^{a}e_{S}$ is central exactly when it commutes with every $e_{i}$, since the $e_{i}$ and $c$ generate $G$, that is, when $b(S, \{i\}) = 0$ for every $i$: when $S$ lies in the radical of $b$. Here $b(S, \{i\}) = |S| + [i \in S]$. If $S$ is neither empty nor $\{1, \dots, n\}$, taking $i \in S$ and $i' \notin S$ gives $|S| \equiv 1$ and $|S| \equiv 0$, which is impossible; $\emptyset$ is always in the radical, and $\{1, \dots, n\}$ is exactly when $n + 1 \equiv 0$, that is $n$ odd. So the radical is $\{\emptyset\}$ for $n$ even and $\{\emptyset, \{1, \dots, n\}\}$ for $n$ odd (as in clause (iii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}), which gives the centre. For $n$ even, the centre, the commutators and the squares are all $\{1, c\}$ by (ii) ($n \ge 2$), so the subgroup they generate is $\{1, c\}$ as well, and $G$ is extraspecial of order $2^{1+n}$ (for a finite $2$-group the subgroup generated by squares and commutators is the Frattini subgroup). Central elements of order $2$: $c$, and for $n$ odd $c^{a}e_{1 \cdots n}$ exactly when $(c^{a}e_{1 \cdots n})^{2} = c^{q(\{1, \dots, n\})} = 1$. Here $q(\{1, \dots, n\}) = \binom{n}{2} + q$, and for $n = p + q$ odd, $\binom{n}{2} + q$ is even exactly when $p - q \equiv 1 \bmod 4$: writing $p - q = n - 2q$, both conditions are unchanged when $q$ grows by $2$ and both flip when $q$ grows by $1$ (since $n - 2q$ then drops by $2$), and for $q = 0$ the first reads $n \equiv 1 \bmod 4$, which is the second.

\emph{(iv)} Let $\Phi : G \to G'$ be an isomorphism with $\Phi(c) = c'$. It induces a group isomorphism $\phi : G/\langle c\rangle \to G'/\langle c'\rangle$, that is, a linear bijection of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$, and $\Phi(g)^{2} = \Phi(g^{2})$ reads $c'^{\,q'(\phi(S))} = c'^{\,q(S)}$, so $q' \circ \phi = q$. Conversely, let $q' \circ \phi = q$. Then also $b' \circ (\phi \times \phi) = b$, $b$ being the polar form of $q$. Choose $g_{i} \in G'$ over $\phi(\{i\})$. By (ii) for $G'$, $g_{i}^{2} = c'^{\,q'(\phi(\{i\}))} = c'^{\,s_{i}}$ and $g_{i}g_{j} = c'^{\,b(\{i\}, \{j\})}g_{j}g_{i} = c'\,g_{j}g_{i}$ for $i \ne j$, and $c'$ is central with $c'^{2} = 1$. By the presentation of (i) there is a homomorphism $\Phi : G \to G'$ with $\Phi(e_{i}) = g_{i}$ and $\Phi(c) = c'$; its image contains $c'$ and elements over the basis $\phi(\{1\}), \dots, \phi(\{n\})$, hence every coset of $\langle c'\rangle$ and all of $G'$; so $\Phi$ is onto, and an isomorphism because $|G| = |G'| = 2^{n+1}$. For $n \ge 2$, $c$ is the only commutator other than $1$ in $G$ and $c'$ in $G'$, and isomorphisms carry commutators to commutators.

\emph{(v)} $\Z[G]$ is free on the $2^{n+1}$ elements $c^{a}e_{S}$. As $c$ is central, the two-sided ideal generated by $c + 1$ is $(c + 1)\Z[G]$, which is spanned over $\Z$ by the $(c + 1)c^{a}e_{S}$; since $c(c + 1) = c + c^{2} = c + 1$, these are the $(1 + c)e_{S}$. So $\Z[G] = \bigoplus_{S}(\Z e_{S} \oplus \Z\,c\,e_{S})$ and $(c + 1) = \bigoplus_{S}\Z(e_{S} + c\,e_{S})$; in each summand $e_{S}$ and $e_{S} + c\,e_{S}$ form a $\Z$-basis (the change of basis from $e_{S}, c\,e_{S}$ has determinant $1$), so $A = \bigoplus_{S}\Z e_{S}$, free with basis the images of the $e_{S}$, with $c\,e_{S} \mapsto -e_{S}$. The product follows from (ii).

\emph{(vi)} $v^{2} = \sum_{i}a_{i}^{2}e_{i}^{2} + \sum_{i < j}a_{i}a_{j}(e_{i}e_{j} + e_{j}e_{i})$, and $e_{i}e_{j} + e_{j}e_{i} = (c + 1)e_{j}e_{i}$ maps to $0$ in $A$, while $e_{i}^{2} = c^{s_{i}}$ maps to $(-1)^{s_{i}}$. So $v^{2} = \sum_{i}(-1)^{s_{i}}a_{i}^{2} = Q(v)$; no element $\tfrac12$ is used.

\emph{(vii)} Tensoring the exact sequence $(c + 1) \to \Z[G] \to A \to 0$ with $R$ gives $A_{R} = R[G]/(c + 1)$, free over $R$ on the $1 \otimes e_{S}$, which are products of the $\iota(\epsilon_{i}) = e_{i}$ ($\epsilon_{i}$ the standard basis of $R^{n}$). Uniqueness: $A_{R}$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by $\iota(R^{n})$. Existence: put $u_{i} = f(\epsilon_{i})$. Then $u_{i}^{2} = Q(\epsilon_{i})\,1 = (-1)^{s_{i}}$, and for $i \ne j$, $(u_{i} + u_{j})^{2} = Q(\epsilon_{i} + \epsilon_{j}) = (-1)^{s_{i}} + (-1)^{s_{j}}$ gives $u_{i}u_{j} + u_{j}u_{i} = 0$. Each $u_{i}$ is a unit, with inverse $(-1)^{s_{i}}u_{i}$, and in the unit group of $B$ the elements $u_{1}, \dots, u_{n}$ and $-1$ satisfy the relations of the presentation in (i): $-1$ is central with square $1$, $u_{i}^{2} = (-1)^{s_{i}}$, $u_{i}u_{j} = (-1)u_{j}u_{i}$. So there is a group homomorphism $\psi : G \to B^{\times}$ with $\psi(e_{i}) = u_{i}$ and $\psi(c) = -1$; its $R$-linear extension $R[G] \to B$ is a unital algebra homomorphism that kills $c + 1$, hence factors through $A_{R}$ as $F$, and $F(\iota(x)) = \sum_{i}x_{i}u_{i} = f(x)$. The tensor algebra of $R^{n}$ modulo the ideal generated by the $x \otimes x - Q(x)$ has the same universal property (that of the tensor algebra, passed to the quotient), so the two are isomorphic by the unique isomorphism compatible with the maps from $R^{n}$; $\iota$ is injective because the $e_{i}$ are part of an $R$-basis. For $R = \R$ the universal property is that of Definition \claimref{obj.std-algebra.clifford-algebra} for $\R^{n}$ with the form $Q$ of signature $(p, q)$. If $2 = 0$ in $R$ then $-1 = 1$, so $e_{S}e_{T} = e_{S \triangle T}$, which is the multiplication of the group algebra of $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$.

\emph{(viii)} (a) $\Leftrightarrow$ (b) is (iv). (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c): an isomorphism $G \to G'$ carrying $c$ to $c'$ extends to $R[G] \cong R[G']$ carrying $c + 1$ to $c' + 1$. (c) $\Rightarrow$ (d) with $R = \Z$. (d) $\Rightarrow$ (e): let $R \to K$ be a unital homomorphism to an ordered field; then $K \otimes_{R} A_{R} = A_{K}$, so an isomorphism over $R$ gives one over $K$. On $A_{K}$ put $\tau(x, y) = 2^{-n}\Tr(L_{xy})$, the trace of left multiplication on the $K$-vector space $A_{K}$. An algebra isomorphism $\Phi$ satisfies $L_{\Phi(z)} = \Phi L_{z}\Phi^{-1}$, so $\tau$ is carried to $\tau'$. Since $e_{S}e_{T} = \pm e_{S \triangle T}$, $L_{e_{S}}$ maps each basis line to a different one unless $S = \emptyset$, so $\Tr(L_{e_{S}}) = 2^{n}$ for $S = \emptyset$ and $0$ otherwise; hence $\tau(x, y) = \langle xy\rangle_{0}$, $\tau(e_{S}, e_{T}) = 0$ for $S \ne T$, and $\tau(e_{S}, e_{S}) = (-1)^{q(S)}$. Let $P$ be the number of $S$ with $q(S) = 0$ and $U_{\pm}$ the spans of the blades with $e_{S}^{2} = \pm 1$. On $U_{+}$, $\tau(x, x) = \sum x_{S}^{2} > 0$ for $x \ne 0$, and on $U_{-}$, $\tau(x, x) = -\sum x_{S}^{2} < 0$ for $x \ne 0$; a subspace $W$ with $\dim W > P$ meets $U_{-}$ in a nonzero vector, as $\dim W + \dim U_{-} > 2^{n}$. So $P$ is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $\tau$ is positive definite, an isomorphism invariant, and with it the Gauss sum $\sum_{S}(-1)^{q(S)} = 2P - 2^{n}$. (e) $\Rightarrow$ (a): all the forms $q_{(p,q)}$ with the same $n$ have the same polar form $b$, whose radical is $\{0\}$ for $n$ even and $\{0, z\}$, $z = \{1, \dots, n\}$, for $n$ odd. Let $W$ be a complement of the radical ($W = \mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}$ for $n$ even); $b$ is alternating ($b(x, x) = q(0) = 0$) and nondegenerate on $W$, so $W$ has a basis $u_{1}, w_{1}, \dots, u_{m}, w_{m}$ with $b(u_{k}, w_{k}) = 1$ and $b = 0$ on all other pairs of basis vectors (choose $u \ne 0$, then $w$ with $b(u, w) = 1$, and continue in the $b$-orthogonal complement of $\mathrm{span}\{u, w\}$, which is complementary to it and on which $b$ is nondegenerate). On each plane $\mathrm{span}\{u_{k}, w_{k}\}$ the three nonzero values of $q$ add to $1$, since $q(u + w) = q(u) + q(w) + 1$: either two of them are $0$, and the two vectors with $q = 0$ form a new basis of the plane with $b = 1$ (type $H$, Gauss sum $2$), or all three are $1$ (type $P$, Gauss sum $-2$). Gauss sums multiply over $b$-orthogonal sums, since $q(x + y) = q(x) + q(y)$ when $b(x, y) = 0$. Two planes of type $P$ give one of type $H$ and one more: in $\mathrm{span}\{u_{1}, w_{1}, u_{2}, w_{2}\}$, $u = u_{1} + u_{2}$ and $w = w_{1} + u_{2}$ have $q(u) = q(w) = 0$ and $b(u, w) = 1$, and the orthogonal complement of $\mathrm{span}\{u, w\}$ there is a plane of Gauss sum $(-2)(-2)/2 = 2$, so of type $H$. Hence $q|_{W}$ is equivalent to $H^{m}$, Gauss sum $2^{m}$, or to $H^{m-1} \perp P$, Gauss sum $-2^{m}$. For $n$ even this is $q$ itself. For $n$ odd, $q(x + az) = q(x) + a\,q(z)$ for $x \in W$, as $z$ is in the radical. If $q(z) = 1$, the pairing $x \leftrightarrow x + z$ shows that the Gauss sum is $0$, and a plane of type $P$ in $W$ becomes one of type $H$ when $u$ is replaced by $u + z$ ($q(u + z) = 0$, $b$ unchanged), so $q$ is equivalent to $H^{m} \perp \langle z\rangle$ with $q(z) = 1$; if $q(z) = 0$, $q$ is equivalent to $q|_{W} \perp \langle z\rangle$ with $q(z) = 0$, with Gauss sum $\pm 2^{m+1}$, the sign that of $q|_{W}$. In each parity the models have distinct Gauss sums, so two forms with equal Gauss sums are equivalent to the same model, hence to each other. The values: in $\Cl_{\Z}(0,1) = \Z \oplus \Z j$, $j^{2} = -1$, a commutative ring, $(-1)^{\binom{k}{2}} = \langle (1 - j)j^{k}\rangle_{0}$ (both sides are $1, 1, -1, -1$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, 3$ and have period $4$). Grouping the $S$ by $a = |S \setminus N|$ and $b' = |S \cap N|$, $(-1)^{q(S)} = (-1)^{\binom{a + b'}{2} + b'} = \langle (1 - j)j^{a}(-j)^{b'}\rangle_{0}$, so $\sum_{S}(-1)^{q(S)} = \langle (1 - j)(1 + j)^{p}(1 - j)^{q}\rangle_{0}$. With $(1 + j)(1 - j) = 2$, $(1 + j)^{2} = 2j$ and $(1 + j)^{8} = 16$: for $r = p - q = 8m + s \ge 0$ ($0 \le s \le 7$) the product is $2^{q}16^{m}(1 - j)(1 + j)^{s}$, and $\langle (1 - j)(1 + j)^{s}\rangle_{0} = 1, 2, 2, 0, -4, -8, -8, 0$ for $s = 0, \dots, 7$; for $r < 0$, $|r| = 8m + s'$, the product is $2^{p}(1 - j)^{|r| + 1}$, whose scalar part equals that of $2^{p}(1 + j)^{|r| + 1}$ (the automorphism $j \mapsto -j$), and $\langle (1 + j)^{t}\rangle_{0} = 1, 1, 0, -2, -4, -4, 0, 8, 16$ for $t = 0, \dots, 8$. With $n = r + 2q$ (respectively $|r| + 2p$) this is $2^{n/2}$ for $r \equiv 0, 2$, $-2^{n/2}$ for $r \equiv 4, 6$, $2^{(n+1)/2}$ for $r \equiv 1$, $-2^{(n+1)/2}$ for $r \equiv 5$ and $0$ for $r \equiv 3, 7 \pmod 8$, the values of clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.blade-square-signs-f2-quadratic-form}; for fixed $n$ they are distinct on the five classes, which are therefore the classes of (viii).

The check builds the cocycle group for every sign vector with $n \le 4$ and verifies associativity, inverses and the relations; it builds $G$ from its relations by rewriting words for every sign vector with $n \le 4$ and for the standard signatures with $n = 5$, and verifies the normal form, associativity ($n \le 3$), agreement with the product of signed blades in GA with $c \mapsto -1$, the closed forms of $q$ and $b$, and that the squares are $\{1, c\}$; the Heisenberg group modulo $k$ ($2 \le k \le 7$) reads its relation both ways only for $k = 2$, and the cyclic groups of order $2m$ ($2 \le m \le 7$) show the independence at $n = 1$; the centre, the central involutions and the extraspecial property for all $20$ signatures with $n \le 5$; the ideal, a unimodular basis change, integral structure constants equal to GA's and $v^{2} = Q(v)$ for all integer vectors with entries in $[-2, 2]$, $n \le 4$, and rational vectors; the universal property for $27$ maps into $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ (twisted generators), rotor-conjugated frames and the grade involution; the reduction modulo $2$; and, for all pairs of sign vectors with $n \le 3$ and of standard signatures with $4 \le n \le 6$, that an explicit $\mathbb{F}_{2}$-isometry exists exactly when the Gauss sums agree, lifted for $n \le 4$ to anticommuting blades of the right squares whose products are $2^{n}$ distinct signed blades (an isomorphism over $\Z$), with the traces $\Tr(L_{e_{S}})$ and the diagonal of the trace form; and the radical and the scalar part of $(1 - j)(1 + j)^{p}(1 - j)^{q}$ in $\Cl_{\Z}(0,1)$, equal to the Gauss sum and to the tabulated value, for all signatures with $n \le 8$.

synthesis.splits-adapted-to-the-null-pai.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or an ordered field and $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the algebra of $\ell$ modes of Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}: generators $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$ with $Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$, null pairs $v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j})$, $w_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} - f_{j})$, with $v_{i}w_{j} + w_{j}v_{i} = \delta_{ij}$; let $V$ be the span of the generators, $W$ the span of the $v_{j}$ and $W'$ the span of the $w_{j}$ (isotropic, $V = W \oplus W'$). A \emph{split} is a decomposition $V = V_{+} \oplus V_{-}$ into orthogonal subspaces on which $Q$ is positive and negative definite; its \emph{adjoint} is the anti-automorphism $\dagger_{s}$ of the algebra that is $+1$ on $V_{+}$ and $-1$ on $V_{-}$. The stored split, $V_{+}$ spanned by the $e_{j}$ and $V_{-}$ by the $f_{j}$, has the blade inverse $\dagger$ as adjoint. A split is \emph{adapted} (to the isotropic subspaces $W$, $W'$) if its adjoint maps $W$ onto $W'$. Premise (P), positivity of values (Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}; assumed, not derived), is stated relative to a split: a state for the split $s$ is a $k$-linear $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger_{s}}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger_{s}}) = \omega(x)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The isotropic subspaces fix the split up to a positive form; the null pairs as vectors fix it; proved.)} The stored null pairs as vectors determine the stored split, $e_{j} = v_{j} + w_{j}$, $f_{j} = v_{j} - w_{j}$, and its adjoint is the one anti-automorphism exchanging $v_{j}$ and $w_{j}$; what follows concerns the subspaces $W$, $W'$ alone. The adapted splits correspond one to one to the positive definite symmetric bilinear forms $g$ on $W$, by $g(v,v') = vv'^{\dagger_{s}} + v'^{\dagger_{s}}v$; the stored split has $g(v_{i},v_{j}) = \delta_{ij}$. For $A \in \mathrm{GL}_{\ell}(k)$ the vectors $v'_{j} = \sum_{i}A_{ij}v_{i}$, $w'_{j} = \sum_{i}(A^{-1})_{ji}w_{i}$ are null pairs spanning the same $W$, $W'$, and $e'_{j} = v'_{j} + w'_{j}$, $f'_{j} = v'_{j} - w'_{j}$ is an orthonormal frame of an adapted split. For $\ell = 1$ the adapted splits are the lines $V_{+} = k(v_{1} + cw_{1})$, $V_{-} = k(v_{1} - cw_{1})$, $c > 0$ in $k$; an orthonormal frame over $k$ exists exactly when $c$ is a square in $k$, $c = t^{-2}$, and is then $e' = tv_{1} + t^{-1}w_{1}$, $f' = tv_{1} - t^{-1}w_{1}$, with the same two null lines and the same parity $f'e' = f_{1}e_{1}$ (over $\Q$, $c = 2$ gives a split with no orthonormal frame: $Q(v_{1} + 2w_{1}) = 2$); $t = 4$ is the boosted frame $\tfrac{17}{8}e_{1} + \tfrac{15}{8}f_{1}$, $\tfrac{15}{8}e_{1} + \tfrac{17}{8}f_{1}$ of clause (vi) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}. So the isotropic subspaces $W$, $W'$ do not determine the adjoint of (P); a choice of dual bases $v_{j}$, $w_{j}$ does, and what the subspaces leave open is a positive definite form on $W$, $\ell(\ell+1)/2$ numbers.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(What the null pairs do fix; proved.)} The number element $N = \sum_{j}w_{j}v_{j}$ is the same for every pair of dual bases of $W$ and $W'$, and $N^{\dagger_{s}} = N$ for every adapted split. Hence the sector projectors $Q_{n} = \prod_{m \ne n}(N - m)/(n - m)$, $0 \le n \le \ell$ (idempotent, with sum $1$ and $\langle Q_{n}\rangle_{0} = \binom{\ell}{n}2^{-\ell}$), the vacuum projector $Q_{0}$ (the atom $\Pi_{0}$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, clause (i)) and the total parity are self-adjoint for every adapted split; so $Q_{0}$ is an atom for each of them, and by clause (iii) of that theorem the vacuum state $x \mapsto \langle Q_{0}x\rangle_{0}/\langle Q_{0}\rangle_{0}$ is the one state sharp on it for every adapted split.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The functionals real for every adapted split; proved, with the case $\ell = 2$ by a complete finite computation.)} A $k$-linear functional $\omega$ satisfies $\omega(x^{\dagger_{s}}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$ and all adapted splits $s$ if and only if $\omega(x) = \langle h(N)x\rangle_{0}$ for a polynomial $h$ of degree at most $\ell$: a space of dimension $\ell + 1$. Such a functional is a state for one adapted split if and only if it is a state for all of them, if and only if $\omega = \sum_{n}q_{n}\,\langle Q_{n}x\rangle_{0}/\langle Q_{n}\rangle_{0}$ with $q_{n} \ge 0$ and $\sum_{n}q_{n} = 1$. These are the states of (P) that do not depend on the choice of adapted split; they include the vacuum state, the state of $Q_{\ell}$ and the products $\prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 + rp_{j})$ with one common $r$, $|r| \le 1$, $p_{j} = f_{j}e_{j}$. If only the splits adapted to each mode separately are admitted ($g$ diagonal in the $v_{j}$), the functionals real for all of them are the $\langle h(w_{1}v_{1}, \dots, w_{\ell}v_{\ell})x\rangle_{0}$, a space of dimension $2^{\ell}$, which contains every product $\prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 + r_{j}p_{j})$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(States that need the split; proved.)} Every other state of the stored split fails to be a state for some adapted split. In particular the pair state $\rho_{12}$ of clause (v) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.mode-split-of-the-clifford-algebra-and-its-klein-twist-to-the-tensor-product} with $cs \ne 0$ is not real for the split with $v'_{1} = 2v_{1}$ (at $c = \tfrac35$, $s = \tfrac45$ its values on $w_{1}w_{2}$ and on the adjoint of $w_{1}w_{2}$ for that split are $\tfrac{12}{25}$ and $\tfrac{48}{25}$). For $\ell = 2$ and the directions $a_{i} = x_{i}e_{1} + z_{i}p_{1}$, $b_{j} = x'_{j}e_{2}p_{1} + z'_{j}p_{2}$ of clause (vii) of the CHSH theorem, a state of the family (iii) gives the CHSH element the value $Z\,\omega(p_{1}p_{2})$, $Z = z_{1}(z'_{1} + z'_{2}) + z_{2}(z'_{1} - z'_{2})$, of absolute value at most $2$; since the family (iii) is the same for every choice of dual bases, the same holds for the directions built from the frame of any one adapted split. In that setting a value above $2$ requires a state that depends on the split.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Scope.} A state for one split assigns numbers in $[0,1]$ to the projectors of that split only; for an idempotent that is self-adjoint for another adapted split its value can lie outside $[0,1]$, as in the stored example with the value $\tfrac{17}{4}$. The statements are about the algebras $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ and the splits adapted to the isotropic subspaces of their null pairs; Premise (P) as stored names the null pairs as vectors, which fix the split, so the result does not show that a datum is missing from the stored premise, only that the split is not forced by the relations the pairs satisfy. That a boost changes the positive structure is clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time} (only positive structures carry states, and no positive structure is preserved by a boost); the present result classifies the adapted ones for the mode algebras over $k$. The classification (iii) uses the reality clause for every adapted split; whether the functionals that are only normalised and non-negative on $xx^{\dagger_{s}}$ for every adapted split form the same family is not addressed. Splits that are not adapted exist for $\ell \ge 2$ and are not treated. Nothing here says which split, if any, the series' other premises select.
synthesis.splits-adapted-to-the-null-pai.technical:
Premise (P), positivity of values, is stated relative to a split of the generators into those of square $+1$ and those of square $-1$, because the adjoint is defined by the split; (P) is assumed, not derived. For the mode algebras $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ this result says how much of the split the modes themselves fix. The modes are given by null pairs $v_{j}$, $w_{j}$; as vectors these fix the split ($e_{j} = v_{j} + w_{j}$), and the question here is what remains fixed if only the two complementary isotropic subspaces $W$ and $W'$ they span are given, that is, the pairs up to a change of dual bases. The splits whose adjoint exchanges $W$ and $W'$ correspond exactly to the positive definite forms on $W$: for one mode a single positive number, the scale $t$ in $e' = tv + w/t$, and the stored boosted frame with the value $17/4$ of the CHSH combination is $t = 4$. So the isotropic subspaces do not determine the adjoint. They do determine the number element $N$, its sector projectors, the vacuum projector and the total parity, which are self-adjoint for every adapted split.

Under (P) for a given split, the states that are states for every adapted split are exactly the mixtures of the normalised sector projectors of $N$: a family with $\ell$ free weights, containing the vacuum and the product states with one common occupation for all modes. If the scale of each mode is free but the modes are kept apart, the common states are the number-diagonal ones, which include all thermal products. Every state with coherence between sectors, such as the stored pair states, is tied to one split; and with one mode per party the split-independent states give the CHSH combination at most $2$. The correspondence, the invariance of $N$ and the classification are proved; the classification uses scalings of single modes and a complete finite computation for two modes.
synthesis.splits-adapted-to-the-null-pai.lay:
The series' assumption (P) about averages uses a mirror operation on the algebra, and that operation depends on dividing the basic directions into two kinds. Given that assumption and the series' description of its modes by pairs of light-like directions, this result asks how much of the division is fixed if only the two families of light-like directions are given and not the particular pairs chosen in them. The answer is: not all of it. For one mode a single positive number, a scale, is left free; for several modes a whole table of such numbers. A known example in the series where the limit on correlations seems to be broken is just a change of this scale.

Assuming (P), the result then finds which states make sense whatever the scale is: only those that are a mixture of "this many modes are occupied" with nothing more specific, such as the empty state or a thermal state with the same occupation for every mode. States in which two modes are entangled depend on the scale, and under the same assumption the states that do not depend on it never exceed the classical limit 2 in the simplest two-party arrangement. So if only the two families are given, some further datum has to supply the scale; the series' premise as stored names particular pairs, which do supply it, and the result shows that this choice is not forced by the relations the pairs satisfy.

proofs.main:
\emph{Preliminaries.} Write $\tau = \langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$ and $u \cdot u' = \tfrac12(uu' + u'u)$ for vectors. By Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}, $W$ and $W'$ are isotropic and $2v_{i} \cdot w_{j} = \delta_{ij}$, so the form pairs $W$ with $W'$ perfectly. An orthogonal linear map $M$ of $V$ extends uniquely to an automorphism and (composed with the reverse) to an anti-automorphism of the algebra; the adjoint of a split is the anti-automorphism extending the reflection $M_{s}$ that is $+1$ on $V_{+}$ and $-1$ on $V_{-}$, and for the stored split it is the blade inverse of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate} (it fixes $e_{j}$ and negates $f_{j}$). The composition of two adjoints is the automorphism extending the product of the two reflections.

\emph{(i).} Let $s$ be adapted and $M = M_{s}$. For $v, v' \in W$, $g(v,v') = 2v \cdot Mv'$; it is symmetric because $M$ is an orthogonal involution ($v \cdot Mv' = Mv \cdot M^{2}v' = Mv \cdot v'$). For $v \ne 0$ the vector $v + Mv$ is fixed by $M$, so it lies in $V_{+}$, and it is nonzero because $W \cap W' = 0$; hence $0 < Q(v + Mv) = 2v \cdot Mv = g(v,v)$, using $Q(v) = Q(Mv) = 0$. Conversely let $g$ be positive definite and symmetric on $W$, and let $\theta : W \to W'$ be the linear map with $2v \cdot \theta v' = g(v,v')$ (it exists and is injective because the pairing is perfect and $g$ nondegenerate). Put $V_{\pm} = \{v \pm \theta v\}$. Then $Q(v \pm \theta v) = \pm g(v,v)$, $(v + \theta v) \cdot (v' - \theta v') = \tfrac12(-g(v,v') + g(v',v)) = 0$, and $V_{+} \cap V_{-} = 0$, so by dimension $V = V_{+} \oplus V_{-}$ is a split; its reflection sends $v$ to $\theta v$, so it is adapted and its form is $g$. The two constructions are inverse to each other. For $A \in \mathrm{GL}_{\ell}(k)$: $2v'_{i} \cdot w'_{j} = \sum_{a}A_{ai}(A^{-1})_{ja} = \delta_{ij}$, so the $e'_{j}$, $f'_{j}$ are orthonormal with squares $1$, $-1$, the reflection of this frame exchanges $v'_{j}$ and $w'_{j}$, and the split is adapted. For $\ell = 1$ a form on $W = kv_{1}$ is $g(v_{1},v_{1}) = c > 0$, with $\theta v_{1} = cw_{1}$ and $Q(v_{1} \pm cw_{1}) = \pm c$; a vector of square $1$ in $V_{+}$ exists exactly when $c$ is a square in $k$. That the stored pairs fix the stored split is $e_{j} = v_{j} + w_{j}$, $f_{j} = v_{j} - w_{j}$. For $A = (t)$: $e' = tv_{1} + t^{-1}w_{1} = \tfrac12(t + t^{-1})e_{1} + \tfrac12(t - t^{-1})f_{1}$, which at $t = 4$ is $\tfrac{17}{8}e_{1} + \tfrac{15}{8}f_{1}$, and $f'e' = (tv_{1} - t^{-1}w_{1})(tv_{1} + t^{-1}w_{1}) = v_{1}w_{1} - w_{1}v_{1} = f_{1}e_{1}$. The space of symmetric forms on $W$ has dimension $\ell(\ell+1)/2$.

\emph{(ii).} If $v'_{j} = \sum_{i}A_{ij}v_{i}$ is another basis of $W$ and $w'_{j}$ the dual basis of $W'$, then $w'_{j} = \sum_{i}(A^{-1})_{ji}w_{i}$ and $\sum_{j}w'_{j}v'_{j} = \sum_{i,a}\bigl(\sum_{j}(A^{-1})_{ji}A_{aj}\bigr)w_{i}v_{a} = \sum_{i}w_{i}v_{i}$. For an adapted split with form $g$ choose a basis $v'_{j}$ of $W$ and put $w'_{j} = v_{j}'^{\dagger_{s}} \in W'$; if $g$ has an orthonormal basis this gives dual bases and $N^{\dagger_{s}} = \sum_{j}(w'_{j}v'_{j})^{\dagger_{s}} = \sum_{j}w'_{j}v'_{j} = N$. In general let $G_{ij} = g(v'_{i},v'_{j})$; the dual basis of $W'$ is $\sum_{i}(G^{-1})_{ji}w'_{i}$, so $N = \sum_{i,j}(G^{-1})_{ji}w'_{i}v'_{j}$ and $N^{\dagger_{s}} = \sum_{i,j}(G^{-1})_{ji}w'_{j}v'_{i} = N$ because $G$ is symmetric. The elements $n_{j} = w_{j}v_{j}$ are commuting idempotents ($w_{j}v_{j}w_{j}v_{j} = w_{j}(1 - w_{j}v_{j})v_{j} = w_{j}v_{j}$), so $N$ satisfies $\prod_{m=0}^{\ell}(N - m) = 0$, the $Q_{n}$ are the idempotents of its spectral decomposition, polynomials in $N$, hence self-adjoint for every adapted split; $Q_{n}$ is the sum of the $\binom{\ell}{n}$ products $\prod_{j \in I}n_{j}\prod_{j \notin I}(1 - n_{j})$, $|I| = n$, each of scalar part $2^{-\ell}$ since $n_{j} = \tfrac12(1 - p_{j})$; and the total parity is $\prod_{j}(1 - 2n_{j}) = \sum_{n}(-1)^{n}Q_{n}$. $Q_{0} = \prod_{j}(1 - n_{j}) = \prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 + p_{j})$ is the vacuum projector of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, clause (i), with corner $kQ_{0}$; the corner does not depend on the adjoint, so $Q_{0}$, being self-adjoint for every adapted split, is an atom for each, and clause (iii) of that theorem, whose proof uses only that the adjoint is an anti-automorphism with positive definite $\tau(x^{\dagger_{s}}x)$ preserving $\tau$, gives the uniqueness of the sharp state for each.

\emph{(iii).} The condition is linear in $\omega$. Sufficiency: $h(N)$ is self-adjoint for every adapted split by (ii), and $\tau(x^{\dagger_{s}}) = \tau(x)$ for every split (an anti-automorphism extending an orthogonal map preserves the scalar part), so $\tau(h(N)x^{\dagger_{s}}) = \tau((xh(N))^{\dagger_{s}}) = \tau(h(N)x)$. The functionals $\tau(N^{j}\,\cdot)$, $0 \le j \le \ell$, are independent because $1, N, \dots, N^{\ell}$ are and $\tau(y^{\dagger}y) > 0$ for $y \ne 0$. Necessity. Step 1: let $\omega$ be real for the stored split and for the split with $A = \operatorname{diag}(t_{1}, \dots, t_{\ell})$. Then $\omega$ is invariant under the composition of the two adjoints, the automorphism with $v_{j} \mapsto t_{j}^{2}v_{j}$, $w_{j} \mapsto t_{j}^{-2}w_{j}$. The ordered monomials $w_{I}v_{J}$ ($I$, $J$ subsets of the modes) are a basis, and this automorphism multiplies $w_{I}v_{J}$ by $\prod_{j \in J}t_{j}^{2}\prod_{i \in I}t_{i}^{-2}$; taking $t_{j} = 2$ for one $j$ in the symmetric difference of $I$ and $J$ and $t = 1$ elsewhere gives $\omega(w_{I}v_{J}) = 0$ unless $I = J$. So $\omega$ is determined by the numbers $c_{I} = \omega(\prod_{j \in I}n_{j})$; this already proves the statement about splits adapted to each mode separately (dimension $2^{\ell}$; sufficiency there as above, the $n_{j}$ being self-adjoint for such splits). Step 2, $\ell = 2$: the script computes the space of functionals real for the four splits $A = 1$, $\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, $\operatorname{diag}(1,3)$ and the shear $v'_{2} = v_{1} + v_{2}$; it has dimension $3$ and equals the span of $\tau(N^{j}\,\cdot)$, $j = 0, 1, 2$. The conditions have rational coefficients, so the dimension is the same over every $k$. In particular $c_{\{1\}} = c_{\{2\}}$. Step 3, general $\ell$: fix two modes $i \ne j$ and a set $I$ of other modes, and put $\omega_{I}(y) = \omega(\prod_{m \in I}n_{m}\,y)$ for $y$ in the subalgebra of the modes $i$, $j$. An adapted split of that two-mode algebra, extended by the stored split on the other modes, is an adapted split of the whole, its adjoint fixes $\prod_{m \in I}n_{m}$, which commutes with $y$; so $\omega_{I}$ is real for every adapted split of the two modes, and by Step 2 $\omega_{I}(n_{i}) = \omega_{I}(n_{j})$, that is $c_{I \cup \{i\}} = c_{I \cup \{j\}}$. Hence $c_{I}$ depends only on $|I|$, the space has dimension at most $\ell + 1$, and with sufficiency it is the span of the $\tau(N^{j}\,\cdot)$; the script confirms dimension $4$ for $\ell = 3$. States, in the sense of Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values} read for the split $s$: write $h(N) = \sum_{n}h(n)Q_{n}$. If $\omega$ is a state for one adapted split then $\omega(Q_{n}) = h(n)\tau(Q_{n}) \ge 0$, as $Q_{n} = Q_{n}Q_{n}^{\dagger_{s}}$, and $\sum_{n}h(n)\tau(Q_{n}) = 1$; conversely for every adapted split each $x \mapsto \tau(Q_{n}x)/\tau(Q_{n})$ is a state (the functional of an element $Q_{n}Q_{n}^{\dagger_{s}}$; clause (iii) of the CHSH theorem, whose proof applies to the blade inverse of any orthonormal frame, and for a split without orthonormal frame over $k$ by extending $k$), so the convex combinations are. The vacuum state is $q_{0} = 1$; $\prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 + rp_{j}) = \prod_{j}\bigl(\tfrac{1+r}{2}(1 - n_{j}) + \tfrac{1-r}{2}n_{j}\bigr)$ is a function of the $n_{j}$ symmetric in them with coefficient depending only on the number of occupied modes, hence a function of $N$; with distinct $r_{j}$ it is a function of the $n_{j}$.

\emph{(iv).} A state of the stored split that is a state for every adapted split is real for all of them, hence of the form (iii). For the pair state of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.mode-split-of-the-clifford-algebra-and-its-klein-twist-to-the-tensor-product}, clause (v), $\rho_{12}$ contains $cs(w_{1}w_{2} + v_{2}v_{1})$, so its functional $x \mapsto 4\tau(\rho_{12}x)$ is nonzero on the monomial $w_{1}w_{2}$ paired against $v_{2}v_{1}$, a monomial with $I \ne J$, and Step 1 excludes it; the two values are the script's. For the CHSH element: as in the cited clause (vii), $a_{i}b_{j} = x_{i}x'_{j}\,e_{2}f_{1} + x_{i}z'_{j}\,e_{1}p_{2} + z_{i}x'_{j}\,p_{1}e_{2}p_{1} + z_{i}z'_{j}\,p_{1}p_{2}$, using $e_{1}e_{2}p_{1} = e_{2}f_{1}$. The second and third terms are odd, and $e_{2}f_{1} = (v_{2} + w_{2})(v_{1} - w_{1})$ is a combination of monomials $w_{I}v_{J}$ with $I \ne J$ (after ordering, $v_{2}v_{1}$, $w_{1}v_{2}$, $w_{2}v_{1}$, $w_{2}w_{1}$); a functional of the family (iii) vanishes on all of these by Step 1. So $\omega(C) = Z\omega(p_{1}p_{2})$. The family (iii) and the elements $N$, $Q_{n}$ do not depend on the dual bases, so the argument applies verbatim to the directions built from the frame $e'_{j}$, $f'_{j}$ of any adapted split. That a boost changes the positive structure in the Hermitian setting is clause (iv) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.positive-structure-is-twistor-form-at-imaginary-time}, cited for comparison only. $|\omega(p_{1}p_{2})| = |q_{0} - q_{1} + q_{2}| \le 1$, and $|Z| \le |z'_{1} + z'_{2}| + |z'_{1} - z'_{2}| \le 2$ since $|z_{i}| \le 1$ and $|z'_{j}| \le 1$.

synthesis.switch-planes-on-a-two-state-s.formal:
Let $F$ be a field in which $2 \ne 0$, $E = \mathrm{End}_{F}(F^{2})$, $E_{0} \subset E$ the maps of trace zero, and let a \emph{switch} be a pair $(a, b)$ in $E$ with $a^{2} = b^{2} = 0$, $ab + ba = 1$ (as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If $V \subseteq E$ is a subspace of dimension at least $2$ in which every element squares to a scalar, then $V \subseteq E_{0}$. On $E_{0}$, $x^{2} = -\det x =: Q(x)$, and in the basis $h = wv - vw$, $v + w$, $v - w$ of a fixed switch $(v,w)$, $Q = \alpha^{2} + \sigma^{2} - \tau^{2}$.
\item[(ii)] Let $V \subseteq E_{0}$ be a plane. Its nonzero elements of square zero form two lines exactly when $V$ is spanned by a switch, one line exactly when $Q|_{V}$ is degenerate, and no line otherwise. No plane of $E_{0}$ is totally null.
\item[(iii)] If $F$ is ordered, an orthogonal basis of $V$ has squares of signs $(+,+)$, $(+,-)$ or $(+,0)$, and no other. If moreover every positive element of $F$ is a square, $V$ is spanned by a switch exactly in the case $(+,-)$.
\item[(iv)] $V$ generates $E$ as an algebra when $Q|_{V}$ is nondegenerate, and a subalgebra of dimension $3$ (conjugate to the upper triangular matrices) when it is degenerate.
\item[(v)] $V \mapsto \{\ker a, \ker b\}$, for any switch $(a,b)$ spanning $V$, is a well-defined bijection from the planes spanned by a switch to the unordered pairs of distinct lines of $F^{2}$, and any two such planes are conjugate under $\mathrm{GL}_{2}(F)$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.switch-planes-on-a-two-state-s.technical: On a two-state system the operations whose squares are numbers are, apart from the numbers themselves, the trace-free ones, and they form a three-dimensional quadratic space with two positive directions and one negative. A plane of such directions contains two independent operations of square zero exactly when it is spanned by a set-and-clear pair; it contains one when the form degenerates on it, and none otherwise. Over the reals the three cases are the signatures $(2,0)$, $(1,1)$ and degenerate, so a plane of directions that generates all operations is either Euclidean, with no operation of square zero, or the hyperbolic plane of a switch. The switch planes correspond one to one with the unordered pairs of distinct lines, the two states.
synthesis.switch-planes-on-a-two-state-s.lay: Suppose a system has just two states, and you look for a pair of independent directions acting on it. There are only two kinds that produce everything: a pair of ordinary perpendicular directions, or a pair made of one direction that squares to plus one and one that squares to minus one. Only the second kind contains operations that, done twice, give nothing, like switching on. And each such pair corresponds to exactly one choice of what the two states are.

proofs.main:
Throughout, $(v, w)$ is a fixed switch in $E$, for instance set and clear in a basis of $F^{2}$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}(i)), $h = wv - vw$, and $hw = w$, $wh = -w$, $hv = -v$, $vh = v$, $h^{2} = 1$ by the relations of a switch.

\emph{(i)} Every $x \in E$ satisfies $x^{2} = (\operatorname{tr}x)\,x - \det x$, so $x^{2}$ is a scalar exactly when $x$ is a scalar or $\operatorname{tr}x = 0$. Suppose $x \in V$ has $\operatorname{tr}x 
e 0$. Then $x$ is a scalar $\lambda 
e 0$. Take $y \in V$ independent of $x$; $y$ is not a scalar, so $\operatorname{tr}y = 0$, and $x + y$ is not a scalar and has trace $2\lambda 
e 0$, so $(x + y)^{2}$ is not a scalar, a contradiction. On $E_{0}$, $x^{2} = -\det x$. By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.set-and-clear-of-a-bit-generate-the-hyperbolic-plane}(ii) and (iv), $h$, $v + w$, $v - w$ is a basis of $E_{0}$ of pairwise anticommuting elements of squares $1$, $1$, $-1$, so $Q(\alpha h + \sigma(v + w) + 	au(v - w)) = \alpha^{2} + \sigma^{2} - 	au^{2}$.

\emph{(ii)} A nonzero $n \in E_{0}$ with $n^{2} = 0$ is a null vector of $Q$, and for $x, y \in E_{0}$, $xy + yx = (x + y)^{2} - x^{2} - y^{2}$ is the scalar $2B(x,y)$, $B$ the polar form of $Q$. Let $n_{1}, n_{2} \in E_{0}$ be independent with $n_{1}^{2} = n_{2}^{2} = 0$. A nonzero map of square zero on $F^{2}$ is conjugate to $w$, so choose the basis of $F^{2}$ with $n_{1} = w$. For $y = \alpha h +  eta w + \gamma v$, $wy + yw = \alpha(wh + hw) + \gamma(wv + vw) = \gamma$. If $n_{1}n_{2} + n_{2}n_{1} = 0$, then $n_{2} = \alpha h +  eta w$ and $n_{2}^{2} = \alpha^{2} + \alpha eta(hw + wh) = \alpha^{2} = 0$, so $n_{2}$ is a multiple of $w$, which is excluded. Hence $n_{1}n_{2} + n_{2}n_{1} = \gamma 
e 0$. In particular $(n_{1} + n_{2})^{2} = \gamma 
e 0$: no plane is totally null. And $(n_{1}, \gamma^{-1}n_{2})$ is a switch spanning the plane. Conversely, on a plane spanned by a switch $(a, b)$, $Q(\alpha a +  eta b) = \alpha eta$, with exactly the two null lines $Fa$ and $Fb$. If $Q|_{V}$ is degenerate, its radical is a line (not $V$, as $V$ is not totally null) of null vectors, and it is the only null line, since a second would be orthogonal to it and make $V$ totally null. If $Q|_{V}$ is nondegenerate and has a null vector $n$, choose $y \in V$ with $ny + yn 
e 0$; then $y -  rac{Q(y)}{ny + yn}\,n$ is null (expand the square) and independent of $n$. So a nondegenerate plane has no null line or two.

\emph{(iii)} Let $x, y$ be an orthogonal basis of $V$ (it exists since $2 
e 0$). The plane $P = \operatorname{span}\{h, v + w\}$ has $Q > 0$ on its nonzero vectors, a sum of two squares in an ordered field. $V \cap P 
e 0$ by dimensions, so $Q$ takes a positive value on $V$, and not both of $Q(x), Q(y)$ are $\le 0$. If both were negative, $Q$ would be negative on the nonzero vectors of $V$, against $V \cap P 
e 0$. If one were negative and the other zero, or both zero, the same contradiction or (ii) applies ($Q \le 0$ on $V$, respectively $V$ totally null). This leaves $(+,+)$, $(+,-)$, $(+,0)$. A switch plane contains $a + b$ and $a - b$ of squares $1$ and $-1$, orthogonal: case $(+,-)$. Conversely if $Q(x) = \lambda > 0 > -\mu = Q(y)$ and $\mu/\lambda = ho^{2}$, then $ho x \pm y$ are independent null vectors, and (ii) applies.

\emph{(iv)} If $Q|_{V}$ is nondegenerate, take an orthogonal basis $x, y$: they anticommute and have nonzero scalar squares, so both are invertible. If $\alpha +  eta x + \gamma y + \delta xy = 0$, conjugating by $x$ changes the sign of the last two terms, so (as $2 
e 0$) $\alpha +  eta x = 0$ and $(\gamma + \delta x)y = 0$, hence $\gamma + \delta x = 0$; since $x$ is not a scalar, all four coefficients vanish. So $1, x, y, xy$ are independent and span $E$. If $Q|_{V}$ is degenerate, take $n$ in the radical, a basis of $F^{2}$ with $n = w$, and $y \in V$ independent of $n$; by the computation in (ii), $y = \alpha h +  eta w$ with $\alpha 
e 0$, and $yw = \alpha w$, $wy = -\alpha w$, so the algebra generated is $\operatorname{span}\{1, w, h\}$, the upper triangular matrices in the basis $(s_{\mathrm{off}}, s_{\mathrm{on}})$.

\emph{(v)} By (ii) any switch $(a, b)$ spanning $V$ has $a$ and $b$ on the two null lines of $V$, so $\{\ker a, \ker b\}$ depends only on $V$. A nonzero map of square zero on $F^{2}$ has image equal to its kernel, a line. If $\ker a = \ker b = \ell$ then $\operatorname{im}a = \operatorname{im}b = \ell$ and $ab = ba = 0$, against $ab + ba = 1$: the two lines differ. A nonzero map of square zero is determined up to a scalar by its kernel, so the pair of lines determines the two null lines of $V$ and hence $V$: the map is injective. Given distinct lines $\ell_{0}, \ell_{1}$, choose $s_{\mathrm{off}} \in \ell_{0}$, $s_{\mathrm{on}} \in \ell_{1}$; set and clear in this basis are a switch with $\ker w = \ell_{0}$, $\ker v = \ell_{1}$: the map is onto. $\mathrm{GL}_{2}(F)$ acts transitively on pairs of distinct lines, and conjugation carries switch planes to switch planes compatibly with the map.
