synthesis.the-sign-is-the-rotor-at-infin.formal:
Let $\Cl_{\Q}(2,0)$ be the rational Clifford algebra of the plane (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.division-gives-the-rationals}), $B = e_{1}e_{2}$, so $B^{2} = -1$, and $U_{\Q} = \{a + bB : a, b \in \Q,\ a^{2} + b^{2} = 1\}$. For $t \in \Q$, $1 + tB$ is invertible with $(1 + tB)^{-1} = (1 - tB)/(1 + t^{2})$; put
\[
R_{t} = (1 - tB)(1 + tB)^{-1} = \frac{(1 - t^{2}) - 2t\,B}{1 + t^{2}}, \qquad R_{\infty} = -1 .
\]
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Rational rotors.)} Each $R_{t}$ lies in $U_{\Q}$, so $R_{t}\widetilde{R_{t}} = 1$, and $v \mapsto R_{t}v\widetilde{R_{t}}$ maps the rational vectors $V_{\Q}$ to themselves preserving $Q$. $R_{0} = 1$, $R_{1} = -B$ (the half turn, $v \mapsto -v$), $R_{\infty} = -1$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Composition is tangent addition.)} $R_{s}R_{t} = R_{s \oplus t}$ on $\Q \cup \{\infty\}$, where $s \oplus t = (s + t)/(1 - st)$ for $st \ne 1$, $s \oplus t = \infty$ for $st = 1$, $\infty \oplus t = t \oplus \infty = -1/t$ for $t \ne 0, \infty$, $\infty \oplus 0 = \infty$ and $\infty \oplus \infty = 0$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The sign is the rotor at infinity.)} $t \mapsto R_{t}$ is a group isomorphism from $(\Q \cup \{\infty\}, \oplus)$ onto $U_{\Q}$, with inverse $a + bB \mapsto -b/(1 + a)$ for $a \ne -1$ and $-1 \mapsto \infty$. The sign $-1$, the residue of two distinctions passing each other (Premise (F2)), is the rotor at the point at infinity of the parameter line. As a map of vectors it is the full turn, $R_{\infty}v\widetilde{R_{\infty}} = v$, while the rotor itself is $-1$.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The path to the sign has length $\pi$.)} Over $\R$ (Premise (F4)), with $|a + bB|^{2} = \langle (a + bB)(a + bB)^{\sim}\rangle_{0} = a^{2} + b^{2}$ on the even part, the curve $t \mapsto R_{t}$, $t \in [0, \infty)$, closed by $R_{\infty}$, traces the half of the unit circle of the even part with $b \le 0$ exactly once, from $1$ to $-1$, with speed $|dR_{t}/dt| = 2/(1 + t^{2})$. Its length is therefore half the length of the unit circle, $\pi$, and $\pi = \int_{0}^{\infty} 2\,dt/(1 + t^{2})$.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.the-sign-is-the-rotor-at-infin.technical: In the rational algebra of the plane, the unit bivector $B$ squares to $-1$, and the Cayley form $R_{t} = (1 - tB)/(1 + tB)$ gives a rotor for every rational $t$, with rational coefficients. Every rational rotor arises this way, composition is the tangent addition law $(s + t)/(1 - st)$, and the parameter needs one extra point, $t = \infty$, which gives the rotor $-1$. So the sign bit of the foundation is the rotor at the point at infinity of a projective line, completed exactly as the transport principle completes the line for $1/0$. Acting on vectors that rotor is a full turn, which does nothing, while the rotor itself is $-1$: the spinor sign. The sign is reached algebraically, but the distance to it is not: over the reals the path of rotors from $1$ to $-1$ is half the unit circle, of length $\pi$, and $\pi$ is irrational (classical, not proved here). The continuum enters at exactly that step.
synthesis.the-sign-is-the-rotor-at-infin.lay: Turning something round in a plane can be done entirely with fractions: every rotation by a "rational" amount is described by one fraction $t$, and doing two rotations one after the other combines their fractions by a simple rule. One rotor is missing from the fractions, the one that turns everything by a full circle, and it sits at "$t$ = infinity", the same point at infinity that makes $1/0$ meaningful elsewhere on this site. That rotor is $-1$: a full turn leaves every arrow where it was, yet the algebra remembers it as minus one, the sign that electrons and other spinning particles are known to pick up. Getting to it is algebraic; measuring how far it is takes $\pi$, which no fraction equals.

proofs.main:
Work in $\Cl_{\Q}(2,0)$, which exists by Theorem \claimref{synthesis.division-gives-the-rationals} (the integer algebra of Premise (F3) with every non-null vector inverted). Its even part $\{a + bB : a, b \in \Q\}$ is commutative, since $B$ commutes with $1$ and with itself, and $(a + bB)^{\sim} = a - bB$ because reversion reverses $e_{1}e_{2}$ to $e_{2}e_{1} = -B$. Hence $(a + bB)(a + bB)^{\sim} = a^{2} - b^{2}B^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$.

\emph{Invertibility.} $(1 + tB)(1 - tB) = 1 - t^{2}B^{2} = 1 + t^{2}$, a nonzero rational, so $(1 + tB)^{-1} = (1 - tB)/(1 + t^{2})$ and $R_{t} = (1 - tB)^{2}/(1 + t^{2}) = ((1 - t^{2}) - 2tB)/(1 + t^{2})$.

\emph{(i)} With $a = (1 - t^{2})/(1 + t^{2})$ and $b = -2t/(1 + t^{2})$, $a^{2} + b^{2} = ((1 - t^{2})^{2} + 4t^{2})/(1 + t^{2})^{2} = 1$, so $R_{t} \in U_{\Q}$ and $R_{t}\widetilde{R_{t}} = 1$. For $R \in U_{\Q}$ and $v \in V_{\Q}$, $RvR^{\sim}$ is a product of two even elements and one odd one, hence odd, and in $\Cl(2,0)$ the odd elements are the vectors, so $RvR^{\sim} \in V_{\Q}$; its square is $RvR^{\sim}RvR^{\sim} = Rv^{2}R^{\sim} = Q(v)$. The values $R_{0} = 1$ and $R_{1} = -2B/2 = -B$ are direct; $(-B)e_{1}(-B)^{\sim} = -Be_{1}B = -e_{1}$ and likewise $e_{2} \mapsto -e_{2}$, the half turn.

\emph{(ii)} The even part is commutative, so for rational $s, t$
\[
R_{s}R_{t} = \frac{(1 - sB)(1 - tB)}{(1 + sB)(1 + tB)} = \frac{(1 - st) - (s + t)B}{(1 - st) + (s + t)B}.
\]
If $st \ne 1$, divide numerator and denominator by $1 - st$: this is $R_{u}$ with $u = (s + t)/(1 - st)$. If $st = 1$ then $s + t \ne 0$ (as $s, t$ are rational with $st = 1 > 0$, they have the same sign), and the quotient is $(-(s + t)B)/((s + t)B) = -1 = R_{\infty}$. With infinity: $R_{\infty}R_{t} = -R_{t}$, and for $t \ne 0$, $R_{-1/t} = (t + B)/(t - B)$ (multiply numerator and denominator of $(1 + B/t)/(1 - B/t)$ by $t$), while $-R_{t} = (tB - 1)/(1 + tB)$; multiplying numerator and denominator of $(t + B)/(t - B)$ by $B$ gives $(tB - 1)/(tB + 1)$, so $-R_{t} = R_{-1/t}$. Also $R_{\infty}R_{0} = -1 = R_{\infty}$ and $R_{\infty}R_{\infty} = 1 = R_{0}$.

\emph{(iii)} We show the map is a bijection onto $U_{\Q}$; by (ii) it then carries $\oplus$ to the product of the group $U_{\Q}$, so $\oplus$ is a group law with identity $0$ and the map is an isomorphism. Injective: if $a + bB = R_{t}$ with $t$ rational then $1 + a = 2/(1 + t^{2}) \ne 0$ and $-b/(1 + a) = (2t/(1 + t^{2}))/(2/(1 + t^{2})) = t$, so $t$ is recovered, and $R_{t} \ne -1 = R_{\infty}$ since $1 + a \ne 0$. Surjective: let $a^{2} + b^{2} = 1$ with $a \ne -1$ and put $t = -b/(1 + a) \in \Q$. Then $1 + t^{2} = ((1 + a)^{2} + b^{2})/(1 + a)^{2} = (2 + 2a)/(1 + a)^{2} = 2/(1 + a)$, so $(1 - t^{2})/(1 + t^{2}) = (2 - (1 + t^{2}))(1 + a)/2 = a$ and $-2t/(1 + t^{2}) = b$; and $a = -1$ forces $b = 0$, the element $-1 = R_{\infty}$. Finally $R_{\infty}vR_{\infty}^{\sim} = (-1)v(-1) = v$.

\emph{(iv)} Over $\R$ (Premise (F4)) the formulas of (i) to (iii) hold verbatim for real $t$, the even part with $|a + bB|^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}$ being the Euclidean plane in the coordinates $(a, b)$. For $t \ge 0$, $b(t) = -2t/(1 + t^{2}) \le 0$, and $a(t) = (1 - t^{2})/(1 + t^{2})$ has $a'(t) = -4t/(1 + t^{2})^{2} < 0$ for $t > 0$, so $a$ decreases strictly from $1$ at $t = 0$ towards $-1$ as $t \to \infty$; since $a^{2} + b^{2} = 1$ and $b \le 0$, the point $(a, b)$ is determined by $a$, and the curve runs once along the lower half of the unit circle from $(1, 0)$ to $(-1, 0)$, the endpoint being $R_{\infty}$. Its length is half the length of the unit circle, which is $\pi$ by definition. Differentiating, $b'(t) = -2(1 - t^{2})/(1 + t^{2})^{2}$, and
\[
a'(t)^{2} + b'(t)^{2} = \frac{16t^{2} + 4(1 - t^{2})^{2}}{(1 + t^{2})^{4}} = \frac{4(1 + t^{2})^{2}}{(1 + t^{2})^{4}} = \frac{4}{(1 + t^{2})^{2}},
\]
so the speed is $2/(1 + t^{2})$ and the length is $\int_{0}^{\infty} 2\,dt/(1 + t^{2}) = \pi$. $\square$

The check verifies (i) to (iii) in exact rational arithmetic with GA.py (the rotor property and the vector action for a grid of rationals, the composition law on all pairs from a set of rationals including the cases $st = 1$ and infinity, and the bijection on every rational point of the circle with height at most $60$), the speed identity as an identity of rational functions, and brackets the length $\int_{0}^{\infty} 2\,dt/(1 + t^{2})$ between rational Riemann-sum bounds, which it compares with rational bounds on $\pi$ from Machin's formula.

synthesis.three-party-trade-off-of-chsh-.formal:
Notation, hypotheses and clause numbers of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate} (the base) are used: $k$ is $\Q$ or any ordered field, $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ the Clifford algebra of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} with coefficients in $k$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.division-gives-the-rationals}), $\dagger$ the linear extension of the inverse on blades, an \emph{observable} an $x$ with $x^{\dagger} = x$, $x^{2} = 1$, and \emph{Hypothesis (P), positivity of values:} values are given by a \emph{state}, a $k$-linear $\omega : \Cl_{k}(p,q) \to k$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$; (P) is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}, assumed, not derived. The adjoint is defined by the chosen generators. In definite signature it does not depend on the orthonormal frame; in indefinite signature it depends on the split into generators of square $1$ and of square $-1$, so observables, states and (P) are relative to that split, and each statement holds for every fixed split. Let $A_{1}, A_{2}$; $B_{1}, B_{2}$; $D_{1}, D_{2}$ be observables such that elements of different pairs commute, and
\[
C_{AB} = A_{1}(B_{1} + B_{2}) + A_{2}(B_{1} - B_{2}), \qquad C_{AD} = A_{1}(D_{1} + D_{2}) + A_{2}(D_{1} - D_{2}), \qquad A_{\pm} = A_{1} \pm A_{2} .
\]
The shared party uses \emph{the same} two observables $A_{1}, A_{2}$ in both CHSH elements; every statement below about two CHSH values is under this condition.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The diagonals anticommute; proved.)} $A_{+}A_{-} + A_{-}A_{+} = 0$, $A_{+}^{2} + A_{-}^{2} = 4$, and $C_{AB} = A_{+}B_{1} + A_{-}B_{2}$, $C_{AD} = A_{+}D_{1} + A_{-}D_{2}$. The self-adjoint elements $A_{+}B_{1}$ and $A_{-}D_{2}$ anticommute, as do $A_{-}B_{2}$ and $A_{+}D_{1}$, and $(\lambda A_{+}B_{1} + \mu A_{-}D_{2})^{2} = \lambda^{2}A_{+}^{2} + \mu^{2}A_{-}^{2}$ for scalars $\lambda, \mu$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Trade-off, under (P), same $A_{1}, A_{2}$ in both; proved.)} For every state
\[
\omega(C_{AB})^{2} + \omega(C_{AD})^{2} \le 8 .
\]
So the two CHSH values that share party $A$ with the same two observables cannot both exceed $2$ in absolute value, and $\omega(C_{AB})^{2} = 8$ forces $\omega(C_{AD}) = 0$ for every third pair tested with the same $A_{1}, A_{2}$. This clause uses of (P) only $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(1) = 1$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The values $2$ and $4$, under (P); proved.)} If $A_{1}A_{2} = A_{2}A_{1}$ then $C_{AB}^{2} = 4$ and $\omega(C_{AB})^{2} \le 4$ (base, clause (iii)). If all four of $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{1}, B_{2}$ lie in a commutative subalgebra spanned by orthogonal self-adjoint idempotents $q_{1}, \dots, q_{m}$ with sum $1$, then $C_{AB} = \sum_{i}\gamma_{i}q_{i}$ with every $\gamma_{i} \in \{2, -2\}$, and $\omega(C_{AB})$ is an average of these with the weights $\omega(q_{i}) \ge 0$. For arbitrary commuting observables $\omega(A_{i}B_{j})^{2} \le 1$, so $|\omega(C_{AB})| \le 4$. Under (P) and for observables the value $4$ is not reached (base, clause (iii)); it is reached when positivity is dropped (base, clause (v)) and exceeded when self-adjointness is dropped (base, clause (vi)).
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Three modes of $\Cl_{\Q}(3,3)$ with nested Klein twists and parity-odd directions; proved, the sample values computed.)} With generators $e_{j}, f_{j}$ ($Q(e_{j}) = 1$, $Q(f_{j}) = -1$) and $p_{j} = f_{j}e_{j}$, the three pairs $\{e_{1}, p_{1}\}$, $\{e_{2}p_{1}, p_{2}\}$, $\{e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}, p_{3}\}$ consist of anticommuting observables and commute across pairs: the second and third are twists of modes $2$ and $3$ by $p_{1}$ and by $p_{1}p_{2}$, as in Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} with one and with two planes, and with the single factor $p_{1}$ in place of $p_{1}p_{2}$ the third pair would not commute with the second. The elements $e_{1}$, $e_{2}p_{1}$, $e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}$ are odd under the total parity. For the state $\omega_{\rho}$, $\rho \propto (1 + e_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1})(1 + e_{1}\,e_{3}p_{1}p_{2})(1 + p_{1}p_{2}p_{3})$, and the settings $A = (e_{1}, p_{1})$, $B_{1} = B_{2} = e_{2}p_{1}$, $D_{1} = D_{2} = e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}$ the two values are $(2, 2)$: the bound of (ii) is attained over $\Q$. With $I_{B} = e_{2}p_{1}p_{2}$, $I_{D} = e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}$ and $y = (1 + \tfrac15I_{B})(1 - \tfrac14I_{D})$, the state of $y\rho y^{\dagger}$ has, at the same settings, the values $(\tfrac{24}{13}, \tfrac{30}{17})$, both nonzero, with sum of squares $\tfrac{318564}{48841} < 8$ (computed). The pure state of modes $1, 2$
\[
\rho_{AB} = \tfrac45\,y'\rho_{0}y'^{\dagger}, \qquad \rho_{0} = \tfrac14(1 + e_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1})(1 - p_{1}p_{2}), \qquad y' = 1 - \tfrac12e_{2}p_{1}p_{2},
\]
has value $\tfrac{14}{5}$ at the blade settings $(e_{1}, p_{1}; e_{2}p_{1}, p_{2})$ (it is not the pair state of clause (v), whose value at the blade settings is at most $2$); so for every state $\omega$ with $\omega(C_{AB}) = \tfrac{14}{5}$, for instance that of $\rho_{AB}\cdot\tfrac12(1 + p_{3})$, every CHSH value of the same $A_{1}, A_{2}$ with a third pair has square at most $8 - (\tfrac{14}{5})^{2} = \tfrac{4}{25}$; for the instance named the values with party $D$ at rational directions are all $0$.
\item[(v)] \emph{(What a pair state leaves a third party, same $A_{1}, A_{2}$ in both; proved, with a computed instance.)} If $\omega(C_{AB}) = S$ then $\omega(C_{AD})^{2} \le 8 - S^{2}$ for every third pair tested with the same $A_{1}, A_{2}$. For \emph{amplitudes} $c, s$ with $c^{2} + s^{2} = 1$ and $r = c^{2} - s^{2}$, the pair state of modes $1, 2$ with amplitude $c$ on $\ket{00}$ and $s$ on $\ket{11}$ is
\[
\rho_{c,s} = \tfrac14(1 + p_{1}p_{2})(1 + rp_{1}) + cs\,(w_{1}w_{2} + v_{2}v_{1}), \qquad v_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} + f_{j}), \quad w_{j} = \tfrac12(e_{j} - f_{j}),
\]
a self-adjoint idempotent with $\langle\rho_{c,s}\rangle_{0} = \tfrac14$ (the element that the stored account reads as an eviction pair). Its correlations in the directions of the two parties are $\omega(e_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1}) = 2cs$, $\omega(p_{1}p_{2}) = 1$, $\omega(e_{1}p_{2}) = \omega(p_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1}) = 0$, and the settings $(p_{1}, e_{1}; zp_{2} + x\,e_{2}p_{1}, zp_{2} - x\,e_{2}p_{1})$, $x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$, have value $S = 2(z + 2cs\,x)$, with $S^{2} \le 4(1 + 4c^{2}s^{2}) = 4(2 - r^{2})$. At amplitudes $(c, s) = (\tfrac35, \tfrac45)$ and direction $(x, z) = (\tfrac{20}{29}, \tfrac{21}{29})$: $S = \tfrac{402}{145}$, so a third pair tested with the same $(p_{1}, e_{1})$ is left $\omega(C_{AD})^{2} \le \tfrac{6596}{21025}$, against $4r^{2} = \tfrac{196}{625}$ in the limit of the best directions.
\end{enumerate}
synthesis.three-party-trade-off-of-chsh-.technical:
When one party shares correlations with two others, the two Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt values are not independent: with the shared party's two quantities the same in both, the sum of their squares is at most $8$, the Toner-Verstraete relation. Here it is proved in the rational Clifford algebra of the foundation, for commuting self-adjoint elements of square one, under Hypothesis (P) of the stored CHSH bound, positivity of values: values are given by a state, a linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$ for all $x$; (P) is assumed, not derived. The proof uses one fact about the shared party: the sum and the difference of its two quantities anticommute, like the diagonals of a rhombus, and their squares add to $4$. Each CHSH element is a sum of two products with these diagonals, the products pair up across the two CHSH elements into anticommuting pairs, and for anticommuting self-adjoint elements the squared values add up to at most the value of the sum of the squares. No dimension and no square root enters, and no step uses real coefficients. For quantities in a commutative subalgebra the combination takes the values $\pm 2$ on its points; the bound $4$ for the square when one party's quantities commute, the fact that $4$ is not reached under the hypothesis, that it is reached without positivity and exceeded without self-adjointness, are the stored bound's.

Two settings are recorded side by side. The general statement applies to parity-even observables with two modes for each party, which need no twist. The realisation given here is the other one: three modes of the split-signature algebra with two nested Klein twists and directions that are odd under the total parity. There the bound is attained over the rationals at the point $(2, 2)$, and a state entangled across all three parties with values $(24/13, 30/17)$ is given. A pair of modes in the pair state with amplitudes $c$, $s$ has squared value up to $4(2 - r^{2})$, $r = c^{2} - s^{2}$, and so leaves a third party tested with the same two quantities of the shared mode a squared value of at most about $4r^{2}$, below the local value (remark, resting on the stored pair-state reading of the eviction pairs and on parity-odd elements counting as observables; under parity superselection it is empty).
synthesis.three-party-trade-off-of-chsh-.lay: If one experimenter shares strong quantum correlations with a second, there is less left to share with a third. For the standard measure of such correlations the rule is exact, provided the shared experimenter uses the same two measurements in both comparisons: the squares of the two values add up to at most 8, so if one pair reaches the quantum maximum the other pair, tested with those same two measurements, shows no correlation of this kind at all, and two pairs can never both beat the limit of 2 that holds for a world of pre-existing answers. This is a known theorem. Here it is proved inside the algebra of directions that the series builds from its simplest assumptions, using only fractions, from one geometric fact: the sum and the difference of two unit directions are perpendicular. The proof assumes the rule called (P), positivity of values: averages are given by a rule that is linear, gives the trivial measurement the value 1, never gives a quantity times its mirror image a negative average, and gives a quantity and its mirror image the same average; this is assumed, not derived. The result also places the three familiar numbers: 2 for measurements that do not interfere with each other, 2 times the square root of 2 as the quantum maximum, and 4 as a value that no allowed assignment of averages reaches.

proofs.main:
\emph{Premise.} Hypothesis (P) of the statement is Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}; every statement below about the values of states is under it, relative to the fixed split of the generators.

\emph{Preliminaries.} From Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate} (the base), whose algebra is that of Theorems \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} and \claimref{synthesis.division-gives-the-rationals}: $\dagger$ is an anti-automorphism, states exist, and for a state and self-adjoint $h$, $\omega(h)^{2} \le \omega(h^{2})$ and $\omega(h^{2}) = \omega(hh^{\dagger}) \ge 0$; a functional $\langle\rho\,\cdot\,\rangle_{0}/\langle\rho\rangle_{0}$ with $\rho = \sum_{r}y_{r}y_{r}^{\dagger} \ne 0$ is a state.

\emph{(i).} $A_{+}A_{-} = A_{1}^{2} - A_{1}A_{2} + A_{2}A_{1} - A_{2}^{2} = -[A_{1},A_{2}]$ and $A_{-}A_{+} = [A_{1},A_{2}]$; $A_{\pm}^{2} = 2 \pm (A_{1}A_{2} + A_{2}A_{1})$. Regrouping, $C_{AB} = (A_{1} + A_{2})B_{1} + (A_{1} - A_{2})B_{2}$, and likewise for $D$. Put $U = A_{+}B_{1}$, $V = A_{-}D_{2}$. Since $B_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ commute with $A_{1}, A_{2}$ and with each other, $U^{\dagger} = B_{1}A_{+} = U$, $V^{\dagger} = V$, $U^{2} = A_{+}^{2}$, $V^{2} = A_{-}^{2}$, and $UV + VU = (A_{+}A_{-} + A_{-}A_{+})B_{1}D_{2} = 0$. So $(\lambda U + \mu V)^{2} = \lambda^{2}A_{+}^{2} + \mu^{2}A_{-}^{2}$. The same holds for $U' = A_{-}B_{2}$, $V' = A_{+}D_{1}$ with $A_{+}$ and $A_{-}$ exchanged.

\emph{(ii).} Let $a = \omega(A_{+}^{2})$; then $a \ge 0$ and $4 - a = \omega(A_{-}^{2}) \ge 0$. Write $u = \omega(U)$, $v = \omega(V)$, $u' = \omega(U')$, $v' = \omega(V')$, so that $\omega(C_{AB}) = u + u'$ and $\omega(C_{AD}) = v' + v$. By (i) and the preliminaries, for all scalars $\lambda, \mu$,
\[
(\lambda u + \mu v)^{2} \le \lambda^{2}a + \mu^{2}(4 - a), \qquad (\lambda u' + \mu v')^{2} \le \lambda^{2}(4 - a) + \mu^{2}a . \tag{$*$}
\]
\emph{Case $0 < a < 4$.} Put $\tau = u^{2}/a + v^{2}/(4 - a)$ and take $\lambda = u/a$, $\mu = v/(4 - a)$ in the first inequality: $\tau^{2} \le \tau$, so $\tau \le 1$. Likewise $\tau' = u'^{2}/(4 - a) + v'^{2}/a \le 1$. The identity
\[
4\Bigl(\frac{u^{2}}{a} + \frac{u'^{2}}{4 - a}\Bigr) - (u + u')^{2} = \frac{\bigl((4 - a)u - au'\bigr)^{2}}{a(4 - a)} \ge 0
\]
and the same identity for $v'$, $v$ (with $a$ under $v'$) give $(u + u')^{2} + (v + v')^{2} \le 4(\tau + \tau') \le 8$. \emph{Case $a = 0$.} From ($*$): $\mu = 0$ gives $u = 0$, and $\lambda = 0$ gives $v^{2} \le 4$; in the second, $\lambda = 0$ gives $v' = 0$ and $\mu = 0$ gives $u'^{2} \le 4$. So the sum of squares is $u'^{2} + v^{2} \le 8$. \emph{Case $a = 4$} is the same with the roles exchanged. If both values exceeded $2$ in absolute value the sum of squares would exceed $8$. Only positivity and normalisation of $\omega$ were used.

\emph{(iii).} The first sentence is clause (iii) of the base. In the commutative case each observable is $\sum_{i}\epsilon_{i}q_{i}$ with $\epsilon_{i}^{2} = 1$ (its square is $1 = \sum q_{i}$), so $C_{AB} = \sum_{i}\gamma_{i}q_{i}$ with $\gamma_{i} = \alpha_{1}(\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}) + \alpha_{2}(\beta_{1} - \beta_{2})$ for signs $\alpha, \beta$; one of $\beta_{1} \pm \beta_{2}$ is $0$ and the other $\pm 2$, so $\gamma_{i} = \pm 2$. $\omega(q_{i}) = \omega(q_{i}q_{i}^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\sum_{i}\omega(q_{i}) = 1$. For commuting observables $A$, $B$ the product $AB$ is an observable, so $\omega(AB)^{2} \le \omega(1) = 1$, and $|\omega(C_{AB})| \le 4$ by the triangle inequality. The last sentence cites clauses (iii), (v) and (vi) of the base.

\emph{(iv).} The adjoint fixes $e_{j}$ and negates $f_{j}$; $p_{j}$ is self-adjoint of square $1$ and anticommutes with $e_{j}$, $f_{j}$, and commutes with the generators of the other modes. The twists are those of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} with the plane of mode $1$ and with the planes of modes $1, 2$; the lines needed are these. $e_{2}p_{1}$ has square $e_{2}^{2}p_{1}^{2} = 1$ ($p_{1}$ commutes with $e_{2}$) and commutes with $e_{1}$, $f_{1}$ (each anticommutes with $e_{2}$ and with $p_{1}$), as in clause (vii) of the base. $p_{1}p_{2}$ has square $1$, commutes with $e_{3}$, and anticommutes with each of $e_{1}, f_{1}, e_{2}, f_{2}$; so $e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}$ has square $1$ and commutes with each of these four generators (two sign changes), hence with the algebra of modes $1, 2$, which contains $e_{1}, p_{1}, e_{2}p_{1}, p_{2}$; $p_{3}$ is even in mode $3$ and commutes with modes $1, 2$. Both twisted elements are self-adjoint (a product of commuting self-adjoint factors). $e_{3}p_{1}$ anticommutes with $e_{2}p_{1}$, since $e_{3}$ and $e_{2}$ anticommute. The total parity $p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}$ anticommutes with $e_{1}$, $e_{2}p_{1}$ and $e_{3}p_{1}p_{2}$. The three factors of $\rho$ are $1 + g$ for commuting observables $g$ (the check verifies this and the values), so $\rho$ is a positive multiple of a self-adjoint idempotent; with $B_{1} = B_{2}$, $C_{AB} = 2A_{1}B_{1}$ and $\omega_{\rho}(A_{1}B_{1}) = 1$, likewise for $D$. The state of $y\rho y^{\dagger}$ is a state by the preliminaries; its two values are computed by the check. $\rho_{0}$ is a product of two commuting self-adjoint idempotents, $y'^{\dagger}y' = 1 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac54$ ($I_{B}^{\dagger} = -I_{B}$, $I_{B}^{2} = -1$), so $\rho_{AB} = y'\rho_{0}y'^{-1}$ is a self-adjoint idempotent; its value $\tfrac{14}{5}$ is computed by the check. $p_{3}$ commutes with modes $1, 2$, so $\rho_{AB}\cdot\tfrac12(1 + p_{3})$ is a self-adjoint idempotent with the same value of $C_{AB}$. The bound $\tfrac{4}{25}$ is (ii). For this instance and a direction $a$ of mode $1$, $d = x\,e_{3}p_{1}p_{2} + z\,p_{3}$ of party $D$: the term with $e_{3}$ has no scalar part, because no blade of $\rho_{AB}\cdot\tfrac12(1 + p_{3})$ or of $a$ contains $e_{3}$ without $f_{3}$; the term with $p_{3}$ has scalar part $\tfrac{z}{2}\langle\rho_{AB}\,a\rangle_{0}$, and $\langle\rho_{AB}\,e_{1}\rangle_{0} = \langle\rho_{AB}\,p_{1}\rangle_{0} = 0$ (computed by the check; the blades of $\rho_{AB}$ other than $1$ are $e_{1}f_{2}$ and products $A_{i}B_{j}$). So all values of $C_{AD}$ are $0$ for this instance, which the check asserts; it is a trivial sample of the bound $\tfrac{4}{25}$.

\emph{(v).} The first statement is (ii). \emph{The pair state.} $\rho_{c,s}$ is self-adjoint ($\dagger$ exchanges $v_{j}$ and $w_{j}$, so $(w_{1}w_{2})^{\dagger} = v_{2}v_{1}$). With $m = cs$, $\rho_{c,s}^{2} - \rho_{c,s}$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$ in $(r, m)$ with coefficients in the algebra, and the amplitudes lie on the conic $r^{2} + 4m^{2} = 1$; a polynomial of degree at most $2$ that vanishes at five points of an irreducible conic vanishes on it, and the check verifies $\rho_{c,s}^{2} = \rho_{c,s}$ at five rational points of the conic. $\langle\rho_{c,s}\rangle_{0} = \tfrac14$ since the other terms are not scalars. So $\omega(x) = 4\langle\rho_{c,s}x\rangle_{0}$ is a state. \emph{Correlations.} The expression is $\rho = \rho^{(0)} + r\rho^{(1)} + cs\,\rho^{(2)}$ with fixed elements $\rho^{(i)}$, so each correlation is $\alpha + \beta r + \gamma\,cs$ with rational constants, and the check evaluates all four at three weight pairs whose vectors $(1, r, cs)$ are linearly independent, which determines the constants: $2cs$, $1$, $0$, $0$ (these are the values $2cs$ and $1$ are those of the amplitudes $c$ on $\ket{00}$ and $s$ on $\ket{11}$: $e_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1}$ exchanges the two terms and $p_{1}p_{2}$ fixes both). With $B_{\pm} = zp_{2} \pm x\,e_{2}p_{1}$: $C = p_{1}(B_{+} + B_{-}) + e_{1}(B_{+} - B_{-}) = 2z\,p_{1}p_{2} + 2x\,e_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1}$, of value $2z + 4cs\,x$; by the Cauchy inequality $(z + 2cs\,x)^{2} \le (z^{2} + x^{2})(1 + 4c^{2}s^{2})$, and $4c^{2}s^{2} = 1 - r^{2}$. The numbers at the stated point are arithmetic.

tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.formal: Let $A$ be a unital real algebra and $m \geq 1$. Then: (i) $Z(\Mat_m(A)) = Z(A)\cdot 1_m$; (ii) if $A$ is simple, so is $\Mat_m(A)$; (iii) $\Mat_m(\Mat_r(D)) \cong \Mat_{mr}(D)$ for any unital $D$; (iv) $\Mat_m(A_1 \oplus A_2) \cong \Mat_m(A_1) \oplus \Mat_m(A_2)$.
tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.technical:
For a unital real algebra $A$ and $m \geq 1$, passing to $m \times m$ matrices over $A$ preserves the basic structure. The centre is $Z(\Mat_m(A)) = Z(A) \cdot 1_m$; $\Mat_m(A)$ is simple whenever $A$ is; nested matrix algebras regroup, $\Mat_m(\Mat_r(D)) \cong \Mat_{mr}(D)$ for any unital $D$; and amplification distributes over direct sums, $\Mat_m(A_1 \oplus A_2) \cong \Mat_m(A_1) \oplus \Mat_m(A_2)$.

The first two statements follow from computations with the matrix units $E_{kl}$; the last two are regroupings of indices.
tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.lay: Replacing an algebra by square matrices whose entries come from that algebra changes its size but not its essential character. The centre stays the same, simplicity is kept, matrices of matrices are just larger matrices, and a direct sum of algebras splits into a direct sum of matrix algebras.
tower.matrix-amplification-structural-pr.typing_note: Self-contained computation with matrix units and no store references, so no edges.

proofs.main: Parts (i) and (ii) are \claimref{std-algebra.morita-amplification}(i) and (ii); the computation runs as follows. (i) Let $z = (z_{ij})$ be central. The entries of $z E_{kl} = E_{kl} z$ are $(z E_{kl})_{ij} = z_{ik}\,\delta_{lj}$ and $(E_{kl} z)_{ij} = \delta_{ik}\, z_{lj}$; equality for all $i, j, k, l$ forces $z_{ik} = 0$ for $i \neq k$ and $z_{kk} = z_{ll}$, so $z = a \cdot 1_m$ with $a := z_{11}$, and commuting with $b \cdot 1_m$ for all $b \in A$ forces $a \in Z(A)$. The converse inclusion is clear. (ii) A nonzero two-sided ideal $I$ contains some $x$ with an entry $x_{kl} = a \neq 0$; then $E_{ik}\, x\, E_{lj} = a E_{ij} \in I$ for all $i, j$, so $I \supseteq \Mat_m(AaA) = \Mat_m(A)$, since $AaA = A$ by simplicity. (iii) and (iv) are regroupings of indices and entrywise splittings.

tower.morita-equivalence-algebra-amplifi.formal: For any unital ring $A$ and $m \geq 1$, the column module $A^m$ is a $\Mat_m(A)$-$A$-bimodule implementing an equivalence of module categories: $A$ and $\Mat_m(A)$ are Morita equivalent. \emph{Provenance:} classical Morita theory, \cite[\S\S 17--18]{Lam1999}.
tower.morita-equivalence-algebra-amplifi.technical: For any unital ring $A$ and any $m \geq 1$, the column module $A^m$ is a $\Mat_m(A)$-$A$-bimodule implementing an equivalence between the categories of modules over $\Mat_m(A)$ and over $A$. Hence $A$ and its amplification $\Mat_m(A)$ are Morita equivalent; this is classical Morita theory.
tower.morita-equivalence-algebra-amplifi.lay: Replacing an algebra by the algebra of square matrices with entries in it does not change its module theory: the two have equivalent categories of modules. This is a classical result imported from ring theory.

transport.centre.formal: For $n \geq 1$, the centre of $\Cl(p,q)$ is $\R \cdot 1$ if $n$ is even, and $\R \cdot 1 \oplus \R \cdot \omega$ if $n$ is odd, where $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$ is the pseudoscalar.
transport.centre.technical:
Let $n = p + q \geq 1$ and let $\omega = e_1 e_2 \cdots e_n$ be the pseudoscalar of $\Cl(p,q)$. The centre $\Zc$ of the algebra depends only on the parity of $n$: for even $n$ it is just the scalars, $\Zc = \R \cdot 1$, while for odd $n$ it is two-dimensional, $\Zc = \R \cdot 1 \oplus \R \cdot \omega$.

The standard reason is that each basis blade either commutes or anticommutes with each generator $e_j$, and the only blades commuting with every generator are $1$ and, when $n$ is odd, $\omega$.
transport.centre.lay: The centre of an algebra is the set of its elements that commute with everything else in it. For the Clifford algebra of a space with an even number of dimensions, only the ordinary numbers do this. With an odd number of dimensions there is one more such element, the product of all the basis directions, so the centre becomes two-dimensional.

transport.classification-idempotent-orbi.technical:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ be nondegenerate, so that by the classification $A \cong \Mat_m(D)$ or $\Mat_m(D) \oplus \Mat_m(D)$ with $D \in \{\R, \C, \HH\}$, acting on $D^m$ (or a pair of copies). The rank of an idempotent is the $D$-dimension of its image, a rank pair in the split case. Two idempotents are conjugate under inner automorphisms if and only if they have the same rank data; in particular $e$ and $1 - e$ are conjugate if and only if $\mathrm{rank}\,e = m - \mathrm{rank}\,e$, componentwise in the split case.

An idempotent is central if and only if its conjugation orbit is a single point. This makes the boundary between obstruction types P and C orbit-theoretic: type C idempotents are those conjugation cannot move, type P those it moves through a full rank class.
transport.classification-idempotent-orbi.lay: Idempotents are elements equal to their own square, like projections onto a subspace. This result sorts them in any nondegenerate real Clifford algebra: two are related by an internal change of viewpoint exactly when they project onto subspaces of the same size (in each of the two blocks, when the algebra splits into two). The ones that no such change can move at all are exactly the ones that commute with everything, and this is how the series separates two of its types of obstruction.
transport.classification-idempotent-orbi.typing_note: Added the classification theorem, cited in the statement's hypothesis and named in context_refs; version bumped to 2 for the derivation change, so transport.pair-canonical-label-bit's pin @1 is now stale. Levels pass: the lay now keeps the nondegeneracy hypothesis and the split-case rank pairs.

proofs.main:
(1) Conjugation preserves rank, since $geg^{-1}$ has image $g(\mathrm{im}\, e)$. Conversely let $e, e'$ be idempotents of equal rank $r$ on $V = D^m$, on which $A \cong \Mat_m(D)$ acts (\claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}). Each splits $V$: $V = \mathrm{im}\,e \oplus \ker e$, both summands free (a finitely generated submodule of a free module over a division ring is free, with well-defined dimension); choose $D$-bases of $\mathrm{im}\,e$ and $\ker e$, and likewise for $e'$. The $D$-linear map $g$ carrying the first adapted basis to the second is invertible and satisfies $g e g^{-1} = e'$, both sides being the projection onto $g(\mathrm{im}\,e) = \mathrm{im}\,e'$ along $g(\ker e) = \ker e'$. In the split case, invertible elements are pairs of invertibles and conjugation acts componentwise (inner automorphisms preserve the two ideals, which are the algebra's minimal central summands), so the same argument applies in each slot and no inner automorphism exchanges slots.

(2) is (1) applied to the pair, $\mathrm{rank}(1-e) = m - \mathrm{rank}(e)$.

(3) If $e$ is central its orbit is $\{e\}$. Conversely, if $geg^{-1} = e$ for every invertible $g$, then $e$ commutes with every invertible element, hence with every sum of two of them, hence with all of $A$ by Lemma \claimref{transport.units-span}: $e$ is central. The identification of the singleton-orbit idempotents with the taxonomy's type C, and of the moved ones with type P, is then Definition \claimref{obj.transport.obstruction-types} read against (1).

transport.classification-real-clifford-a.formal:
Let $d \equiv p - q \pmod 8$. Then $\Cl(p,q)$ is isomorphic, as a real associative algebra, to
\[
\begin{array}{llll}
d = 0:\ \Mat_{k}(\R), &
d = 1:\ \Mat_{k}(\R) \oplus \Mat_{k}(\R), &
d = 2:\ \Mat_{k}(\R), &
d = 3:\ \Mat_{k}(\C), \\[2pt]
d = 4:\ \Mat_{k}(\HH), &
d = 5:\ \Mat_{k}(\HH) \oplus \Mat_{k}(\HH), &
d = 6:\ \Mat_{k}(\HH), &
d = 7:\ \Mat_{k}(\C),
\end{array}
\]
with $k$ in each case determined by $\dim_\R \Cl(p,q) = 2^n$. In particular $\Cl(p,q)$ is a simple algebra except when $d \in \{1, 5\}$, i.e.\ except when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where it is the direct sum of two isomorphic simple algebras.
transport.classification-real-clifford-a.technical:
The real Clifford algebra $\Cl(p,q)$ is, as a real associative algebra, a full matrix algebra over $\R$, $\C$ or $\HH$, or a direct sum of two copies of one, and which case occurs depends only on $d \equiv p - q \pmod 8$: $\Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 0, 2$; $\Mat_k(\R) \oplus \Mat_k(\R)$ for $d = 1$; $\Mat_k(\C)$ for $d = 3, 7$; $\Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 4, 6$; and $\Mat_k(\HH) \oplus \Mat_k(\HH)$ for $d = 5$. In each case the size $k$ is fixed by $\dim_\R \Cl(p,q) = 2^n$.

Consequently $\Cl(p,q)$ is a simple algebra except when $d \in \{1, 5\}$, that is when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, where it is the direct sum of two isomorphic simple algebras.
transport.classification-real-clifford-a.lay: Clifford algebras built from a space with p positive and q negative directions turn out to be familiar objects in disguise: square tables of numbers (matrices) whose entries are real numbers, complex numbers or quaternions, or a pair of such tables side by side. Which of these appears depends only on p minus q, in a pattern that repeats every eight steps. Usually the algebra is a single indivisible block; it splits into two identical pieces exactly when p minus q leaves remainder 1 on division by four.

transport.corner-even-subalgebra.formal: Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ with $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, split by the central idempotents $\varepsilon_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm \omega)$, let $\Cl^0(p,q)$ be its even subalgebra, and let $B_\gamma = A \oplus A\nu$ be its one-generator ascent. The map $\phi : \Cl^0(p,q) \to \varepsilon_+ A$, $\phi(a) = \varepsilon_+ a$, is an isomorphism of unital algebras (with unit $\varepsilon_+$ on the right-hand side). Moreover $\varepsilon_+ B_\gamma\, \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_+ A$.
transport.corner-even-subalgebra.technical:
In the setting where $A = \Cl(p,q)$ with $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ splits along the central idempotents $\varepsilon_\pm = 	frac12(1 \pm \omega)$, and $B_\gamma$ is its extension by an orthogonal generator $
u$, the map $\phi(a) = \varepsilon_+ a$ is an isomorphism of unital algebras from the even subalgebra $\Cl^{0}(p,q)$ onto the corner $\varepsilon_+ A$, whose unit is $\varepsilon_+$. Injectivity uses that $\omega$ is odd, and surjectivity a dimension count.

Moreover the extension adds nothing to the corner: $\varepsilon_+ B_\gamma\, \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_+ A$, because $B_\gamma = A \oplus A
u$ and $
u\,\varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_-\,
u$.
transport.corner-even-subalgebra.lay: When an algebra splits into two blocks, each block can be compared with the algebra's even part, built from products of an even number of directions. This result shows each block is an exact copy of that even part. It also shows that enlarging the algebra by one extra direction and then cutting back down to the block returns the same block.
transport.corner-even-subalgebra.typing_note: Both edges are cited premises and kept; the section's standing type C hypothesis is not added as an edge, to avoid a version bump for a setting-level citation.

proofs.main:
$\phi$ is an algebra map because $\varepsilon_+$ is a central idempotent of $A$: $\phi(a)\phi(b) = \varepsilon_+ a\, \varepsilon_+ b = \varepsilon_+^2 ab = \phi(ab)$, and $\phi(1) = \varepsilon_+$. Injectivity: if $a$ is even and $\varepsilon_+ a = 0$, then $a = (\varepsilon_+ + \varepsilon_-)a = \varepsilon_- a$, i.e.\ $2a = a - \omega a$, i.e.\ $\omega a = -a$. But $\omega$ has odd grade ($n$ odd) while $a$ is even, so $\omega a$ is odd and $-a$ is even; a common value is possible only if both vanish, so $a = 0$. Surjectivity follows by dimension: $\dim \Cl^0 = 2^{n-1} = 	frac12 \dim A = \dim \varepsilon_+ A$ (the first equality is \claimref{std-algebra.z2-grading}), the last equality because $x \mapsto (\varepsilon_+ x, \varepsilon_- x)$ splits $A$ into two summands exchanged (linearly) by the grade involution, which maps $\varepsilon_+ x \mapsto \varepsilon_- \hat{x}$ and is bijective. For the second statement: $\varepsilon_+ B_\gamma \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_+ A \varepsilon_+ + \varepsilon_+ A 
u \varepsilon_+$ by Lemma \claimref{transport.decomposition-commutation}; the first term is $\varepsilon_+ A$ (centrality in $A$), and the second vanishes: $
u \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_- 
u$ (Proposition \claimref{transport.ascent-renders-grade-involution-inner}), so $\varepsilon_+ a 
u \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_+ a \varepsilon_- 
u = (\varepsilon_+ \varepsilon_-) a 
u = 0$.

transport.even-subalgebra-one-dimensiona.technical:
Adjoin to $\Cl(p,q)$ one generator $

transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exact.formal: Let $n$ be odd and consider the two real forms of the Lorentzian algebra in dimension $n$, $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ (time of square $+1$) and $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ (time of square $-1$). Then $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ is type C if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and in each case the other real form has complex type. The two real forms have the same complexification, which is split for every odd $n$: over $\C$, realised as $\Cl(V) \oplus \Cl(V)I_{\hat V}$ with $V$ the $n$-dimensional space and $I_{\hat V}$ the central pseudoscalar of the odd extension $\hat V$ of $V \oplus \R f$ ($f$ one further vector), which squares to $-1$ and commutes with every vector (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), the element $\omega' = \omega$ or $I_{\hat V}\omega$, whichever has square $+1$, is central, and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are its central idempotents. Thus the obstruction is present in every odd Lorentzian dimension; the real form decides whether it is visible as a splitting or hidden as a central complex structure.
transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exact.technical:
For odd $n$ compare the two Lorentzian real forms $\Cl(1,n-1)$, with $Q = +1$ on the time generator, and $\Cl(n-1,1)$, with $Q = -1$ on it. Using the commuting-square theorem on where the obstruction sits among one-dimensional extensions, $\Cl(1,n-1)$ is of type C if and only if $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\Cl(n-1,1)$ is of type C if and only if $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and in each case the other real form has complex type.

Both forms have the same complexification, which is split for every odd $n$: over $\C$, with complex unit $I_{\hat V}$, the central pseudoscalar of an odd extension of $V \oplus \R f$, whichever of $\omega$ and $I_{\hat V}\omega$ squares to $+1$ is a central involution $\omega'$, and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are central idempotents. So the obstruction is present in every odd Lorentzian dimension, and the real form decides whether it appears as a splitting or as a central complex structure.
transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exact.lay: In an odd number of spacetime dimensions there are two ways to set up the algebra, depending on whether time is given a positive or a negative square. Exactly one of the two breaks into two pieces, and which one depends on the dimension modulo four; the other hides the same feature as a built-in square root of minus one. Over the complex numbers the two choices agree, and the result always splits.
transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exact.typing_note: Kept the single edge to the commuting-square theorem, which the proof applies; the complexification step is self-contained.

proofs.main: $\Cl(1,n{-}1)$ is the spacelike extension of $\Cl(1,n{-}2)$, an even-dimensional algebra with $p - q = 3 - n$, which is $\equiv 2 \pmod 4$ iff $n \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\equiv 0$ iff $n \equiv 3$; Theorem \claimref{transport.where-obstruction-lies-commuting-square}(a) gives the first claim and the complex type of the other case. $\Cl(n{-}1,1)$ is the extension of $\Cl(n{-}2,1)$, $p - q = n - 3$, by a generator of square $+1$, obstructed iff $n - 3 \equiv 0$, i.e.\ $n \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, complex type otherwise. For the complexification: by Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension} applied to the even-dimensional $V \oplus \R f$, $\Cl(\hat V)$ is its complexification with central unit $I_{\hat V}$, and the subalgebra generated by $V$ and $I_{\hat V}$ is $\Cl(V) \oplus \Cl(V)I_{\hat V}$ (the summands meet in $0$, since the blades of the second contain $f$), the complexification $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \C$ with complex unit $I_{\hat V}$; in it the substitution $e_k \mapsto I_{\hat V}e_k$ on the generators of square $-1$ turns the relations of $\Cl(p,q)$ into those of $\Cl(n,0)$, so $\Cl(p,q) \otimes \C$ depends only on $n$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification}); the volume element remains central, and if $\omega^2 = -1$ then $(I_{\hat V}\omega)^2 = +1$, so $\omega'$ as defined is a central involution and $\tfrac12(1 \pm \omega')$ are orthogonal central idempotents summing to $1$. The script checks the alternation, with its complex-type complement, in dimensions $3, 5, 7, 9, 11$.

transport.sign.formal: $\displaystyle \omega^2 = (-1)^{\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}} (-1)^q = (-1)^{\tfrac{(p-q)(p-q-1)}{2}}$. In particular $\omega^2 = +1$ if and only if $p - q \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.
transport.sign.technical:
For the pseudoscalar $\omega = e_1 \cdots e_n$ of $\Cl(p,q)$, with $n = p + q$, the square is fixed by a count of signs: reversing the order of the $n$ generators costs $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$, and $\omega$ times its reverse is the product of the $Q(e_i)$, which is $(-1)^q$. Hence $\omega^2 = (-1)^{n(n-1)/2}(-1)^q$.

This depends only on $p - q$, namely $\omega^2 = (-1)^{(p-q)(p-q-1)/2}$, and in particular $\omega^2 = +1$ exactly when $p - q \equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 4$.
transport.sign.lay: Multiplying all the basis directions of a Clifford algebra together gives a special element called the pseudoscalar. Its square is always plus one or minus one, and this result says which. The answer depends only on the number of positive directions minus the number of negative ones: the square is plus one when that difference leaves remainder 0 or 1 on division by four, and minus one otherwise.
